parties:
Shamuj Ali and ors -------- Appellants
Vs.
Kamalarma Bibi and others -------- Respondent
case_source: From the Judgment and order of the High Court Division dated July 24, 1979 passed in S.M.A. No. 45 of 1970.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—This appeal by appeal leave nits In question a judgment and order of the High Court Division dated July 24, 1979 in S.M.A. No. 45 of 1970 reversing the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge who on setting aside the judgment and order of the Trial Court held that an application for restitution under section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code is governed by Article 181 of Schedule 1 of the Limitation Act, 1908 and not by Article 182 of the said Act. The High Court Division further held that even if Art. 181 applies to an application for restitution the three years period of limitation provided thereunder will begin from the date of the final decree in second appeal and not from she date of the decree of the first appellate Court reversing that of the court of the first instance. In other words, right to apply" for restitution as referred to in Art. 181 accrues on "the date of the final decree of the appellate court." 
2. Facts of the case are rather simple. The respondent-plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 63 of 1956 against the appellant-defendants for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land. The suit was decreed by the Munsif on 29th May, 1957 and the plaintiffs by putting the decree into execution got delivery of possession of the land on 26th August, 1957. But the defendants filed an appeal against the decree which was allowed and the decree was set aside by the Subordinate Judge, by an order dated 26th June, 1958. The plaintiffs preferred a second appeal being S. A. No. 142 of 1959, in the High Court Division which was dismissed on 26th May, 1965. Thereafter, the defendants filed an application on 29th May, 1967 for restitution under section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code. The application was resisted by the plaintiffs contending that it was barred by limitation Under section 181 of the Limitation Act as it was filed beyond the period of three years as prescribed in that Article. This contention was rejected by the learned Munsif who held that an application for restitution is in fact an application for execution of a decree and as such it is governed by Art. 182 of the Limitation Act which provides that for an application for execution of a decree the period of limitation of three years begins "where there has been an appeal, from the date of the final decree" On that principle the application for restitution was found to have been filed within the period of limitation. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, took the view that the application for restitution is not an application in execution but it is an independent application for which no specific provision having been made elsewhere in the Limitation Act or in the Civil Procedure Code will be governed by the residuary provision of Art 181 and that the three years period of limitation under this Article begins from the date of the decree of the first appellate court reversing the original decree and that on this date the right to apply accrues. In this case the decree of reversal by the first appellate court having been made on June 26, 1958 the suit was not filed within three years from that date and as such the suit was barred by limitation. 
3. The question involved in this appeal is a question which has been agitated for about a century in the superior Courts of the Sub-continent and conflicting opinions have been expressed as to the nature of an application for restitution of a property in pursuance of an adverse appellate decree. For proper appreciation of this question relevant provisions of Law are quoted below: 
Section 144, Civil Procedure Code. 
S. 144 (1). Where and in so far as decree is varied or reversed the Court of first instance shall, on the application of any party entitled to any benefit by way of restitution or otherwise, cause such restitution to be made as will, so far as may be, place the parties in the position which they would have occupied but for such decree or such part thereof as has been varied or reversed; and for this purpose the Court may make any orders, including orders for the refund of costs and for the payment of interest, damages, compensation and manse profits, which are properly consequential or such variation or reversal. 
(2) No suit shall be instituted for the purpose of obtaining any restitution or other relief which could be obtained by application under sub section 1” 
Articles 181 and 182 of Schedule 1 of the Limitation Act        

Description of application

Period of limitation

 

Time from which period of limitation begins to run

 

Art, 181. Application for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in this schedule or by section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Three years

When the right to apply accrues

Art. 182. For the execution of a decree or order of any Civil Court rot provided for by section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

 

Three years; or where a certified copy of the decree or order has been registered, six years.
  1. The date of decree or order, or
  2. Where there has been an appeal, the date of the final decree or order of the Appellate Court, or the withdrawal of the appeal....
4. The first and foremost question is whether an application for restitution is an application for execution of a decree as referred to in Art.182, Limitation Act and within the meaning of s. 47 of the Civil Procedure Code. If it is so, the problem is solved easily, for Art. 182 will straight away apply thereto and the period of limitation, which is same as under Art. 181 i,e. three years, will start from the date of the decree of the first appellate court reversing that of the trial court if no appeal is filed, but if an appeal is filed from the date of the final decree of the appellate court. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned counsel for the appellants has taken pains to press his point that the nature and scope of an application for restitution are quite different from those of an application for execution and as such restitution is not part of an execution proceeding, nor is it in the nature of an execution proceeding. In support of this contention Mr Ahmed has relied upon a number of Indian decisions, particularly the following cases: Parmeswar Singh Vs. Sitaldin Dube AIR 1934 All. 626 F.B Saraj Bhushan Vs. Devendranath AIR 1932 Cal 30, Hari Mohan Dala Vs. Parmeshwar Shau. AIR 1928 Cal 646, Khwaja Allawali Vs. Kesarimal AIR 1947 Nag. 239, Balmukund Marwari vs. Basata Kumari Dasi AIR 1925; part 1.
5. In the Full Bench case of Allahabad High Court as referred to above, Solaiman C J in his illuminating judgment elaborated the differences between an application for execution and an application for restitution and has tried to show that an application for restitution does not come under an execution proceeding in any way and, therefore. Art, 182 Limitation Act, is not attracted to such an application. The salient points of difference between an application for execution and that for restitution as pointed out by the learned Judge may be summarized thus: Section 144 C.P.C. does not make any reference to execution and this section has been put in a different part of the Civil Procedure Code namely, Part XI, under the head "Miscellaneous", whereas an application for execution and all matters connected therewith have been put in Part II under the Head Execution in the said Code that if an application for restitution is same as an application for execution then a separate section like s. 144 is superfluous. Definition of 'decree' in s. 2 C.P.0 includes the determination of an application under s. 47 and also the determination of an application under s. 144; if restitution is covered by "execution" then the definition of 'decree' would have covered both execution and restitution and these two terms would not have been specifically mentioned therein. Similarly, if restitution is covered by execution a suit for restitution is barred as provided under s. 47 and for that purpose a separate provision such as sub-section(2) of s. 144 will be superfluous. If restitution application is an application for execution It will be inconsistent with s. 38 of the Civil Procedure Code, which provides that a decree may be executed either by the Court which passed it or by the Court to which it is sent for execution, whereas an application for restitution is to be filed only in the court of the first instance. Restitution was provided for in s. 583 of the Civil Procedure Code of 1882. That station specifically laid down that any benefit by way of restitution might be available by tiling an application for execution of the decree of reversal passed by the appellate court but in s. 144 of the present Code, all reference to execution of a decree have been avoided. By avoiding any such reference conscious effort was made by the law makers to keep an application for restitution independent of and separate from an application for execution. The scope of an application for restitution is much wider than that of an application for execution in that the Court on an application for restitution, may allow, besides restoration of a property, refund of money, payment of compensation, damage and mesne profits, where the executing court will only execute the decree as it is. In view of these differences the learned Judge concluded thus: 
"An application for restitution under s. 144 is not an application for the execution of a decree within the meaning of Art, 182, Limitation Act and that this Article does not apply to it. It is an application not specifically provided for and is governed by Art, 181, Limitation Act'; 
6. In the Patna case (AIR 1925- Pat 1) it has been held; 
"Execution presupposes a decree or order capable of being carried into effect, restitution presupposes an act of the court which has done an injury to the suitors. Execution will be issued as a matter of course; but in cases of the code, restitution is not a matter of course but depends upon the discretion of the court and will be ordered only when the justice of the case calls for it. The jurisdiction as to restitution bears only a superficial resemblance to the Jurisdiction as to execution. The jurisdiction to order restitution is inherent in the court and it flows not from any power which it may have to carry into effect the decree or order of the court but from the recognition of the duty which it owes to the suitors to take care that no injury is done to them by its acts." 
7. In the Calcutta case Saraj Bhushan Ghosh vs. Debendra Nath ,Ghosh Rankin, C.J. after considering a number of decisions came to the same finding as "An application for restitution under s. 144 Civil Procedure Code is not an application for execution and such applications are governed by Art, 181 of the Limitation Act and not by Article 182. 
8. But the contrary view has also been followed persistently even in a greater number of cases, by different High Courts particularly of Bombay and Madras. Some of those cases are Samasundaram vs. Chokiam Lingam AIR 1917 Mad, 185, Venkataraj vs. Suraynarayana. AIR 1943 Mad. 248 Kurgodii gouda vs. Ningangouda AIR 1917 Bom. 210. Hamidcali vs. Ahmedali AIR 1921 Bom. 67 Bhaunath vs. Kedar Nath AIR 1934 Pat 246 (2). This view, as has been set out earlier in this judgment, is that an application for restitution is an application in execution and as such is governed by Art, 182 of the Limitation Act. 
9. The Indian, Supreme Court in the case Mahijbhai vs, Manibhai" AIR 1965 S C, 1477, considered the two conflicting view, expressed in as many as 20 cases decided by the different Indian High Courts including the cases which have been already referred to in this judgment and finally settled, though by a split judgment of 4 to 1 this question agreeing with the view that an application for restitution is an application for execution and rejecting the view that it is not so, and that it is Art, 182 and not Art, 81 that applies in an application for restitution. The dissenting judgment of Sarkar, J. followed more or less the line of reasoning of Solaiman, C.J. in the Full Bench case of Allahabad High Court as already referred to above, Sarkar, J. pinpointed the difference between an application for restitution and that for an execution and laid particular stress on two points. One is that s. 144, which provides that an application for restitution is to be made to the court of first instance, will be inconsistent with s. 38 which provides that a decree may be executed either by the court which passed it or by the court to which it is sent for execution the other point is that total avoidance of any reference to execution in s. 144. which repeals s. 583 of the preceding Code of 1882 wherein specific reference was made to execution clearly indicates the legislative intent to keep restitution completely separate from execution. In respect of the last paint the learned Judge observed: 
“Indeed the old section leads to the contrary view, for while it expressly provided that restitution would be by way of execution, the present section deliberately omits reference to execution. This departure in the terminology used, would tend to the view 'that it was intended that the procedure under the new section would not be by way of execution." 
As to the nature of an application for restitution the learned Judge held that It is an application for which no limitation has been provided 'elsewhere' and observed: 
"Apart from the fact that the application is not described as one in execution; the provision for the making of an order for the purpose of effecting restitution would lead to the conclusion that it is this order which is to be executed for obtaining restitution. The section obviously could not contemplate two applications for execution, and, therefore, the earlier application resulting in the order mentioned in the section, could not be one for execution. It seems to be impossible, looking at the terms of the section alone and without more, we have no right to look at anything else to say that the application contemplated in it is one in execution. 
10. Subba Rao, J. who expressed the majority view in that case having traced the history of s. 144 of the Civil Procedure Code of 1908 found that in the ultimate analysis what an application for restitution seeks is the fruit of an appellate decree of reversal and that this fruit derived by executing the decree, and on that consideration, held that an application for restitution was never intended to be an original application but it is an application In connection with a case in which a wrong decree passed earlier has been corrected, in appeal. The conclusion arrived at by the learned Judge is quoted below: 
"The section does not either expressly or by necessary implication change the nature of the proceedings. Its object is limited. It seeks to avoid conflict and to make the scope of the restitution clear and unambiguous. It does not say that an application for restitution, which, till the new Procedure Code was enacted, was an application for execution, should be treated as an original petition. Whether an application is one for execution of a decree or is an original application depends upon the nature of the application and the relief asked for. When a party, who lost his property in execution of a decree, seeks to recover the same by reason of the appellate decree in his, favour, he is not initiating any' original proceeding, but be is only concerned with the working out of the appellate decree in his favour. The application flows from the, appellate decree and is filed to implement or enforce the same. He is entitled to the relief of restitution, because the appellate decree enable; him to obtain that relief, either expressly or by necessary implication. He is recovering the fruits of the appellate decree." 
11. The learned Judge was fully aware reasons for the contrary view emanating from eminent Judges and realised that "the opposite construction for which the appellate contended is also a possible one," but observed that it ignores the history of the legislation and the anomalies that it introduces" and held: 
"On a procedural matter pertaining to execution when a section yields to two conflicting constructions, the Court shall adopt a construction which maintains rather than disturbs the equilibrium in the field of execution". 
12. Restitution under s. 144 C.P.C. means restoration of a right or of a property to a person who has been deprived thereof by wrongful order of the Court which is reversed. In English law the concept of restitution has found clear exposition in Halsbury’s Laws of England, (2nd Edn., Vol. 14 P. 38) In the following terms: 
"Where a wrongful or irregular execution has been set aside, or where a judgment or order has been reversed after execution thereon has taken place, restitution will be made to the successful party. The order setting aside the execution or reversing the judgment or order should provide, for this and if it does execution may issue upon it in the ordinary course. If the order dies not so provide, another order may be made, or a writ called a writ of restitution be issued, commending the judgment creditor to restore the property or pay over the proceeds of sale". 
The English law GS quoted above provides that the court while reversing an erroneous decree may itself give direction for restitution but if it does not do so, a separate order for restitution might be issued without, however, indicating, by whom. Reference to the English law, therefore, does not give us much assistance in the interpretation of s. 144. 
13. In "Jai Berham Vs. Kedar Nath Marwari", AIR 1922 P.C. 269, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council considered the scope of s. 144 and duty of the court to effect restitution and held: 
"It is the duty of the Court under s. 144 of the Civil Procedure Code to place the parties in the position which they would have occupied, but for such decree or such part thereof as has been varied or reversed. Nor indeed does this duty or jurisdiction arise merely under the said section. It is inherent in the general jurisdiction of the Court to act rightly and fairly according to the circumstances towards all parties involved." 
This decision also does not appear to be very much helpful in our attempt to find the answer of the question before us namely, whether an application under s. 144 is an application in execution of a decree.
14. Prior to the enactment of s. 144 of the Civil Procedure Code of 1908, s. 583 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 1882 contained the procedure for restitution. Restitution thereunder was to be effected by an application for execution of the decree of reversal. Section 583 is quoted below: 
"When a party entitled to any benefit, by way of restitution or otherwise, under decree passed in an appeal under this chapter desires to obtain execution of the same, he shall apply to the Court which passed the decree against which the appeal was preferred; and such Court shall proceed to execute the decree passed in appeal, according to the rules herein before prescribed for the execution of decrees in suits" 
Section 144 has already been quoted at pace 3 of this judgment Upon reading of these two sections it is clear that in s. 583 provision was made for obtaining restitution by executing the decree and it is this provision which led to the interpretation that restitution is same as execution proceeding. But if an application for restitution under s. 144 is same as an execution proceeding under s. 47 why the old section 583 was replaced by s. 144 in which no reference to execution has been made at all, Both Sarkar, J. and Subba Rao, J who expressed the two conflicting views in the Indian case agreed that the old notion contained some "conflict" or "anomaly" and observed that the new section was brought in just to remove the conflict or anomaly. But what we find is that by removing the conflict, anomaly or confusion; whatever it might be, the legislature made its intention clear in the new section hat restitution is completely separate from execution and that these two provisions which have been set out in separate section and under separate Chanters should not be Intermixed or confused If the legislative intention was to provide restitution through an execution proceeding then either s. 144 would have simply contained a provision to the effect that restitution will be available in the same manner as the execution of a decree under section 47, or s. 83 would have been altogether deleted without re-enacting it in the form of s. 144. If restitution falls under an execution proceeding the entire section 144 Is then superfluous for, restitution will be obtainable by putting into execution the decree of reversal like any other decree. Similarly, inclusion in the definition of "decree" of the provision "the determination of any question within section 144 or the provision barring a suit for restitution contained in s. 144(2) will also be unnecessary". Conscious avoidance of any reference to execution in s. 144 clearly shows that an application for restitution is an independent application, no matter its object is the recovery of the fruit of a decree passed earlier but subsequently reversed. Application for restitution is an application for which no limitation has been specifically provided for in the law and as such it attracts the residuary prevision of Article 181 We are, therefore, firmly of the view that a restitution application is not an application for execute on of a degree and as such it is not governed by Art. 182 but it is governed by Art. 181 of the Limitation Act. 
15. The next question is when the period of limitation provided under Articles 181; Limitation Act begins to run. In other words, when the right to apply accrues under Article 181. The High Court Division has expressed the view that "the right to apply" accrues on the date of the final decree when appeal is preferred from the appellate decree of reversal. On the interpretation of this Article also there is conflict of views, one view being that the right to apply for restitution accrues on the data of the decree of the first appellate court reversing the decree of the trial court, and the other view being that this right accrues on the date of the final decree when appeal is preferred from the decree of the first appellate court. 
16. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has contended that the appropriate time for the application is the date of the decree if the first appellate court whether any appeal therefrom is filed or not and that once the limitation begins to run it cannot be suspended by the filing of an appeal and in the absence of any order of stay. In support of this contention be has cited a number of decisions particularly the decision of Sundrawardy, J. which was upheld by Rankin, C.J. and Buckland, J, disagreeing with the contrary view of Graham J, in the case "Hari Mohan Dulal Vs Prarneshwar Shau". (32 CWN 917 corresponding AIR 932 Cal 308) In that case both the Benches took as settled that Art 181 and not Art. 182 governs a restitution application but difference arose as to when the right to apply for restitution accrues. The question considered was whether, by the plaintiffs appealing from the decree of the District Judge (first appellate court) the defendant’s right to claim restitution was suspended or whether the doctrine of suspension is applicable in such a case. In the opinion of the learned Judge "there is no principle of law under which the period sanctioned by that Article can be extended", and it was observed that under s. 9. Limitation Act, "once time has begun to run no subsequent disability or inability to sue stops it". The learned Judge, disagreeing with the previous view of the same High Court expressed in "Atul Chandra Sinha Vs. Kunja Behary Sinha 27 CLj 451 (1970) to the effect that "an application for restitution immediately on reversal of the preliminary decree by the first appellate court would have been futile by the second appeal," held, "The fact that the plaintiffs appealed from the decree of District Judge cannot in my judgment suspend, take away, restrict or extinguish the right of the defendants to seek restitution." As to the argument that if no extension is allowed for the period spent during the pendency of the second appeal hardship would be caused to minors and other disabled persons who would be deprived of the benefits of section 6 & 7 of the Limitation Act, the learned Judge observed that in the matter of interpretation of statutes equitable consideration Is out of place and held: 
"The cause of action or right to apply under s. 144 accrued to the defendants on the very next day after the decree of the first court was modified by the appellate court and nothing has happened since then to suspend or stay or, to be more precise, to revive or give a fresh start to the exercise of rights." 
17. This view of the High Court however did not find favour with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case Nagendranath De vs. Surenara De, ILR 1933 Cal, 1. Their Lordships of the Privy Council held; 
"It is at least an intelligible rule that, so long as there Is any question sub fake between any of the parties, those affected shall not be compelled to pursue the so often thorny path of execution, which, if the final result is against them, may lead to no advantage. Nor in any such case as this, is the judgment-debtor prejudiced, He may indeed obtain the boon of delay, which is so dear to the debtors, and, if he is virtuously inclined, there is nothing to prevent him paying what he owes into court." 
In a case where second appeal is filed challenging the decree of reversal of the first appellate court and restitution takes place during pendency of the second appeal, the restitution may be set at naught by the reversal of the decree in the second appeal and possession of the property will change bands once again. When appeal is the extension of the original cause we find no reason why the "right to apply" should not be taken to accrue on the date of the final decree of the appellate court if appeal is preferred from the decree of reversal of the first appellate court.
In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.
End.

lawyer: Abdul Aziz Chowdhury, Advocate—For the Petitioner Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Hares Mia (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Khorsheda Khatun and others  ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Civil Revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order dated 25-10-93 passed by Mr. Md. Mohshin Mollah, Senior Assistant Judge, District Kishoreganj in OC Execution Case No. 4 of 1993 rejecting the application dated 2-9-1993 of the Judgment-debtor for dismissing the Execution case which arises out of OC Suit No. 105 of 1979 of the said Court. 

	2. Short facts involved in the case is that, the predecessors of Opposite Party Nos. 1(a)-(f) as plaintiffs filed OC Suit No. 105 of 1979 in the First Court of Munsif, Kishoreganj against the petitioner and the predecessors of these opposite party Nos. 2(a)-2(f), 2 and 3 for ejectment of tenant. 

	3. The petitioner and the opposite party No. 3 filed written statements and contested the suit. 
	4. The suit of the plaintiff was decreed wherein the judgment was passed on 25-5-81 and the decree was signed on 3-6-1981. Against the aforesaid decree the tenant preferred OC Appeal No. 141 of 1981 before the learned District Judge Mymensingh who by his judgment dated 26-9-88 and decree dated 29-9-88 set aside the trial Court's aforesaid decree and thereafter the landlord filed Civil Revision No. 949 of 1988 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division by the judgment dated 17-2-93 set aside the appellate decree and restored that of the trial Court and that against the High Court Judgment the tenant preferred a review petition which was rejected by the High Court Division on 26-5-93 and a Leave Petition No. 282 of 1993 was filed before the Appellate Division against the High Court Judgment by the tenant but the same was •ejected by the Appellate Division on 2-9-93 and in the meanwhile the landlord (plaintiff) filed Execution Case No. 4 of 1993 on 10-4-1993 and thereafter on 2-9-93 the tenant filed an application in the aforesaid execution case for dismissal of the execution case on ground of limitation and the said application was rejected by the Executing Court by an order dated 25-10-93 and against this order the present revisional application has been filed by the petitioner and the petitioner obtained the Rule on 9-1-94 

	5. Mr. AA Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that the judgment and order dated 25-10-93 is bad in law, arbitrary, unwarranted, illegal and liable to be set aside. Mr. Chowdhury has further submitted that the learned Court below failed to consider the question of limitation and thus came to an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Chowdhury has further submitted that the judgment being passed on 25-5-1981 and the decree being signed on 3-6-81 arising out of which the Execution Case in question was filed on 10-4-93 and the Execution Case was barred under Article 181 of the Limitation Act but the learned trial Court without considering this point of limitation was very much pleased to refer to one unrelated decision and came to an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Chowdhry further submitted that the Execution Case in question should have been dismissed and in not doing so the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law occasioning a failure of justice. 

	6. Mr. Chowdhury in support of his contention has referred to 1 PLR 215 and has submitted that "limitation for an application to execute the decree or order runs from the date of decree or order sought to be executed". Mr. Chowdhury appearing for the petitioner then referred to 36 DLR (AD) 5 and has submitted that Article 182 requires that first application for execution is to be made within 3 years of the decree. 

	7. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(f), has filed an affidavit in-opposition on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(f), and has stated that the petitioner intentionally did not state the facts that the present opposite parties predecessor filed OC Suit 105 of 1979 for ejectment of the monthly tenant (the present petitioner) from a shop on ground of bonafide requirement. Mr. Bhuiyan has given the dates of the trial Court's judgment and decree and the date of the Appellate Court's judgment and the date oo. the judgment passed in the connected Civil Revision restoring that of the trial Court's judgment and decree and lastly, the date of judgment rejecting the leave petition of the tenant. Mr. Bhuiyan has submitted that in this case there was a continuation of proceeding and though the trial Court's judgment was made on 25-5-81 and the decree was signed on 3-6-81 and thereafter by the judgment of the Appellate Court the decree of the trial Court was set aside and the decree of the landlord was a non entity till it was restored in the Civil Revision on 17-2-93 and the plaintiff (the landlord) could not file execution case to execute the decree which was a non entity till 17-2-93 and in such view of the matter the landlord (the plaintiff) is in time in filing the execution case.

	8. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has submitted that after the judgment of High Court Division dated 17-2-93 restoring the judgment of the trial Court the filing of the execution case on 10-4-93 is within time, in view of the provisions of Article 182 of the Limitation Act and, as a matter of fact, Article 182 of the Limitation Act is applicable in the instant case and Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case the decision reported in 36 DLR (AD) 5 does not apply as the facts of the two cases are different. 

	9. Mr. Bhuiyan has referred to 12 DLR 730 and has submitted that an appeal includes revision and limitation runs from the order in revision under clause 2 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act. 

	10. Mr. Bhuiyan then referred to 33 DLR (AD) 101 and has submitted that a right to apply accrues on the final decree of the appellate Court or the revisional court as the case may be (with effect from the date of the final decree) and in view of Article 182 of the Limitation Act, time should run from the date of the final decree and Mr. Bhuiyan referred to Article 182 of the Limitation Act which runs as follows: 

	Description of application Period of Limitation Time from which period appealed from 182: For the execution of a decree Three years or, where a certified copy 1. The date of the decree or order, or 2. (Where there has been an appeal) the date or order of any civil of the decree or order of the final decree or order of the appellate Court, Court other than,— (1) applications to which section 48 of the has been registered, six years. s or the withdrawal of the appeal, or Code of Civil 3. (Where there has been a review of Procedure, 1908, applies and judgment) the date of the decision passed on the r review, or. (2) applications (Where the decree has been amended) the provided for by Article date of amendment, or 183. 5. (where the application next hereinafter mentioned has been made) the date of (the final order passed on an application made) in accordance with law to the proper Court for execution or to take some step in aid of execution of the decree or order, or 6. (in respect of any amount recovered by execution of the decree or order which the decree holder has been directed to refund by a decree passed in a suit for such refund)the date of such last mentioned decree. Or (in the case of an appeal therefrom) the date of the final decree of the Appellate Court or of the withdrawal of the appeal, or 7. (Where the application is to enforce any payment which the decree or order directs to be made at a certain date) such date.

	11. From the reading of sub-clauses 2, 3 and 6 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act I feel that time should run from the date of the final decree or order of the appellate Court or from the date of the decision passed on revision or review and from the date of such last mentioned decree or in the case of an appeal from the date of the final decree of the appellate Court. I think sub-clauses 2, 3 and 6 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act should be read together and there is no difficulty to say that the time should run from the date of the final decree and the right to apply for execution accrues on the date of the final decree of the appellate Court or revisional Court. 

	12. In view of the discussions made above I find that the Court below committed no error of law in rejecting the application of the petitioner and I find no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

 
End.

MI Farooqui with MA Wahab and M Saleem Ullah, Advocates—For the Appellant 
Fakir Abdul Mannan and Md. Ozair Farook Advocates—For the Opposite Party
parties:
Zarina Khatoon ----- Appellant
Vs.
Nazma Hafeez and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
F H M Habibur Rahman J: This appeal at the instance of defendant Zarina Khatoon is directed against the judgment and order passed on 21-11-83 by Mr. A J Mustafa, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Misc. Case No. 1052/80 arising out of Title Suit No. 74/73 of the said court.

2. Plaintiff Nazma Hafiz instituted Title Suit No. 74/73 on 21-7-73 against defendant No. 1 Zarina Khatun, wife of Md. Waliullah, 3/1, Kailash Ghosh Lane, PS Kotwali, Dhaka and defendant No. 2 Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka praying for a decree for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit property described in the schedule i.e. 06 acre of land being Municipal Holding No. 66 and CS plot No. 97 (part) of CS Khatian No. 157 in Mouza Baje Kakrail, PS Ramna, Dhaka. Defendant No. 1 Zarina Khatun, according to the plaintiff, entered into a written agreement dated 7-1-71 to sell the suit property to the plaintiff for Taka 55,000.00 after accepting advance consideration money of Taka 45,000.00 and gave delivery of possession of the suit property to the plaintiff on the same date. Plaintiff rented out the property to Mrs. Safia Ali, wife of Mr. SM Ali who stayed there till January, 1973 and thereafter the said tenant vacated the suit property and since then the plaintiff has been residing in the said property. It was stipulated in the agreement dated 7-1-71 that the defendant No. 1 shall execute and register the deed of sale in favour of plaintiff on receipt of the balance consideration money of Rs. 10,000.00 before 31st December, 1971 after getting necessary income tax clearance certificate and gain tax, etc. Thereafter plaintiff offered the balance consideration money of Rs. 10,000.00 from 1971 to 9th July, 1973 and asked defendant No.1 to execute and register the sale deed but defendant No. 1 ultimately refused to execute and register the deed in favour of the plaintiff on 9th July, 1973. The plaintiff therefore, was compelled to institute this title suit. By amendment of the plaint the plaintiff added in the plaint that the plaintiff has acquired an equitable title in the suit property by virtue of the written agreement dated 7-1-71 executed by defendant no.1 in favour of the plaintiff, that the letter dated 4-3-73 issued by defendant No. 4, Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh is illegal and that the Government of Bangladesh had no right to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit property. The plaintiff also added Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Public Works as defendant Nos. 3 and 4.

3. On 11-5-74 the suit was decreed ex parte by the learned Subordinate Judge.

4. On 14-6-74 the Government of Bangladesh filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree and for restoration of the said Title suit. This was numbered as Misc. Case No. 299/74. This Misc. Case was dismissed for default on 6-12-74. On 31-12-80 defendant No. 1 Zarina Khatun as petitioner filed Misc. Case No. 1052/80 under Order 9 rule 13 CPC praying for setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 11-5-74. in the present Title Suit No. 74/73 and to restore the same to its file and number directing the District Registrar, Dhaka making the endorsement of setting aside the said decree on the deed being No. 1079/4402 dated 2-3-76 executed and registered by the Subordinate Judge in Title Execution Case No. 29/74 with a further direction not to deliver the said document to the opposite party or to anyone else. The appellant petitioner alleged that she never received any notice of Title Suit No. 74/73 and that her husband also was never asked to receive any summons of the said title suit. She contended that she lived the whole year of 1973 in Comilla in her mother's house along with her husband, that she first came to know about the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 74/73 in the abandoned property cell by the Ministry of Works in the Secretariat of the Government of Bangladesh on 15-12-80, that she went to the court of the Subordinate Judge and submitted an information slip on 18-12-80, that she learnt about the ex parte decree definitely on 18-12-80 and that she promptly filed Misc. Case No. 1052 /80 on 31-12-80 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting aside the ex parte decree as aforesaid.

5. The plaintiff-respondent filed written objection to the effect that the summons of Title Suit No. 74 /73 was duly served upon the petitioner on 21-8-73 in presence of her husband Mr, Waliullah and witnesses and that in spite of receipt of summons of the said Title Suit No. 74/73 the petitioner defendant no. 1 did not enter appearance while the Government entered appearance and that ultimately on 11-5-74 the suit was decreed ex parte against the petitioner defendant No. 1 as well as against the Government. According to the plaintiff-respondent, as the service of summons was made on defendant No. 1 on 21-8-73, she (defendant No. 1) had knowledge of the suit and therefore, the application by defendant No. 1 in Misc. Case No. 1052/80 made on 31-11-80 is barred by limitation.

6. Both the parties examined witnesses. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the said Misc. No. 1052 of 1980 on 21-11-83 Thereafter defendant No. 1 Zarina Khatun has preferred this appeal against the said judgment and order dated 21-11-83.

7. At the time of hearing of the said Misc. Case on behalf of the defendant No. 1 petitioner Zarina Khatun, 4 witnesses, namely, PW 1 Waliullah, PW 2 Anwar Ali Khan, PW 3 Md. lqbal and PW 4 Md. Anwar were examined. On behalf of the respondent opposite party 7 witnesses, namely OPW 1 Faizuddin OPW 2 NC Paul OPW 3 Golam Mohammad OPW 4 Enamul Hafiz OPW 5 Azmal Ansari, OPW 6 Abu Jafar, and OPW 7 Fazle Elahi were examined.

8. PW 11 Waliullah the husband of petitioner defendant no.1 stated that he holds the registered power of attorney executed by his wife in his favour, that the suit property was rented out to SM Ali, that the said tenant SM Ali being a non-local Urdu speaking person went away during the liberation struggle, that the Government took over the suit property as abandoned property as appellant petitioner Zarina Khatun's husband's house at 3/1 Koilash Chose Lane PS Kotwali Dhaka was found vacant by the Government because defendant No. 1 and her husband had gone away to Comilla to defendant No. 1's mother's house and that after the said house at 3/1 Koilash Ghosh Lane was taken over by the Government as abandoned property, it was subsequently sold to defendant No. Is husband by registered deed dated 10-1-80 by the Government for Taka 100.00 in pursuance of the policy of the Government? He further deposed that neither PW 1 Waliullah nor his wife defendant No. 1 was asked to receive any summons of Title suit No. 74/73 of the 3rd Court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka at any time and that they did not know anything about the institution of the Title suit No. 74/73 and that neither defendant No. 1 nor PW 1 knew anything about the suit till the middle of December, 1980. No service of summons was made by the process server on defendant No.1. In his examination-in-chief PW I stated that he his wife defendant No.1 never resided at House No. 12-C 17/47 of Mirpur (House No. 47 Lane 7, Block C, Section 12, Mirpur) in 1973 or at any other time and that therefore, the question of service of summons at the aforesaid address at Mirpur does not arise at all. In his cross-examination PW 1 Waliullah stated that the application was written according to the statement of his wife defendant No.1, that PW 1 never went to see the suit property in 1972, that subsequently he could not go to the suit property out of fear although he came to know that the plaintiff was occupying the suit property and that his wife defendant No. 1 remained in Comilla since 1972, she could never go to the suit property.

9. PW 2 Anwar Ali Khan, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh corroborated PW 1 ownership and possession of the suit house by PW 1 and himself defendant No. 1, PW 3 and 4 deposed that PW 1 and his wife never resided in Mirpur.

10. OPs. 2-7 admittedly did not see the process server OPW 1 Faizuddin to serve any summons of this suit on defendant No. 1 in Mirpur. The fact that the process server OPW No. 1 Faizuddin deposed falsely will appear from the following discussion.

<u>11. It appears from the report made in the body of the summons Ext, 7 that OPW 1 Faizuddin, the process server, has reported that he did not find defendant No. 1 Mst. Zarina Khatun, wife of PW 1 Md. Waliullah at 3/1 Kailash Ghosh Lane, PS Kotwali, Dhaka, that on hearing that the said defendant No.1 resides at Mirpur House No. 12-C, L-7 /47 he on his own will went to Mirpur and at his convenience miraculously found defendant No. 1"s husband Waliullah there and asked him to receive the summons but the said Waliullah refused to accept the same or to grant receipt and that, therefore, he served the notice by hanging on the front door of the house at Mirpur on 21-8-73 in presence of Asgar Hossain, Shamsuddin, Lalu and Kalu Mia most of whom have been examined in this case. Rule 73 of Chapter III of Volume I of Civil Rules and Orders provides as follows:</u>

<u>"If the person addressed is absent from his residence at the time of attempted service and there is likelihood of his returning there within a reasonable time and there is no agent empowered to accept service on his behalf "nor any other person on whom service can be made, service shall be affected in the manner directed in Or. 5, r, 17. It should be proved according to the circumstances of the case by the declaration of the serving officer and, if necessary, by the affidavit or solemn declaration of some other person or persons (if any) acquainted with the facts that the person was absent from his residence at the time of attempted service and that there was no likelihood of his returning within a reasonable time and that there was no agent empowered to accept service, nor any other person on whom service could be made; and in any case that the house, on the outer door or some conspicuous part on which a copy of the process was affixed, was the ordinary residence or place of business of the person addressed at the time when it was so affixed. The court may also proceed under Or. 5 r. 19"</u>

<u>Rule 77 of Chapter III of Volume I of Civil Rules and Orders provides as follows:</u>

<u>"If the person addressed has no place of residence and he cannot be found or if he is dead, these facts shall be stated in the report together with the names and addresses of at least two persons from whom the facts are ascertained. If the persons addressed has ceased to live at the place, his present address, if available, and the source of information should be reported."</u>

<u>12. There is thus no doubt that the process server OPW I absolutely illegally and collusively showed that he on his own (without any order of the court) went to Mirpur to serve his notice on the false plea of serving the notice in question for which he had no legal authority in any manner, on behalf of the plaintiff. Respondent PW 3 Golam Mohammad stated that he is the son of late Lal Meah alias Lalu that he knows that PW 1 Md. Waliullah" used to reside in section 12 of Mirpur as he had seen him there in section 12 after the liberation of Bangladesh. But he does not remember when or for how many days he had seen him. No reliance can be put on his statement because undisputedly he had not seen PW 1 Waliullah residing with his wife (defendant No.1) in any house in section 12 of Mirpur.</u>

<u>Mere statement that the process server's report Ext A Ext. 7 contains the signature of his late father Lalu does not prove that defendant 1's husband PW 1 Waliullah was asked to receive the summons of the title Suit in question and that the said summons was served by hanging on the front door of a house in Mirpur where PW 1 Waliullah used to reside at the relevant time.</u>

13. We, therefore, hold that the summons were not duly served by the process server OPW 1 on defendant No.1 Zarina Khatun.

<u>14. Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan submits that the petitioner defendant Zarina Khatun knew about the ex parte decree passed on 11-5-74 because she knew that plaintiff was residing in the Suit property. There is no evidence to show that the defendant No. 1 or her husband personally has seen the plaintiff residing in the suit property after the liberationa war or after the aforesaid ex parte decree. PW1 Waliullah has merely stated that in 1973 he heard that the plaintiff was possessing the suit land but he himself could not pluck up courage to go to see the suit property. There is no reason for us to find that the defendant No. 1 has knowledge of passing of the ex parte decree dated 11-5-74 before 15 December, 1980. Furthermore, it is well settled that if it is found that the summons was not duly served on the defendant the ex parte decree must be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of the suit. In the case of Abdur Rashid vs. Abdul Barek reported in 35 DLR (AD) 162 it has been held:</u>

<u>"Under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code if summons is not duly served on the defendant, which is a good ground for setting aside the ex parte decree. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Code it will be apparent that due service of summons is an essential condition, which must be satisfied before the court can proceed to give judgment under Order 9 rule 13. If a party satisfies a Court that the summons has not been duly served upon him, the court is bound to set aside the ex parte decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex parte decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of the institution of the suit. No provision of law could be pointed out by the learned Counsel for the respondent which dispenses with the necessity of proper service of summons."</u>

15. In the instant case there was neither any service of summons on defendant No.1 Zarina Khatun nor there is any reason to hold that defendant No. 1 had knowledge of the institution of the suit.

16. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge on 21-11-83 are set aside. The Misc. Case No. 1052/80 is allowed.

The suit being Title Suit No. 74 of 1973 is restored to its file and number.

End.

case_source: Appeal against the Order of Mr. H. Huq, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court of Zilla Dacca dated the 28th day of May, 1979 passedin miscellaneous case, No.77 of 1977.
full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossain, J.- This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28.5.82 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge 3rd Court, Dacca in Miscellaneous case No. 77 of 1977 arising out of money suit No. 26 of 1974.

2. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid money suit No. 26 of 1974 in the 3rd Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dacca against the proforma respondent Nos. 2 and 3 for recovery of money alleged to be due on account of loan advanced to the said proforma respondent Nos. 2 and 3 against hypothecation of goods. The appellant Bangladesh Power Development Board was made proforma defendant No.4 in that suit. The proforma defendant No. 4 filed written statement and was contesting the suit. The suit was fixed on 79.12.76 for pre-emptory hearing. Defendants were found absent on call and the suit was decreed ex parte. Thereafter, the appellant defendant filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C giving rise to Misc. Case No. 77 of 1977 for setting aside the ex parte decree. The miscellaneous case was opposed by respondent No. 1. The ground on which the application under Order 9 rule 13 was made was stated to be engagement of the lawyer of the petitioner defendant in a case before the Labour Court. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence adduced in the case could not believe the ground and dismissed the miscellaneous case. Being aggrieved the petitioner defendant has preferred this appeal.

3. Mr. Abul Qushem Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant has taken us through the impugned judgment and other relevant materials. The learned Advocate submits that the petitioner defendant has examined his advocate to prove the advocate was engaged in the, labour court and the learned Trial court ought to have accepted the evidence of the Advocate and allowed the miscellaneous case. The learned Advocate further submits that the engagement of the lawyer in another court is a sufficient cause for non-appearance within the meaning of order 9 rule 13 of C.P.C. The learned Advocate has placed before us the decision of Mirza Umar Baksh Vs. Hussan Aara and others reported in P.L.D. 1960 (W.P.) Peshawar 85. In that case, it was held that a general statement of the kind, that counsel's absence, when the case was called because he was elsewhere in his professional activities was not a sufficient ground, will not be conducive to the administration of justice, for which the courts exists. "The absence of the Advocate on account of his being busy elsewhere in his professional activities was held to be a sufficient ground for non-appearance within the meaning of Order 9 rule 13 C.P.G, In the case of Asghar Hossain Vs. Vicarunnisa Begum reported in AIR 1961 Andba. Pra, 128 it was held that "If an Advocate is engaged in another court and is not in a position to appear in a suit or in an appeal, it is a sufficient cause for setting aside an ex-parte decree. If he makes a statement that he was not in a position to appear for particular reasons the statement ought to be generally accepted and not lightly brushed aside." In the case of Gajraj Singh Vs. Suraj Bux Singh and another reported in A.I.R. 1948 Oudh, 116 on which reliance has been placed by Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the respondent, it was however held that "the fact that when the appeal is called for bearing, the counsel of the appellant was preoccupied before another court is no ground for that attending to appeal and is not a sufficient cause." We are of the opinion that no hard and fast rule of law can be laid down as to whether the engagement of a lawyer in another court is or is not a sufficient cause for non-appearance within the meaning or order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. or similar other provisions of the Code. Every case must be considered in that background of the facts and circumstances of that case. In the case of Gajrej Singh vs. Suraj Bux Singh referred above, it was observed that "the question whether sufficient cause for readmission of an appeal dismissed for default has been made out or not is not one which can be decided with the aid of judicial decisions, except insofar as the decisions lay down any principle of universal application, Each case must depend upon its special facts and must be determined upon its own circumstances. There can be no hard and fast rule in determining a simple question of fact as this. “We find our self, with respects, in complete agreement with this observation. In the present case the petitioner has examined the Advocate Mr. Syed Ahmed as P.W. 2 who stated 'on that date I came to court at 10 A.M. and filed an application for adjournment as I was engaged in a part heard case in the Labour Court. After filing the petition I left the Court. It was not possible to move the petition........................... After returning from the Labour Court I find no order was passed on adjournment, petition but the suit was decreed ex-parte. In cross-examination he stated, "filed no papers to show that I was engaged in Labour Court. This was the only evidence adduced on the side of the petitioner defendant to prove that on that date his advocate was engaged in a case before the Labour Court. The evidence of the learned Advocate does not show that he was diligent in the conduct of the miscellaneous case. The learned Advocate had -not even moved the adjournment petition and bad left the court after simply throwing the same in court. This must be deprecated. In such circumstances, the alleged engagement of the lawyer cannot be held to be a sufficient case for non-appearance. In this case, it further appears that the learned Advocate could not produce any paper to show that he was engaged in the Labour Court. Even the diary of the advocate was not produced. We are unable to accept the Andha Pradesh view that the evidence of an advocate given in court should generally be accepted. There is no reason why the testimony of an advocate also should not require some corroboration. The evidence adduced on the said petition of the petitioner could not inspire confidence in the trial court and the trial court had disbelieved the ground of non-appearance alleged by the petitioner. We are unable to find fault with the learned trial court. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case we are of the opinion that the petitioner has failed to prove that he was prevented from appearing when the suit was called for hearing because of this advocate's engagement in another court, and the learned trial court has rightly dismissed the Misc Case.    


The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without any order as to costs.

Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.-I agree.

End.
