case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 5-4-68 passed by the Dacca High Court in S. A. No. 218 of 1968)
full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J.—This appeal by special leave is at the instance of Dacca Improvement Trust (hereinafter referred to as (DIT) against a judgment and order of a Single, Judge of the Dacca High Court reversing a concurrent order of rejection of the plaint, filed in a suit instituted by Respondents No. 1 and 2, under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Respondents No. 1 and 2 instituted the suit against the appellant and the remaining respondents for a declaration that there was no valid and enforceable requisition and or acquisition or eviction notices as served upon the plaintiffs and that the acquisition was in violation of the order dated 8th March, 1966 made by the appellant and also for an injunction restraining the appellant and others from enforcing the requisition and/or acquisition and disturbing thereby the possession of Respondents No. 1 and 2 in the property in suit.

3. After the service of the notices of the suit the appellant, namely, Dacca Improvement Trust, which is defendant No. 1 in the suit, appeared and filed an application stating that the suit was barred under section 93C of the Town Improvement Act, and that as such the plaint was liable to be rejected under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Before this objection of the appellant was heard and plaintiffs-Respondents filed an application on 8-4-67 for amendment of the plaint by substituting the prayer (a) of the plaint by a new prayer to the following effect:

"(a) a decree be passed declaring that the date 13-8-66 contained in Memo  of the D. I. T. Dacca cancelling the permission accorded in letter No. 881- T. P. dated 8-3-66, is illegal, void, malafide, with-out jurisdiction and is not binding upon the plaintiffs and that the subsequent notices upon the plaintiffs on the strength of the said illegal order viz, notices dated 3,9-66 are also illegal, void and inoperative This prayer are amendment of 	the plaint was allowed and the plaint stood amended With the new prayer (a):

4, The trial Court, however, being of the view that the declaration prayed for in the plaint being tantamount to setting at naught the order of requisition came, within the mischief of section 93C of the Town Improvement Act; rejected the plaint under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure by his order dated 10-4-67. On appeal, the Court of Subordinate Judge affirmed the view of the learned Munsif as well as his order rejection of the plaint.

5. A second appeal was filed by the plaintiffs in the Dacca High Court against the said order of` rejection of the plaint. At the time of the hearing of the appeal, a preliminary objection was taken on behalf of the present appellant on the contention that the appeal before the first appellate Court was incompetent, in view. of the fact that no certified copy of the decree was filed along with the Memorandum of appeal as required under Order 41, rule I of the Civil Procedure Code, According to the definition of the term, 'decree' as contained in section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the order of rejection of the plaint passed on the 10th April, 1967 was deemed to be a decree and as such was appealable as a decree, but it was contended on behalf of the present appellant, as the Memorandum of Appeal against the said order of rejection filed on the 12th April, 1967 was not accompanied by a certified copy of the formal decree which was subsequently drawn up and signed on 6.6 67, the appeal was incompetent for contravening the mandatory provision of the Code in regard to the filing of a certified copy of the decree along with a certified copy of the judgment as contained in rule 1 of the Order 41 of the Code. The learned Judge of the Dacca High Court relying upon a decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Jagadish Bhargava Vs. Jawaharlal Bhargava and others in A.I.R. 1961 (SC) 832 took the view that no format decree Court having not been drawn to the defect relating to the filing of a certified copy of the decree, it would not be reasonable to penalize the party for the default of the office in suggestions that it was needful for the party to move the Court for the necessary order and that the decree having ultimately been prepared and formed a part of the record before the appellate Court, it could not be said that the appeal before the First Appellate Court was incompetent.

6. On the merits of the appeal the learned Judge of the High Court has held that the sum and substance of the plaintiff's case is that after the acquisition had been completed, the plaintiffs obtained license to remain on the land and raised structure thereon with the permission of Defendant No. 1 and that the subsequent cancellation of the said permission was without any lawful authority. The learned Jude has taken the view that as the prayer (a) of the plaint having sought for a declaration only with respect to the validity of the order of cancellation of the permission granted by defendant No. 1 and correctness or legality of the order of requisition or acquisition made under Town Improvement Act, having not been challenged, the said prayer cannot be said to be barred under section 93C of the Town Improvement Act. As regards prayer (b) of the plaint in which a decree has been sought for restraining the defendants permanently from enforcing the requisition or acquisition and from disturbing thereby the possession of the plaintiffs in the property in suit, the learned Judge has noted that he did not accede to the prayer in the plaint to which was made before him for amending the of said prayer. in the plaint to which also an exception was taken on the ground that by the said prayer the correctness or validity of the order of requisition and acquisition made under the Town Improvement Act was impugned, and has ultimately held that this part of prayer having not been in accordance with the case made out in the body of the plaint can be ignored.

7. The new point as to the maintainability of the suit under section 14 of the East Bengal Building Construction Act 1952 was sought to be argued at the hearing of the Second appeal on behalf of the defendants on the view that the bar in suit under the aforesaid provision was attracted as the legality of an order made under section 9 of the said Act was challenged. The learned Judge, however, did not entertain this contention on the view that as the said point was not taken before the trial Court, it could not therefore, be entertained by the said Court. The learned Judge has therefore, held that the statements in the plaint having not challenged any order or action under Chapter IV of the Town Improvement Act, 1953, the suit was not barred under section 93C of the said Act. The concurrent order of rejection of the plaint by the two Courts below was set aside and the trial Court was directed to proceed with the suit.

8. Leave was granted by the Supreme Court of Pakistan to appeal against the judgment of the Dacca High Court for considering the following points:

(i) Whether in view of the statements and the prayer made in the plaint the suit was barred under section 93 C of. the Town Improvement Act and as such the plaint was liable to be rejected under Order 7, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

(ii) Whether having regard to the fact that the Memorandum of Appeal against the Order of rejection of the plaint was not accompanied by a certified copy of the order drawn up in the form of a formal decree as required by Order 41, Rule 1 C.P. Code, the said appeal as well as the second appeal before the High Court were competent.

(iii) Whether in view of the facts of the case the suit was barred under section 14 of the East Bengal Building Construction Act, 1952.

9. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, has contended that the case as made out in the plaint being substantially for a declaration which required an adjudication as to the legality of the requisition and acquisition proceedings initiated under the Town Improvement Act, the bar contemplated in section 93 C of the said Act becomes operative. The learned Counsel has submitted that although the original prayer in the plaint has been amended and has been substituted by a new prayer in which there is no explicit reference to the requisition and acquisition proceedings, the averments in the plaint make it sufficient clear that what the plaintiffs were seeking was the undoing of the requisition and acquisition of the plaintiffs land. Moreover, it has been further submitted by the learned Counsel that the first part of the prayer (b) having been made for a decree seeking to restrain the defendants permanently from enforcing the requisition and or acquisition of the disputed land, the case is clearly within the mischief of the bar contained in section 93C of the Town Improvement Act.

10. Mr. M. H. Khandker, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents, has, on the other hand, submitted that the statements in the plaint make it abundantly clear that the Plaintiffs did not seek at all to challenge any action taken or order made relating to requisition or acquisition of the disputed land under Town Improvement Act and that the substantial case made out in the plaint relates to certain arrangements subsequent to the requisition and acquisition of the suit premises leading to the cancellation of the order of requisition and grant of permission by the Chairman of the D.I.T. the appellant, to construct a three storied Commercial building on the disputed land. What has been challenged in the suit, according to the learned Counsel, is the subsequent cancellation of the said permission by the Authorised Officer of the D.I.T. and the notices of eviction served upon the plaintiffs in consequence of such cancellation. Learned Counsel has submitted that the cancellation of the permission and the approval of the plan being, according to the plaint, not under Town Improvement Act, section 93C of the said Act cannot be attracted.

<u>11. Section 93C of the Town Improvement Act prohibits the entertainment by any Civil Court of a suit or application against any order passed or action taken under Chapter IV of the Town Improvement Act except as expressly provided in the said chapter which contains provisions for requisition and acquisition of land for carrying out the purposes of the Act, constitution of a Tribunal for performing the function of compulsory acquisition of land and determination of compensation in respect of such land and the procedure for assessment of compensation. What is meant by this provision is that the correctness or regularity of any order made or action taken under the said chapter can be called in question only in the manner as laid down in the said chapter, and it cannot be challenged in a collateral proceeding in a civil court. On perusal of the plaint it does not appear that any action or order purported to be taken or made under the provision of the Town Improvement Act has been sought to be challenged in the suit. The case made out in the plaint in substance is that the plaintiffs being served with a notice purporting to acquire the land mentioned in the schedule of the plaint approached the Chairman D.I.T. who assured him that the premises in suit would not be required as it fell beyond the proposed alignment for which the acquisition proceeding was started and that it would be returned to him in due time. In pursuance of this assurance the plaintiffs submitted a plan of a three storied commercial building which was approved by an order dated 4.11.65 after vacating the requisition order 20.3.63. In consequence of said order the plan submitted by the plaintiffs was duly approved by the Authorised Officer on 8-3-66 and on the strength of the said permission the plaintiffs started construction of the building and almost completed it incurring a heavy expenditure when the plaintiffs received a letter communicating the order of cancellation of the approved plan and several notices thereafter asking the plaintiffs to vacate the disputed premises, and then the present suit has been instituted with a prayer for declaration that the order cancelling the permission accorded in letter dated 8.3.66 as well as the notices issued upon the plaintiffs on the strength of the said order were illegal, void, malafide and without jurisdiction. The second prayer is for restraining the defendant permanently from enforcing the requisition and or acquisition and disturbing thereby the possession of the plaintiffs property in suit.</u>

12. As it appears from the averments made in the plaint as well as the prayers therein, they do not appear to be directed against any order made or action taken under the Town Improvement Act. The plaintiffs case in fact being that after the notice of acquisition under the Town Improvement Act had been served on the plaintiffs, a new arrangement was brought into effect due to an agreement between the plaintiffs and the Chairman of D.I.T. as a result of which the order of requisition was Vacated and a permission was granted to the plaintiffs to construct a three storyed commercial building and that the subsequent cancellation of the said permission, as well as the notices of the eviction issued on the strength of the said order of cancellation, being void, malafide and without any jurisdiction, the bar contemplated in section 93C of the Town. Improvement Act cannot obviously come into operation as none of the orders or notices challenged where, according to the statement made in the plaint, under any of the provision of Chapter IV of the Town Improvement Act.

<u>13. There is, of course, some reference to the requisition and/or acquisition in the first part of the second prayer made in the plaint in respect of which a prayer for amendment was made before the learned Judge of the High Court but he was pleased not to allow the said amendment. The learned Judge, however, held that the said prayer was redundant and not consistent with the statements made in the plaint which was based on a, new agreement subsequent to the acquisition. As it has been pointed out above, the suit did not purport to challenge the legality or validity of any order of requisition or acquisition made under the Town Improvement Act but it sought to establish that, in view of the subsequent arrangement and the action of Defendant No. 1 the plaintiffs are not liable to be evicted from the disputed premises. The action or order which has been challenged in the suit was not definitely, according to the statements of the plaint, made or taken under the Town Improvement Act By seeking to restrain the enforcement of the order of requisition or acquisition made under the Town Improvement Action the basis of the new right alleged to be arising from a subsequent arrangement between the plaintiffs and defendant No. 1, the plaintiffs are trying to establish that in view of the subsequent arrangement and action taken by defendant No. I the order of requisition and acquisition which might have been good and unexceptionable at the time when it was made has become unenforceable and inoperative because of the subsequent arrangement. It cannot therefore be said that by such a prayer as seeks to establish that the plaintiffs are not liable to be removed from the possession of the disputed premises as a result of the new right arising from the subsequent action of Defendant No. 1, the plaintiffs suit is brought within the mischief of Section 93C of the Act. Whether the plaintiffs will ultimately succeed in establishing their claim in the suit is entirely a different matter, but in view of the nature of the case made in the plaint, it cannot be maintained that the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred under the provision of Section 93C of the Act, We are, therefore, of the opinion that the learned Judge of the High Court was not wrong in holding that the suit was not barred under the said provision.</u>

<u>14. Leave was granted also to consider the question of applicability of section 14 of the East Bengal Building Construction Act, 1912. This objection was not taken in the trial Court not in the First Appellate Court. Such an objection was taken for the first time in the High Court. The learned Judge in deciding the appeal before the High Court did not express any opinion on this objection on ground that it was not mooted in the trial Court but observed that the defendant was at liberty to raise this objection before the trial Court. The Supreme Court of Pakistan having, however, granted leave to consider the question, learned Counsel for the appellant has argued this point and has submitted that the case made out in the plaint sought to impugn the order of the Authorised Officer under section 9 of the East Bengal Building Construction Act, 1952 cancelling the sanction for construction of the three storeyed building and that as such the suit is barred under section 14 of the said Act which provides that every such order shall be final and shall not be called in question in any Civil Court. It is, no doubt, true that the amended prayer (a) specifically calls in question, the order of the Authorised Officer cancelling the permission accorded to the plaintiffs but the plaintiff's case, as it appears from the said prayer, is that such an order of cancellation was void, malafide and without jurisdiction. It is now well established that when an order purporting to be made under a certain provision of a statute is shown to have been made without jurisdiction or malafide such an order cannot be said to have been made under the said statute and that in such a case the statutory provision seeking to bar a suit challenging the said order is not attracted. What is really meant to be prohibited by such a barring provision is a suit challenging the propriety or correctness of an order under a particular statute, which is not a nullity. If the order, though purporting to be made under a statute, being malafide or without jurisdiction, is a nullity, such an order cannot be taken, to have been made under the said statute. Reference may be made to the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Secretary of State for India Vs. Mask & Co., L. B. 67 I. A. 222 same case A.I.R. 1940 P.C. 105 same case 44 C. W.N. 709 and also the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Abdul Pouf and others Vs. Abdul Hanalei Khan in 16 D.L.R. (S.C.) 515 same case P.L.D. 1965 S. C. 671. The case made out in the plaint being that the order of the Authorised Officer was without jurisdiction and malafide the barring provision as contemplated in Section 14 of the East Bengal Building Construction Act, 1952 cannot obviously be attracted. Whether the plaintiffs will ultimately succeed in establishing that the said order was without jurisdiction or malafide is a different question and that will be decided in the suit itself. But upon such a pleading, in any view, the suit cannot be held to be barred under section 14 of the East Bengal Building Construction Act, 1952, and the plaint cannot be rejected Under Order 7, Rule (b) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

15. The procedural question on which, leave was granted relates to the question of the maintainability of the appeal against the order made under Order 7, rule II of the Code, when the memorandum of the Appeal, though filed along with a certified copy of the order under appeal, was not accompanied by a certified copy of the decree as required under Order 41 rule 1 of the Code.

16. It appears that the order rejecting the plaint was made on the 10th April, 1967 and the appeal against the said order was filed on the 12th April, 1967. A certified copy of the order was, of course, filed along with the Memorandum of Appeal but no copy of the decree was filed, although a formal decree appears to have been prepared, and signed in this case on the 6th June, 1967. The appeal was heard and decided on 10.7.67, that if, after the drawing up of a formal decree. The absence of a copy of the formal decree which, as a matter of fact, was prepared and signed, was not taken any notice of by the Court or by the parties and the appeal was decided without such a copy. The learned Judge of the High Court has, however, held that though the appeal was defective in form and the defect could have been rectified by a suitable order of the Court requiring the filing of a certified copy of the decree but that the decree having formed a part of the records after it had been prepared and the said records having been before the Appellate Court at the time of the hearing, the appeal was maintainable. It has been contended by the learned Counsel for the appellant that the learned Judge having taken the view that the appeal was defective in form for the non-filing of a certified copy of the decree was not correct in holding that the defect had been cured by the fact that the original records of the case containing the formal decree prepared before the Court at the time of the hearing. The learned Judge of the High Court appears to have relied upon the judgment of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Jagadish Bhargava Vs. Jawaharlal Bhargava and others in A.I.R. 1961 S. C. 832 to hold that the appeal before the First Appellate Court was not incompetent for the failure of the appellants to file a certified copy of the formal decree under appeal. But that case is not on all fours with the instant case, because in that case of the Indian Jurisdiction, the absence of a certified copy of the decree under appeal was detected before the disposal of the appeal and although the Court was of the view that the provision of Order 41, Rule 1 of the Code Was mandatory, but that the defect could be made good by giving an opportunity to the appellant to file the requisite copy of the decree Gajendra gadakar, J.(as he then was) who delivered the Judgment of the Court explained the provision of Order 41 rule 1 of the Code in the following words.

"The position of law the under Order 41, Rule 1 is absolutely clear. Under the said rule every appeal has to be preferred in the form of a memorandum signed by the appellant or his pleader and presented to the Court or to such officer as it appoints in that behalf and has to be accompanied by a copy of the decree Appealed from and of the judgment on which it is founded. Rule 1 empowers the appellate Court to dispense with the filing of the judgment but there is no jurisdiction in the Appellate Court to dispense with the filing of the decree".

17. The said Court, however, does not appear to have taken a very rigid view about this procedural requirement, and proceeded to consider various situation which may arise as a result of the failure of the appellant to file a certified copy of the decree, in the following passage, at page 837 of the report:

"If at the time when the appeal is preferred a decree has already been drawn up by the trial Court and the appellant has not applied for it in time it would be a clear case where the appeal would be incompetent and a penalty of dismissal could be justified. The position would however be substantially different if at the time when the appeal is presented before the appellate Court a decree, 10 fact had not been drawn up by the trial Court, in such a case if an application has been made by the appellant for a certified copy of the decree then all that can be said against the appeal preferred by him is that the appeal is premature sine a decree has not been drawn up and it is the decree against which an appeal lies In such a case, if the officer of the High Court examines the appeal carefully and discovers the defect, the appeal may be returned to the appellant for presentation with the certified copy of the decree after it is obtained. In the case like the present if the appeal has passed through the stage of admission through the over sight of the officer then the only fair and rational course to adopt would be to adjourn the hearing of the appeal with a direction that the appellant should produce the certified copy of the decree as soon as it is supplied to him. In such a case it could be open to the High court and we apprehend it would be its duty to direct the Subordinate Court to draw up the decree forthwith without any delay. On the other hand, if a decree has been drawn up and an application for its certified copy has been made by the appellant after the decree was drawn up, the office of the appellate Court should return the appeal to the appellant as defective and when the decree is filed by him the question of limitation may be examined on merits. It would then be clear that no hard and fast rule of general applicability can be laid down for dealing with appeals defectively Media under Order 41, Rule 1".

18. We thus find that the said decision, in which the provision of Order 41, rule 1 was held to be mandatory, does not support the conclusion reached by the learned Judge of the High Court, regard being had to the fact that no copy of the decree was filed before the hearing of the appeal despite the fact that such a decree was drawn up and made a part of the record of the trial Court.

19. A similar question was considered again by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Phool Chand Vs. Gopal Lal, reported in A.I.R. 1967, 1470, in which case a decree was not at all drawn up by the trial Court inspite of being moved in that behalf and the appeal was heard without a copy of the decree in the file of the appellate Court. In the exceptional circumstance of that case the Supreme Court of India took the view that although the provision or Order 41, rule 1 of the Code was mandatory, the appeal was maintainable without a copy of the decree, because "the fact that the trial court refused to frame a formal decree cannot in law deprive Gopal Lal of his right to appeal." Similarly, the Supreme Court of India held in the case of Shakuntala Vs Kuntal, reported in A.I.R. 1969 S.C. 575, that an appeal against an order under section 47 C.P. Code would be competent, if the Memorandum of appeal was accompanied by a copy of the judgment alone where no formal decree had been drawn up.

20. The ratio of these cases seems to be that the requirement of filing a certified copy of the decree, though mandatory and the Ming of it cannot be dispensed with by the appellate Court, is not of such basic character as would make the disposal of the appeal without such a copy completely without jurisdiction, but it would rather depend upon the superior court hearing an appeal from such a decision to decide whether the circumstances were of such an exceptional nature as would make the failure of the appellant to file the necessary copy excusable.

21. The facts of these latter two cases have got some similarity with those of the instant case in the sense that the appeal had been ultimately heard without a copy of the decree, but the difference is that no decree had at all been prepared in those cases whereas in the instend case a decree had, as a matter of fact, been formally drawn up.

22. The learned Judge, of the High Court, however, appears to have taken the instant case to be an exceptional one in view of the fact that the attention of none of the parties nor of the Court was attracted to the defect as to the absence of a certified copy of the formal decree before the disposal of the appeal and there was no question of prejudice to any of two parties in regard to the hearing of the appeal without a certified copy of the decree as the original record containing the decree which was subsequently formally drawn up was before the appellate Court.

<u>23. This line of reasoning deems to be quit logical. We need not, however, express any final opinion in this regard, as the decision in this case may be more appropriately founded on a different premise. It appears no doubt from the provision of Order 41, rule 1(1) that the requirement that the Memorandum shall be accompanied by a copy of the decree appealed from is compulsory Under the provision of the said rule the Court has power to dispense with the filing of a copy of the judgment but not of the decree, for the obvious reason that according to the provision of the Code as contained in section 96, it is against a decree that an appeal lies. When a suit has been disposed of by a judgment, a decree shall follow in accordance with the provision of section 33 of the Code and a formal decree is prepared in accordance with the provision of rules 6-19 of Order 20 of the Code. The case of an appeal against an order rejecting the plaint under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code stands, however, on a different footing. Such an order which may be made even before the appearance of a defendant is not strictly an adjudication in respect of any of the rights in controversy between the parties and does not come within the substantive provision of the definition clause as incorporated in section 2(2) of the Code, but it is a decree in view of the inclusive provision of the definition clause, which provides that the expression, 'decree', "shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within section 47 or section 144." The provisions of Order 20 of the Code which lay down procedural rules relating to pronouncement and signing of a judgment and the drawing up of a decree which is to follow such a judgment do not strictly appear to have any application to such an order as is itself deemed to be a decree under the definition clause. It is true that the Civil Rule that the Civil Rules and Orders of the High Court of Calcutta 1935 contained a rule being Rule No. 186 which was to the following effect:</u>

<u>"An order rejecting a plaint being a 'decree' within the meaning of section 2(2), C.P. Code, it shall in every case be followed by a decree whether or not defendant has appeared or costs have been allowed."</u>

24. This rule has, however, been deleted by an order, being No. 429 dated the 29th April, 1941. Reference may also be made to Rule No. 187 (1) which provides as follows:

"Decree or formal orders in the nature of decrees need not be drawn up under the Code in all Cases even though the orders concerned may be adjudication upon right claimed or defence set up, for instance final orders under Orders No. 9 and 13; Order 21 or 2, 38, 91, 92, 99, 100, 101 41 r. 19, 21, 23.47 r. 1 C.P. Code."

<u>25. We thus see that under the amended provisions of the Civil Rule and Orders which were issued under the authority of the Calcutta High Court and which has been adopted in this Court, a formal decree need not be drawn up in respect of an order of rejection of a plaint in accordance with the provision of Order 20 of the Code, and the said Order itself may be taken to be a decree for the purpose of filing an appeal under Order 41 rule 1 of the Code particularly having regard to the provisions of Civil Rules and Orders which do not require the drawing up of a formal decree in case of an order of rejection of a plaint under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code. We are, therefore, of opinion that an appeal against an order of rejection of a plaint under Order 7, rule 11, C.P. Code filed with a copy of the said order, but without a certified copy of a formal decree of such an order was maintainable, even though such a formal decree, as a matter of fact, was prepared after the filing of the said appeal.</u>

<u>The result, therefore, is that the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

parties:
Bangladesh ----- Petitioner
vs
Rafeda Khatun and ors ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md Delwar Hossain J : This Rule was issued calling upon opposite-party Nos. 1-7 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 18-10-2006 passed by the Additional District Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh in Other Appeal No. 250 of 2005 affirming those dated 7-9-2005 passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No. 2 of 2004 decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The opposite-parties as plaintiffs instituted other Class Suit No.2 of 2004 in the Court of Joint District Judge, First Court Mymensingh for declaration of title in respect of the suit land.

3. Plaintiffs' case, in short, was that the nature of the suit land was homestead and pond and it belonged to Maharaja Sitangshu Kumar Acharjee Chowdhury. The predecessor of the plaintiffs, Abdul Hye Sujan took rokka pattan of the suit land on 18th Kartic 1351 BS and since then he had been in possession therein by constructing dwelling house, excavating pond and rearing fish. Preliminary record of right was prepared in the name of Abdul Hye Sujan, but finally was prepared in the name of the Government. Said Abdul Hye Sujan died on 30-9-1996 leaving behind the plaintiffs as his legal heirs. Thus the predecessor of the plaintiffs and after his death the plaintiffs had/have been possessing the suit land for more than 60 years. The plaintiffs came to know about the wrong recording of the record of right in the name of the Government for the first time on 2-5-2002 which created, cloud over their title to the suit land, hence the suit.

4. Defendants contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Zaminder and CS Khatian was prepared in the name of Zaminder and by operation of law the same vested in the Government after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act) came into being. Record of right was correctly prepared in 1962 in the name of the Government. Further case of the defendants was that the plaintiffs had/have no right, title and interest in the suit land. In order to grab the suit land of the Government plaintiffs created some false documents and instituted the present suit.

5. At the trial the plaintiffs examined 5 witnesses and filed some documents in support of their claim to the suit land. The defendants examined one witness and also filed documents. The learned Joint District Judge on consideration of the evidence on record by his judgment and decree dated 31-8-2005 decreed the suit declaring the plaintiffs' title to the suit land. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree of the trial Court the defendants preferred other Appeal No. 250 of 2005 before the District Judge, Mymensingh the said appeal on being transferred was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh who by the impugned judgment and decree dismissed the appeal affirming those passed by the trial Court. Hence this revision by defendant No.1.

6. Mr Zainul Abedin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the Courts below failed to consider the interpolation in the alleged rokka pattan, the very basis of the plaintiffs' claim which was admitted by PW 5, Mohini Mohan Dey and non consideration of the said apparent factual aspect and the evidence of PW 5 resulted in an error occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit. He further submitted that the suit land belonged to Zaminder Maharaja Sitangshu Kumar Acharjee Chowdhury as khash land. After the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force the suit land, being chandina land, vested in the Government as khash land. Accordingly, record of right was correctly prepared in the name of the Government. Therefore, by the alleged pattan the plaintiffs' predecessor did not acquire any title to the suit land, both the Courts below committed error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside.

7. Mr Sikder Mahmudur Raji, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Bakiruddin Bhuiyan for the plaintiff-opposite-parties, on the other hand, submitted that the predecessor of the plaintiffs took rokka pattan of the suit land on 18th Kartic, 1351 BS from Maharaja Sitangshu Kumar Acharjee Chowdhury and since then had been possessing peacefully without any interference from any quarter. Accordingly, they acquired valid right, title and interest in the suit land, but the suit land was wrongly recorded as khash land in the record of right in the name of the Government which they came to know on 2-5-2002 and, as such, they instituted the suit for declaration of their title, the court below rightly decreed the suit. He further submitted that both the courts below having concurrently believed plaintiffs' case of settlement by rokka from its original owner and thus title in the suit land there is no scope of interference with the impugned judgment and decree by this Court in exercising revisional jurisdiction and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

8. We have perused the revision application and the evidence on record both oral and documentary and the impugned judgment and decree.

9. The only point to be decided in this revision is, whether the appellate Court was justified in affirming the decree passed by the trial Court in decreeing the suit.

<u>10. From Exhibit 3 series it appeared that the suit land is Chandina land, so the same vested in the Government after the acquisition of the wholesale interest of the Zamindars pursuant to the provisions of section 3 of the Act, and therefore, neither the plaintiffs' predecessor nor the plaintiffs did acquire any title in the suit land by virtue of the alleged rokka pattern. From Exhibit 3 series, 'Kha' and 'Ga', it is clear that the suit land is Khas land of the Government. PW 5 Mohini Mohan Dey, who was 92 years old and examined to prove the settlement by the Zamindars, stated in his cross-examination to the effect : “দাখিলাগুলিতে ঘষা মাজা আছে।” We have also perused the dakhila and the same appeared to us interpolated which fact alone created doubt as to the genuineness of the same. But unfortunately, none of the courts below considered the said vital piece of evidence of PW 5 and thus fell into an error in finding title of the plaintiffs in the suit land. It is true that the appellate Court is the last court of fact, but it having failed to consider the material evidence as discussed above, the finding of fact arrived by it is not infallible and can be interfered with in revision.</u>

11. Mr Raji relying on the case of Bangladesh vs Har Chandra Nath reported in 10 MLR (AD) 313 tried to argue that the plaintiffs also acquired right, title, and interest in the suit land by virtue of their possession therein for more than 60 years, so the courts below rightly decreed the suit.

<u>12. Both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land for a long continuous period. But the question is, whether they are in possession for more than 60 years, because in order to acquire title by way of adverse possession the plaintiffs must prove their possession for more then 60 years as provided in Article 149 of the Limitation Act, 1908. The rokka pattan by which the plaintiffs' predecessor claimed to have taken pattan though not proved even if taken into consideration for the purpose of possession it appeared that the same is dated 18th Kartic 1351 BS corresponding to 2/3 November, 1944 and the suit was instituted on 2-1-2005, that is, before 60 years. Therefore, the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the suit land by virtue of their possession.</u>

13. However, since the plaintiffs have been in long continuous possession if so advised, they may approach the concerned authority of the government for giving settlement of the same in their favour and if they so approach they shall consider their prayer with sympathy.

14. In conclusion, we are constrained to hold that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title to the suit land so the court below was not justified in affirming the decree of the trial Court decreeing the suit declaring their title.

15. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 18-10-2007 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh in Other Appeal No. 250 of 2005 allowing the appeal affirming those passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No. 2 of 2004 is set aside and the suit is dismissed.

Send down the lower court records.

End.

parties:
Marjina Khatoon ----- Petitioner
vs
Shamsunnahar and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant No. 2 appellant petitioner was issued calling upon the plaintiff-respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 16-9-2001 (decree drawn on 20-9-2001) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Satkhira in Title Appeal No. 61 of 1992 dismissing the appeal, affirming the judgment and decree dated 16-2-1991 (decree drawn on 23-2-1991) passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Satkhira in Title Suit No. 345 of 1980 in decreeing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the suit against the petitioner and others as defendants praying for declaration of title to the suit land in "ka" schedule in respect of 0.0633 acres and khas possession in "kha" schedule out of "ka" schedule measuring 0.01470 acres described in the plaint and for injunction.

3. The plaintiff's (opposite party No. 1) case, in short, was that the defendant No. 1 purchased the 'ka' schedule land in Plot No. 2084 measuring 0.0633 acres along with other lands by a registered kabala dated 7-6-1952 who transferred the same to the plaintiff by registered sale deeds dated 4-7-1965 and 7-6-1966 and delivered possession. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 encroached into the land measuring 0.01470 acres of 'kha' schedule land out of 'ka' schedule in the month of Magh, 1377 BS and constructed house illegally for which the plaintiff requested the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on 20th Chaitra, 1386, for fixing boundary pillars on survey of the land by the Amin which they refused and hence the suit. It has been stated that the plaintiff sold 20 link from the northern side and 18 link from the southern side of plot No. 2038 of the land within the road of Satkhira Paurashava.

4. Defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff after purchase of the suit land got physical possession and constructed pucca wall around the suit land measuring 0.0633 acres of land and she had no land outside the boundary wall. According to the report of the Advocate Commissioner, the plaintiff s purchased land was within the boundary wall. The defendants did not encroach the plaintiffs land. There was 0.07 acres of land within the boundary wall excluding the road. Thus she prayed for dismissal of the suit.

5. Defendant No. 5 Satkhira Paurashava also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff encroached 20 link from southern side and 15 link from northern side in the eastern portion of the road in Plot No. 2038, that is, 1.470 square link.

6. The learned Assistant Judge, hearing the parties and perusing the evidence on record, by his judgment and decree dated 16-2-1991 (decree drawn on 23-2-1991) decreed the suit declaring plaintiff's title in respect of 0.0633 acres of land in 'ka' schedule and she was entitled to get the land measured by survey and fixing boundary pillars and directed the defendant No. 2 to deliver possession in respect of 'kha' schedule land measuring 0.01470 acres to the plaintiff within 2(two) months from the date of decree failing which the plaintiff would be entitled to get possession in accordance with law and also restrained the defendant No. 2 from disturbing the plaintiff's possession in the suit land by a decree of permanent injunction.

7. The defendant No. 2 being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court preferred Title Appeal No. 61 of 1991 before the learned District Judge, Satkhira which on transfer the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Satkhira by his judgment and decree dated 16-9-2001 (decree drawn on 20-9-2001) dismissed the appeal affirming those passed by the trial Court.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, the defendant No. 2 as petitioner filed this civil revision application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

9. None appeared for the petitioner.

10. Mr Parimal Chandra Guha, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, submits that admittedly mother of the petitioner sold 0.0633 acres of land from plot No. 2084 as described in 'ka' schedule to the plaint to the opposite party No. 1 by 2(two) registered sale deeds dated 4-7-1965 and 7-6-1966. Since the petitioner and the opposite party are joint owners in the 'ka' schedule land including the suit land the opposite party No. 1 is legally entitled to get 0.0633 acres suit land from plot No. 2084 by fixing boundary pillars at any time and also she is not required to file partition suit. In support of his submission Mr Guha has referred to the case of Shankar Chandra Das vs Kalachand Das reported in 46 DLR 419. He lastly submits that since both the Courts below, discussing the facts and evidence of the case, arrived at concurrent findings, this Court in revisional jurisdiction has little scope to interfere with the same.

11. I have heard the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, perused the revision application, the judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below.

<u>12. Though none appeared for the petitioner yet the High Court Division in exercise of its supervisory power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure can dispose of the matter on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. Even in the absence of either of the parties the High Court Division can exercise its revisional jurisdiction suo moto. In support of my view, I may quote a passage from the decision in the case of Safaruddin vs Fazlul Haque reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151 wherein the Appellate Division held as under:</u>

<u>"The revisional power of the High Court Division is a supervisory power which may also be exercised suo moto. The natural corollary would be that the High Court Division is not obliged to hear the parties before pronouncing its verdict when the parties concerned had opportunities to appear but refrained from doing so."</u>

13. Let me now consider whether there was any foundation for the plaintiff to lay claim of title to the suit land. It transpires that she purchased 0.0633 acres of land from plot No. 2084 described in schedule-ka to the plaint, the suit land, from the mother of the defendant No. 2. The defendant No. 2 as DW 2 in her examination in cross deposed to the effect “আমরা মায়ের বিক্রীত ০.০৬-৩/১শতাংশ জমি বিক্রীত দাগের মধ্য হইতে প্রদান করিতে বাধ্য।”  So, it is admitted by the defendant No. 2 that the plaintiff purchased 0.0633 acres of land, the suit land, from plot No. 2084. In the instant case, both the courts below concurrently found that the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 were the joint owners of plot No. 2084 including the suit land. Admittedly, the opposite party No. 1 is the owner of 0.0633 acres, the suit land, in plot No. 2084 by purchase from the mother of the petitioner. Thus, the opposite party No. 1 is legally entitled to a declaration of title to the suit land. The Court of appeal being the last Court of fact came to a definite finding that the petitioner (defendant No. 2) failed to prove by evidence either orally or documentary that possession of the suit land in plot No. 2084 was delivered by measurement to the opposite party No. 1 (plaintiff). The opposite party No. 1 thus, is legally entitled to possession of the suit land from plot No. 2084 on measurement by a survey knowing Amin and by fixing boundary pillars.

14. From the grounds taken in the civil revision application, it appears that the petitioner for the first time before this Court has raised the plea that the suit for simple declaration of title without praying for consequential relief by way of partition was not maintainable.

<u>15. On a perusal of the evidence on record it appears that both the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 are the joint owners in plot No. 2084, consequently, the suit for simple declaration of title is quite maintainable without praying for consequential relief by way of partition as provided in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. The decision in the case of Shankar Chandra Das vs Kalachand Das reported in 46 DLR 419 referred to by Mr Parimal Chandra Guha may be looked into. A single Bench of this Court relying on a decision in the case of Joy Narain Sett Mil vs Srikanta reported in AIR 1922 Cal 8 held that the plaintiff and the defendant being in joint possession a simple suit for declaration of title without seeking consequential relief by way of partition is quite maintainable as provided in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. I am in respectful agreement with the said decision and hold that since both the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 are the joint owners in possession in plot No. 2084 as found concurrently by both the Courts below, wherein the opposite party No. 1 is admittedly the owner to the extent of 0.0633 acres by purchase from the mother of the petitioner she can maintain the suit for simple declaration of her title to the suit land without seeking consequential relief by way of partition pursuant to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877.</u>

16. It appears from the evidence on record that the opposite party No. 1 is in possession of some lands of road in plot No. 2038 of Satkhira Paurashava, the defendant No. 5, which is not in any way concerned with the suit land in plot No. 2084, inasmuch as opposite party No. 1 did not purchase any land from plot No. 2038.

17. The last branch of submission on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 is that the findings arrived at by the Courts below are concluded by concurrent finding of facts which should not be disturbed in revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

18. It is well recognised principle of law settled by our Appellate Division in a series of decisions that the concurrent finding of facts arrived at by the Courts below cannot be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) Code of Civil Procedure. This Court in revisional jurisdiction can interfere if it is shown that the findings are based on gross misreading or non-consideration of material evidence or it has been based on misconception or misapplication of law or misinterpretation of any material document or being otherwise it is perverse being contrary to the evidence on record.

<u>19. In view of the legal proposition settled by our Appellate Division the judgments under challenge cannot be said to have been based on misreading or non-consideration of evidence or misinterpretation of any material document. The finding of facts arrived at by the Courts below appear to have been based upon consideration of legal evidence and materials on record which do not suffer from any perversity. The Courts below did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in the impugned judgments and decrees occasioning failure of justice. Thus, the same cannot be disturbed by this Court in its revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

20. From the discussions made above I am of the considered view that there is no sub-stance in the Rule which is liable to be discharged.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged however, without any order as to costs. 22. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

The lower Courts' record be sent down at once.

End.

parties:
Abdul Aziz Matubbar  -----  Petitioner
vs
Government of Bangladesh & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties No. 1-4 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 6-3-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge now Joint District Judge, First Court, Faridpur in Review Miscellaneous Case No. 33 of 1996 affirming the judgment and decree dated 6-4-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge now Joint District Judge, First Court, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 248 of 1983 affirming the judgment and decree dated 24-8-1983 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur in Title Suit No. 183 of 1980 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff-appellant has preferred this revision application and obtained the Rule.

3. The short facts of the plaintiffs case are that he purchased the suit land from Phoenix Chemical Laboratories through its Managing Director, Mr Mohiuddin Ahamed on 10-1-1971 by a registered saf kabala. Thereafter, on 12-3-1980 a modified sale deecl was executed by said Mr Mohiuddin Ahmed in favour of the appellant-petitioner who thus got right title in respect of 4.98 acres of land, the suit land. The defendant Government alleged that the suit land was the excess land of ex-landlord Kiran Chandra Lahiri who surrendered the same to the Government and the latter gave settlement of the said land to the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and hence the plaintiff instituted the suit praying for declaration of his title to the suit land.

4. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement contending that the suit land was surrendered in favour of the Government as excess land by its original owner, Kiran Chandra Lahiri and thereafter leased out the same in favour of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3. Further, it was contended that the plaintiff had no right, title, interest and possession over the suit land and prayed for dismissal of the suit.

5. The trial Court after perusing the evidence on record and hearing both the parties dismissed Title Suit No. 183 of 1980 by judgment and decree dated 24-8-1983. The plaintiff being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree preferred Title Appeal No. 248 of 1983 in the Court of learned District Judge, Faridpur which on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge now Joint District Judge, First Court, Faridpur by judgment and decree dated 6-4-1996 dismissing the appeal and affirming those passed by the trial Court.

6. The plaintiff-appellant as petitioner being aggrieved by judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below filed Review Miscellaneous Case No. 33 of 1996 in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Faridpur under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for review of the judgment and decree dated 6-4-1996 contending that Kiran Chandra Lahiri was not the Managing Director of Phoenix Chemical Laboratories on 30-3-1973 and at that time Zamini Kanto Lahiri was the Managing Director and thereafter, Mr Mohiuddin Ahmed was the Managing Director. Signature on the document of surrender purported to be the signature of Kiran Chandra Lahiri was forged. But even after exercise of due diligence the said fact could not be pressed at the time of hearing.

7. The opposite parties did not raise any objection in the said Miscellaneous Review case.

8. The. Joint District Judge framed the point for determination as follows:

"Whether the petitioner has discovered a new important matter with the exercise of due diligence was not within his knowledge for allowing this review petition."

9. The Subordinate Judge now Joint District Judge, First Court, Faridpur hearing the petitioner by judgment and order dated 6-3-1997 disallowed the said case. Being dissatisfied with the same the petitioner preferred this revision application and obtained the instant Rule.

10. No one appeared for either of the par-ties. Nevertheless, the High Court Division can exercise its revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure either at the instance of party or suo moto. I may quote here profitably the decision in the case of Safaruddin vs Fazlid Haque reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151 where the Appellate Division held as follows:

"The revisional power of the High Court Division is a supervisory power which may also be exercised suo moto. The natural corollary would be that the High Court Division is not obliged to hear the parties before pronouncing its verdict when the parties concerned had opportunities to appear but refrained from doing so."

11. Thus even in the absence of any of the parties High Court Division under its supervisory power as contemplated in section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure can dispose of the matter on consideration of the facts and circumstance of the case. Accordingly, I have taken up this Rule for hearing and disposal though none appeared for either of the parties.

12. The petitioner filed the Miscellaneous Review case under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil. Procedure for review of the judgment and order dated 6-4-1996 passed in Title Appeal No. 248 of 1983 contending that the sale deeds Exhibit 6 and 6 ka was executed by Mr Mohiuddin Ahmed, the Managing Director of Phoenix Chemical Laboratories. The surrender document was purportedly executed under the signature of Kiron Chandra Lahiri styling himself as Managing Director of the said Laboratories was false and forged and the same being new important matter which even after exercise of due diligence was not within his knowledge.

13. Order XLVII, Rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides as follows:

"1(1) Any person considering himself aggrieved (a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred,

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes,

and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order."

14. From the plain reading of the above provision it is found that if a decree or order is to be reviewed then there must be discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of the petitioner who seeks review or could not be produced by him when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record or for any other sufficient reasons. These are the grounds on which only a decree or order may be reviewed under Order XLVII, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure.

15. In this context I may refer the case of Noor Hossain vs Bangladesh reported in 49 DLR (AD) 108 where the Appellate Division has said in the following terms:

"It is well known that a review was never meant and allowed for rehearing the matter………”

16. The Appellate Division in the case of Abul Hossain vs Bangladesh reported in 51 DLR (AD) 116 has decided as under:

"Review may be granted only for sufficient grounds akin to those of Order XLVII, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure."

17. I have perused the revision application and the judgment and order under challenge. From the materials on record, it appears that the suit land admittedly auction purchased by the defendant No.6, the Phoenix Chemical Laboratories in Certificate Case No 4056 A-BK/ 60-61 on getting sale certificate and writ of delivery of possession. The petitioner contended that Kiran Chandra Lahiri was not the Managing Director on the date of alleged execution of the document of surrender and his purported signature therein was forged.

<u>18. Respective parties in the suit adduced both oral and documentary evidence which were marked exhibits. The petitioner was required to prove his case by evidence that Kiran Chandra Laheri was not the Managing Director of the Company on the date of surrender. But he failed to discharge his legal obligation to prove that be could not produce the said evidence before the Courts below after exercise of reasonable care and due diligence which was not within his knowledge. Reading the grounds for review taken in the petition of Review Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 1996 it appears that the petitioner sought opportunity for rehearing of the matter sitting over its own judgment passed by the appellate Court which is not permissible in law as provided in Order XLVII, rule I of the Code as well as the decisions referred to hereinabove.</u>

<u>19. The Joint District Judge has correctly observed that in a review petition the Court cannot sit as appellate Court to consider its own judgment. He further observed that inadvertence of the learned Counsel was not a cogent ground for review. It appears from the impugned order that no resolution book was even produced in support of the ground taken for review of the judgment and decree of the court of appeal below.</u>

20. In view of the discussions made above I do not find that the Joint District Judge committed any error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order dated 6-3-1997 disallowing the Review Miscellaneous Case No. 33 of 1996 and hence does not warrant any interference by this Court in revision.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the Lower Courts Records at once.

End.

parties:

Vs.

full_judgment:
K. M. Subhan, J.:- This appeal by special leave arises out of a Judgment of the High Court Division dated April 25, 1975 passed in Civil Revision No. 1126 of 1974, setting aside the order of the District Judge, Noakhali in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 120 of 1974 affirming the order of the Subordinate Judge, Noakhali, refusing to recall appointment of receiver in Other Class Suit No. 137 of 1974.

2. Short facts necessary for the disposal of this appeal may be stated as follows:-

The appellant, who is the plaintiff, instituted the suit for declaration of his title simplicities. Before institution of the suit as the first party he had filed an application before the Sub-divisional Magistrate, Sadar Noakhali, who drew up a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and attached the proceeding land and appointed Circle Officer, Sahara as receiver of the said land. The Magistrate, having failed to decide the question of possession between the parties, by an order dated May 31, 1969 directed them to have their rights determined by a competent civil court with further direction that the order of attachment was to continue and the receiver was to submit accounts regularly. The appellant filed an application before the Subordinate Judge for appointment of a receiver which was allowed and receiver was appointed, who took over charge and also possession of the suit property from the receiver appointed by the Criminal Court. The respondent filed an application before the trial court for recalling the writ appointing the receiver. The trial Judge rejected the application by his order dated August 12, 1974. The appeal to the District Judge preferred by Respondent No. 1 against the said order was dismissed. A rule was obtained from the High Court Division on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

3. A Division Bench of the High Court set aside the order of appointment of a receiver of the lands under attachment by the Magistrate holding that a receiver could not be appointed by a Civil Court in a suit for declaration of title simplicities of immovable property. The reason for so holding is not because of the problem which, according to the learned Judges arises on the conclusion of the suit in making over possession of the disputed property because the suit was framed in accordance with section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, nor was there a prayer for such relief as required under section 42.

4. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was correct in taking the view that receiver cannot be appointed in a suit filed in consequence of an order passed under section 146 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for a declaration simplicities to the immovable property at ached by the Criminal Court and receiver appointed in the absence of a prayer for making over possession as required under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the question of, delivery of possession of the suit land would arise.

5. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant relying on the proviso of sub-section (2) of section 146 has contended that the Civil Court can make an appointment of a receiver although the Criminal Court has already appointed a receiver while attaching the disputed land. He has further contended that the successful party in the suit will get the possession of the property in consequence of the judgment of the Civil Court from the receiver; the receiver being an agent of the court no execution proceeding for delivery of possession is necessary.

6. As none appeared for the respondent and as the matter involved important question of law, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed was requested to appear as amicus curiae for assisting the Court.

7. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed the learned Counsel has submitted that the consequence of appointment of a receiver by the Criminal Court is that the property becomes custodial legs and as such the plaintiff's prayer for declaration of his title is sufficient and relief by way delivery of possession cannot be sought for because the possession is with the court. He has further contended that in a suit relief is sought for against the defendant himself. A declaration simplicities is sought in a suit where the subject matter is already custodial legis. Relief by way of delivery of possession could not be sought for because the possession of the property is already with the agent appointed by the court.

<u>8. Mr. Ahmed, learned Counsel, has relied for this proposition on the decision, in the case of Nawab Humayun Begum v. Nawab Shah Mohammad Khan (1). In this case the plaintiff instituted a suit against her husband, his son, defendant 2, and two banks in India with whom money had been deposited on fixed deposit receipt and the claim was brought by the lady for a declaration that certain sums of money which were held by the banks on deposit receipt were her property and not her husband's. The Judicial Committee held that the lady was entitled to a declaration against the husband and there was no "other relief" she could properly claim against him, once the banks on their own prayer had been treated as out of the case. There was no other relief which could be claimed against the husband. The money was in the banks and at the disposal of the plaintiff and it would have been impossible to make any other claim against the husband except for a declaration that the money in the banks was money which the plaintiff was entitled to be paid out to her. The Judicial Committee further held that "other relief" in the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, must be "other relief" against the defendant himself against whom the declaration is sought. In this case the banks appeared and submitted to the court that they would pay the money to any one whom the court decides to be entitled to it and thus they ceased to be defendants in the suit.</u>

9. A suit for declaration simplicities is maintainable when no further relief is necessary to be prayed for. The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act requires the plaintiff filing a declaratory suit to seek further relief which is possible in the facts of the case. It is well settled that a person in possession of the land need merely to file a declaratory suit for his title. In a suit reliefs are sought for against the parties to the suit against whom the court can allow such relief. When a property is already under attachment in pursuance of an order passed under sub-section (1) of section 146 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the property on such attachment passes in the possession of the court and to seek for ‘other relief’ as contained in the proviso to section 42, would render it necessary merely to seek the relief against the court itself which is not permissible as the court adjudicating a matter is not a party to the proceeding.

<u>10. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, has also relied upon the decision of Sunder Singh v. Managing Committee, Sunder Singh. (1) In the case, Managing Committee filed the suit through a member claiming a declaration to the effect that the plaintiff Committee is the Managing body, trustee and administrators of the High School and that the defendants have no connection whatsoever with the school or its property, nor have they any right as trustee in the said school and that the committee alone is entitled to the income and authorized to spend it. A perpetual injunction against interference by the defendants was also prayed for. The Judicial Committee held that the plaintiff who is the trustee and administrator of certain institution of which neither he nor defendant is in possession or control of the management could maintain the suit for mere declaration under section 42. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has also relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Deo Kuer v. Sheo Prasad (2). In this decision the Supreme Court placed reliance on bath the decisions of the Privy Council referred to earlier. The Patna High Court wherefrom the appeal went to the Indian Supreme Court decided the matter exactly in the same way as has been done by the Dacca High Court. The Patna High Court held that a suit for declaration of title pending an attachment under section 146 is incompetent under the proviso to section 42, unless recovery of possession is also asked for. The Indian Supreme Court in this case held that further relief contemplated by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is relief against the defendant only. Where the defendant who is not in possession is not in a position to deliver possession to the plaintiff and the plaintiff in such a suit-for a declaration of title to property, need not claim possession. In the case of an attachment under section 146 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as it stood before its amendment in 1955, a suit for a bare declaration of title without a prayer for delivery of possession is competent. The position in the case of an attachment under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is the same. In a suit filed for declaration of title to property when it stands attached under section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code, it is unnecessary to ask for the further relief of delivery of possession. It is unnecessary to ask for possession when the property is in custodial legis. Property under attachment under section 145 of the Code is in custodial legis. The fact that the decree may not be binding on the Magistrate does not affect the competence of the suit.</u>

<u>11. This view has been taken by the Indian Supreme Court in the back ground of a similar decision taken by the Patna High Court. We are in respectful agreement with the decision of the Indian Supreme Court.</u>

12. Before we part with this case we would like to put on record our appreciation of the exhaustive argument of the learned Counsel, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed.

13. The appeal, therefore, is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

Faqueer Shahabuddin Ahmed with Mozammel Huq Bhuiyan, Rabia Bhuiyan and Shah Abu Nayeem, Advocates ----- for the petitioner
