parties:
Messrs R. Ahmed & sons
Vs.
Messrs Eastern Technique & Others
full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen, J:- This Rule, at the instance of the plaintiff, is directed against the order dated 16.6.80 of the learned Subordinate judge, refusing the plaintiff’s prayer for attachment before judgment under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Plaintiff filed Money Suit No. 23 of 1980 for recovery of certain sum of money and made the following prayer:

"for a decree against the defendant No. 1 for realisation of money amounting to Tk. 3,27,02,361/61 (Taka three chore twenty seven lac two thousand and three hundred sixty one and paisa sixty one) only payable by the defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff and also interest @ 12% on the said amount till realisation of the decretal amount"

The suit was filed on 19.5.80 On the same day an application for attachment before judgment under Order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed on behalf of the plaintiff in the said petition the plaintiff stated as follows:-

"1. That the plaintiff petitioner has instituted the above-mentioned money suit for realisation of unpaid price against the defendant No. 1, to the tune of Tk. 3,27,02,361/61.

2. That the plaintiff-petitioner has a very fair chance of success and obtaining decree for the said amount of Tk. 3,27,02,361/61 against the defendant No. 3, from this learned Court.

3. That on receipt of the summons of the above mentioned suit, there is every possibility that the defendant No. 1, shall dispose of all his movable and immovable properties with intent to obstruct and delay the execution of the decree in the above-mentioned suit, if and when, be passed against the defendant No. 1, and hence the properties belonging to the defendant No. 1 and disburse or withdraw the money from the Barter Account maintained in the defendant No. 2 Bank before the finalization of the suit and remove the same from the local limits of the jurisdiction of this learned Court, situated with-in the jurisdiction of this learned Court are required to be placed under attachment before judgment.

4. That the defendant No. 1 has the following properties in the sole name of the proprietor or in the firm name situated within the territorial jurisdiction of this learned Court which are required to be placed under attachment before judgment.

i) Motor Car No. Dacca Gha-75

ii) Current Account No. 10286, with Sonali-Bank, Local Office, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dacca in the name of defendant No. 1.

iii) Tk. 3,27,02,361/61 in China Barter Account lying with Sonali Bank, Local Officer, Foreign Exchange Department, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dacca, the defendant No. 2 out of the amount allocated in favour of the defendant No. 1, in the form of L/Cs. Nos. 79/297047 and 79/207057 and other L/Cs. in the name of the defendant No. 1 or its transferees including Export Performances Licences so that the decree when passed in the above suit may be satisfied. 5. That unless the properties of the defendant No. 1 as have been detailed in para 4 above are attached before judgment the decree obtained in the suit by the plaintiff shall be frustrated and on execution of the decree in the above mentioned suit nothing would be available for the plaintiff to satisfy the decree that may be obtained by the plaintiff. Wherefore, it is most humbly prayed that your honour would be pleased to direct the defendant to furnish security for the properties described in paragraph 4 or to direct the defendant No. 1 to appear at the Court and show cause why he should not furnish security to the extent of the claimed amount of Tk. 2, 27, 02,361/61 and in the meantime pass an order of conditional attachment of the said properties for the ends of justice."

3. On this application the learned Subordinate Judge passed the order No. 2 dated 19.5.80 in the following terms:

“Piffles petition u/s 38 rule 5 C.P.C. supported by an affidavit and prays to direct the defdts No. 1 & 2 to furnish security for the properties described in paragraph 4 or to direct the defdts No. 1 & 2 to appear at the court and show cause why they should not furnish security to the extent of the claimed amount of Tk. 3, 27, 02,277/22 and in the meantime pass an order of conditional attachment of the said properties on the grounds stated therein. Put up tomorrow for order."

4. The matter came up for orders on 20.5.80 and the learned Subordinate Judge passed the following order:

"Plffs. petition and affidavit dt. 19.5.80 are put up today. Heard the Id. Adv. perused the petition, affidavit and documents. Issue notice upon the defdts to show cause within 7 days from the service thereof as to why they shall not be asked to furnish security to the extent of the claimed amount.

In the meantime the property mentioned in sub-parts (ii) and (iii) of para 4 in the petition be provisionally attached subject to furnishing security Urgent requisites at once." Defendant No. 1, in obedience to the aforesaid notice, appeared and filed objection against the plaintiff's prayer for attachment before judgment, denying the material allegations of the plaintiff. Defendant No: 1 contended that the properties in the concerned letters of credit belonged to the principal, viz, the Chaina buyer. It was further stated that the application for attachment before judgment was not maintainable inasmuch as vague and indefinite allegations have been made in the application. An affidavit-in-opposition was filed by the plaintiff against the affidavit filed on behalf of defendant No. 1. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the facts and materials on record available before him rejected the application for attachment before judgment and vacated the ad-interim order of attachment granted by him on 20.5.80 the learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the petition for a attachment before judgment suffered from insufficient materials. He observed as follows:

"From these words it cannot be said that the defendant No. 1 is about to dispose of his property or remove it from the jurisdiction of the court with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of the decree that may be passed against him in this suit when the defdt No. 1 was absolutely in dark about filing of this suit. In order to attach the property before judgment u/s 38 rule 5 C.P.C. there must be some material facts and specific allegations against the defdt No. 1 that he is going to dispose of whole or any part of his properties to frustrate the execution of decree that may be passed which are very much absent here in this petition. The allegations which the plaintiff has made in para 3 of the petition are vague and general allegations and as such it cannot be considered for exercising the powers conferred in Order 38, rule 5 C.P.C. and in this connection the decision reported in 27 D.L.R. page 256 and 31 D.L.R. page 112 (A.D) may be referred."

The learned Subordinate Judge further observed:-

"The rule does not provide any scope to attach item No. 3 of the petition as the defdt No. 1 is not the absolute owner of this property. I do agree with the content ion of the .learned Advocate for the defdt No. 1. In view of the facts discussed above I am of the opinion that the plaintiff has failed to make out a case for getting an order of attachment before judgment."

4. This Rule was obtained by the plaintiff on 23 June, 1980. The Rule was made returnable.

<u>5. Mr. Faqir Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the rule has taken us through the relevant papers filed as annexures to this petition. He has emphatically argued that item No. 3 is described in the petition for attachment before judgment is a property belonging to defendant No. 1 and as such attachable under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. S.R. Pal, the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No. 1, contends that the letters of credit in question are not properties, but they merely represent a promise. In the background of these contentions, we have been taken through some authorities and decisions to which we shall presently refer. Mr. Pal. has drawn our attention to Chapter 20 at page 631 of Paget's Law of Banking, 8th Edition, in support of his proposition that a letter of credit is a mere promise. He has, however, contended that the ingredients of revocable and irrevocable or confirmed letter of credit are different. Mr. S. Pal has referred to the case of Pala and Co. S. P. A. v. Thurmann Neilson. (1) He has specifically relied upon the following passage occurring in the judgment of Lord Justice Denning, as his Lordship then was:-</u>

<u>"The sale of goods across usually arranged by means diets The buyer requests a credit in favour of the world is of confirmed his banker to seller and in now reopen pursuance of that request the banker, or his foreign agent, issue a confirmed credit in favour of the seller. This credit is a promise by the banker to pay money to the seller in return for the shipping documents. Then the seller, when he presents the documents, gets paid the contract price. The conditions of the credit must be strictly fulfilled otherwise the seller would not be entitled to draw on it."</u>

<u>This proposition initially provided for the basis and sanctity of 4 letter of credit in the international commercial world. With the advancement of international trade and commerce, the concept of promise appears to have assumed an improved character as we gather from Uniform Commercial Code, 1972 Official. Text with comments and appendix and the Uniform customs and practice for documentary credits. We refreshed our ideas as to how commercial letters of credits are dealt with in international trade and commerce from the treatise of A. G. Davis, "The law relating to Commercial Letters of Credit." We have also considered the relevant provisions of Negotiable Instruments Act in this connection. On consideration of these authorities it appears that the state of promise is indeed the starting point of international commercial transactions. Initially the property in a letter of credit belongs to the buyer who places his money in a bank of his country. It then becomes the property of the bank according to the terms of contract between the buyer and his bank. In the seller's country, the buyer's bank Issues a request with the promise in terms of the conditions contained in the contract between the parties. On the fulfillment of the terms as contained in the contract, the seller's bank performs its part in the international transactions. Benficiary under the letter of credit holds the property under certain terms So also the Bank in the seller's country. In this view of the matter, Mr. Asrarul Hossain the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No. 2 Sonali Bank has rightly contended that ownership of the property in the letters of credit rests with the persons variously under changing circumstances. The contention appears to be of substance. The authorities referred to above lend support in favour of the contention. In the facts of the instant case it appears that the ownership in the property of the letters of credit is disputed. Mr. Pal contends that it is not the property of defendant No. 1 whereas Mr. Faqir Shahabuddin Ahmed contends that it is the property of defendant No. 1. The bank appears to have taken a neutral position con-tending that it depends on the decision of the Court to whom the ownership of the property in the letters of credit belongs. The Subordinate Judge has found that "defendant No. 1 is not the absolute owner of this property." In such circumstances contention of Mr. Faqir Shahabuddin Ahmed that the properties in the letters of credit belongs to defendant No. 1 does not stand on a sound footing. In the exercise of revisional jurisdiction we are not called upon to determine a question of fact as to whether or not the property in the relevant letters of credit belongs either to the plaintiffs or defendant No.1 or the bank. Evidently the letters of credit other than No. 79/207047 and No. 79/207057 have no nexus in the dispute between the parties. Those other letters of credits are not liable to be attached in any view of the matter. It is not for us to say anything with regard to the performance of the parties. We have been addressed by the learned Advocates that there were defaults on the part of the plaintiff and that there were ladles and non-compliance of the part of defendant No. 1. We do not intend to express our opinion in this behalf. In the exercise of revisional jurisdiction we are not called upon to express our opinion as to the beneficiary's rights under the two letters of credit mentioned earlier. The contention of Mr. Pal that a letter of credit is a mere promise does not appear to stand on a sound footing. In our opinion it is a property. We have already indicated that ownership in the property of the relevant letters of credit is in dispute. Now, the question arises whether such a disputed property is attachable. It has been argued on behalf of the plaintiff that section 60 is no bar to attachment of the property in the letter of credit in question. Section 60 may not be bar, but unless a prima facie ownership of the property is determined, the same is not liable to be attached by an order of the Court. The plaintiff in this behalf appears to have signally failed to make out a prima facie case. We have already quoted the petition for attachment before judgment. Paragraph 3 of the petition appears to be significantly vague. In that paragraph only an apprehension has been expressed without indicating the corresponding objectivity behind the apprehension. The learned Subordinate Judge, in our opinion, correctly construed the application for attachment before judgment and rightly refused the prayer for attachment before judgment. In this behalf, we may also refer to the case of Md. Shamsul Huda v. Mozammel Huq W. In this decision we may profitably quote the following observations of their Lordships:—</u>

<u>"The power which has been conferred on the Court under the said provision is an extraordinary power whereby a party in the suit may be prevented from use and enjoyment of its own properties, before any decree has at all been passed against him, and when there is no certainty that a decree will at all be passed against him. This power must, therefore, be used with utmost caution and should be sparingly exercised. It is clear that before issuing an order under the said provisions of the Code, the Court must be satisfied that the defendant has been trying to frustrate the effect of the decree that may be passed against him by disposing of his property or re-moving it from the jurisdiction of the court. That is to say, the Court must be satisfied not only that the defendant is about to dispose of his property or remove it from its jurisdiction but also that this disposal or removal is with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of any decree that may be passed against him. This satisfaction, however, is to be judicial satisfaction and it must be based on some materials which are to be found in the affidavit filed by the party or otherwise. It is true that an order of attachment under this provision is to be found in the affidavit filed by the party or otherwise. It is true that an order of attachment under this provision is to be passed on the basis of an application made by the plaintiff and an order of conditional attachment may be passed even experte. It is, of course, to be borne in mind that it is difficult to produce any conclusive evidence before the Court to prove the intention of a party which is secretly conceived and sought to be suppeptiously executed, but even then, there must be some concrete allegations before the Court about the actions of the defendant and some materials in support thereof. Otherwise, this provision of law is likely to be turned into an instrument of oppression and great harassment."</u>

<u>In the case of Unimarine S.A. Panama through Local Agent Bengal Shipping Line Limited v. Bangladesh (1) it has been clearly laid down that "vague or general allegations without any material are insufficient to invoke the power or the Court under this provision." The following observations of Lordships of the Appellate Division may be referred to:-</u>

<u>"The only question which arises in this appeal is whether the lighter age was attachable under order 38, rule 5 of the Code. Attachment under the rule could be made if there was an attempt on the part of the defendant to remove the vessel from the jurisdiction of the Court with an intent to obstruct or delay the execution of the decree."</u>

<u>6. We have already referred to the decision in Shamsut Huda's case. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division approvingly referred to the said case and expressed themselves in the following terms:-</u>

<u>"The power is not doubt this extraordinary power exercised and with utmost very extensive but must be sparingly caution, otherwise it may become an instrument of oppression. The Court is to insist upon the proof of the allegation in the petition for attachment before judgment by affidavit or other mode of proof and the opposite party must he served with notice and given an opportunity to show cause. The Court is to be satisfied that the defendant is about to dispose of whole or part of his property or he is about to remove whole or part of his property from the Court's  jurisdiction, and his object is to obstruct or delay the execution or any decree that might be passed against him. The party imputing the motive on the defendant must be ready with the evidence to satisfy the Court, if called upon to do so. Vague or general allegations without any material are insufficient to invoke the power of the court under this provision."</u>

<u>The learned Subordinate Judge appear to have correctly relied upon two decisions referred to in the judgment.</u>

<u>7. A question has been raised by Mr. Pal that the instant Rule under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure was incompetent, since the impugned order was passed under Order 38 rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and as such it was appealable. On consideration of the provisions of the said rule we hold that the impugned order was not passed under the said provisions, but it was made under rule 5 Order 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as follows :-</u>

<u>"(1) Where at any stage of a suit, the Court is satisfied, by an affidavit or otherwise, that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree that may passed against him;</u>

<u>(a) is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property, or</u>

<u>(b) is about to remove the whole or any part of his property from the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, the Court may direct the defendant, with in a time to fixed by it, either to furnish security, in such sum as may be specified in the order, to produce and place at the disposal of the Court, when required, the said property or the value of that same, or such portion thereof as may be sufficient to satisfy the decree, or to appear and show cause why he should not furnish security.</u>

<u>(2) The plaintiff shall, unless the Court other-wise directs, specify the property required to be attached and the estimated value thereof,</u>

<u>(3) The Court may also in the order direct the conditional attachment of the whole or any portion of the property so specified."</u>

<u>The application under Order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge and as such it was not an order appealable under Order 43, rule 1(q) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In our view the revision is competent.</u>

8. It has then been argued on behalf of the defendant No. 1 that a revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure direct to this Court is incompetent. According to the learned Advocate the jurisdiction of the High Court and that of the learned District Judge is concurrent. The learned District Judge being the lower tier in the hierarchy of the Courts it should be approached first. The contention appears to be misconceived. However, let us examine the question. Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure prior to the Law Reforms Ordinance stood as follows:-

"The High Court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears:

(a) to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or

(b) to have failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested, or

(c) to have acted in the exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity, the High Court may make such order in the case as it thinks fit." With the Law Reforms Ordinance coming into force section 115 C.P.0 has been substituted by the following provisions:-

"Revision 115(1) The High Court Division may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinated to the High Court Division and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears to have committed any error of law apparent on the face of the record in the decision, the High Court Division may make such order in the case as it thinks fit.

(2) The District Judge may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to the District Court and in which no subordinate any error record in appeal lies thereto, and if such Court appears to have committed of law apparent on the face of the decision, the District Judge may make such order in the case as he thinks fit.

(3) An application to the High Court Division for revision of an order of the District Judge made under sub-section (2) shall lie where the High Court Division grants leave for revision on an error of an important question of law occasioning failure of justice, and the High Court Division may make such order in the case as it thinks fit."

9. Mr. Pal addressed us as to the scope of section 115(1) and (2). In his view, the jurisdiction is concurrent and the liberty to choose the forum rests with the litigant. Mr. Faqir Shahabuddin, however, contends that the provision in section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is not related to the provisions contained in section 115(2). According to Mr. Ahmed these are two distinct provisions and these provisions are to be read along with other provisions of the Act, and the East Bengal Civil Court Act. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has similarly contended that section 115 of the Code Civil Procedure, as it stands, is to he read in the light of section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 3,6, to 8, 18, 19, 20 and 21 of the Civil Courts Act. Section 6 of the Civil Procedure Code runs as follows:—

"Save in so far as is otherwise expressly provided, nothing herein contained shall operate to give any Court jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject-matter of which exceeds the pecuniary limits ( if any ) of its ordinary jurisdiction."

10. On a scrutiny of these provisions we are inclined to hold that the jurisdiction of this Court cannot be conceived to be concurrent with the Court of the learned District Judge. It may be pointed out that in section 3 of the Bengal Civil Court Act four classes of Courts have been contemplated and they are as follows:—

"(1) The Court of the District Judge,

(2) The Court of the Additional District Judge,

(3) The Court of Subordinate Judge, and,

(4) The Court of the Munsif".

These are the gradations in the hierarchy of the Courts. Chapter III of the said Act contains elaborate provisions relating to the ordinary jurisdiction of the Courts enumerated in section 3 of the said Act. Extent of the original jurisdiction of the District Judge or Subordinate Judge has been stated in section 18. Section 19 speaks of the extent of jurisdiction of the Munsif. Section 20 speaks of appeal from the District and Additional Judges. Section 21 eloquently speaks of appeals from the Subordinate Judges and Munsifs. For our purpose we may confine our considerations to the language used in section 20 and 21 respectively. Section 20 runs as follows:—

"(1) Save as otherwise provided by any enactment for the time being in force, an appeal from a decree or order of a District Judge or Additional Judge shall lie to the High Court.

(2) An appeal shall not lie to the High Court from a decree or order of an Additional Judge in which, if the decree or order had been made by the District Judge, an appeal would not lie to that Court."

Section 21 runs as follows:—

"(1) Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a Subordinate Judge shall lie

(a) to the District Judge where the value of the original suit in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed twenty thousand Rupees and

(b) to the High court in any other case.

(2) Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a Munsif shall lie to the District Judge.

(3) Where the function of receiving any appeals which lie to the District Judge under sub-section (1)' or sub-section (2) has been assigned to an Additional Judge, the appeals may be preferred to the Additional Judge.

(4) The High Court may, with the previous sanction of the Government, direct, by notification in the official Gazette, that appeals lying to the. District Judge under sub-section (2) from all or any of the decree or orders of any Munsif shall be preferred to the Court of such Subordinate Judge as may be mentioned in the notification, and the appeals shall there-upon be preferred accordingly."

<u>11. All orders are not appealable. Only these orders as are appealable as enumerated in Order 43, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for appeal against original decree. Can it be conceived that a court which cannot exercise jurisdiction over a matter in appeal was intended to exercise its revisional jurisdiction? It appears to be inconsistent with the scheme of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Civil Courts Act to invest the District Judge with concurrent jurisdiction in matters where no appeal lies before the District Judge. In appealable decrees there is clear provisions without any ambiguity that it is the District Judge where value does not exceed Tk. 20,000/-, in all other cases it is the High Court Division. As provided in section 104, read with Order 43, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies before the District Judge as well as before High Court Division subject to the pecuniary jurisdiction of the District Judge. In such circumstances the contention of concurrent jurisdiction appears to be inconsistent with the scheme of the Act. The District Judge exercises revisional jurisdiction under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of those cases, where the value of the subject-matters does not exceed Tk. 20,000/-. In all other cases it is the High Court Division which exercises jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure cadre for a Court Section 115(3) of the Code of Civil Pro-stands on a different footing and provides second revisional forum before the High Division with the leave of the said Division on the grounds of failure of justice or an error of law. It need not be said afresh that right of appeal is a creature of statute. Where no appeal is provided for, revision is available to an aggrieved person before the Court empowered to exercise such jurisdiction. An aggrieved person cannot, as of right, claim a revision before the High Court Division or the District Judge. The element of discretion should not overlooked. The High Court Division, in our opinion, may, under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, exercise its revisional jurisdiction in any case, and its jurisdiction is not controlled by sub-Section (2) of Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. For the reasons stated above we hold that the instant revision is competent.</u>

12. It has been argued by the learned Advocates appearing on all the sides that a sort of anarchy prevails in the District Court as regards the Court-fee payable on application for revision under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. We have been told that in certain cases court-fee is realised on an application under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the rate of Tk. 7/50 or Tk. 15/- according to the value of the subject-matter, and in certain other cases an application is entertained on a court-fee of Tk. 1/- We are not aware of any provision in the Court-fees Act prescribing special Court fee for a revision under section 115(2) before the learned District Judge. So far as the revisions before the High Court Division are concerned the law appears to be clear and the fee is covered by Article 13A of Schedule 1 and Article 13A of Schedule 1 of the Court-fees Act runs as follows:—

"13A-Application to a High Court for the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Where the application is for revision of an order and the amount of value of the subject-matter is of less than two thousand rupees Seven rupees and fifty paisa.

Where the applications Fifteen for the revision of an rupees order and the amount or value of the subject-matter is two thousand rupees or more.

Where the application is for the revision of an appellate decree

The fee loveable on a memorandum of appeal

Article 13A of the Court-fees Act does not authorise the District Judge to charge Court-fees at the rates mentioned therein for a revision under Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In our opinion, the application for a revision before the learned District Judge should contain a Court fee of Tk. 1/- only in terms of Article 1 of Schedule of the Court fees Act. The relevant provision stands in the following terms:—

"Scheduled II

Fixed fees.

1. Application or petition (a) When presented to any

(b) or when presented to a Civil, Criminal or Revenue Court, or to a Collector, or any Re-venue officer having jurisdiction equal or Subordinate to a Collector, or to any Magi’s Taka one trade in his executive capacity, and not otherwise provided for by this Act."

By specific provisions in Article 13A of Schedule 1 read with Article 1 of Schedule II (d) (i) (a) and (b), Court fee is charged at the rate of Tk. 7/50 or Tk. 15/- as the case may be in the case of an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed before the High Court Division. It cannot be contended that the High Court's power of revision has been delegated to the District Judge. This appears to be a new provision as contained in section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Legislature did not make appropriate provision in the Court-fees Act in that behalf. This indicates that it was not intended by the legislature to impose any special fee on an application for revision before the District Judge under Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thus we conclude that the appropriate Court-fee for an application under Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure to the District Judge is Tk. 1/- as prescribed by Article of Schedule II of the Court-fees Act and this is not controlled by Article 13A of the Schedule 1 of the Court-fees Act.

13. On a consideration of the questions raised in this Rule we are of the view that the plaintiff has failed to make out a case for attachment before judgment under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The allegations made in the paragraph 3 of the petition are vague, general, without materials in proof and insufficient to warrant the jurisdiction of the Court under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

14. We would like to direct the learned Subordinate Judge dispose of this suit as expeditiously as possible after providing lawful opportunities to the contending parties. Send down the records at once.

15. Mr. Mozammel Huq Bhuiya the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that he has instruction to pray for special leave to appeal before the Appellate Division. In that view of the matter he prays for stay of the Operation of this order.

16. The prayer is allowed so far as Laces Nos. 79/207047 and 79/207057 are concerned. Let the operation of this order be stayed till 22nd August, 1980 in respect of the aforesaid two letters of credit only.

17. On a perusal of the application for addition of parties we are not inclined to allow the prayer at this stage. The plaintiff, if necessary, may file an appropriate application before the trial Court for addition of the proposed parties. The application is accordingly rejected.

End.

parties:
Liakat Rice and Oil Mills & Another
Vs.
Janata Bank
full_judgment:
Syed Mohammad Ali, J:—This Rule obtained by the defendant-petitioners is directed against the order dated 2-8-78 passed by Mr. M.I. Khan. Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Mortgage Suit No. 63 of 1974 amending the preliminary decree passed on 19-4-78 under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

2. The facts of the case are that Defendant No. 2 (proprietor of Defendant No. 1 firm) and Defendant No. 1 (a firm) took a loan of Tk. 1,00,000/- as overdraft from his account No. 508 from the plaintiff Janata Bank on 24-12-63 on mortgage of properties promising to repay the loan with interest at the rate of 9% per-annum. Subsequently having failed to repay the loan the defendants by mutual arrangement with the plaintiff Bank executed a fresh promote for Tk. 1,43,000/- on 14-11-66 on renewal of equitable mortgage promising to repay the loan with 11% annual interest. When the defend-ants failed to repay on demands, the plaintiff opposite party filed Mortgage Suit No. 630 of 1974 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for realisation of an amount of Tk. 1,99,418.87 which had become due to the plaintiff Bank with interest on the date of filing the Suit. The defendants filed joint written statement stating inter alia that the suit is not maintainable, barred by limitation and interest claimed by the plaintiff is penal and unconscionable. The suit was previously decreed exparte on 13-5-75 with interest by the said court. Subsequently the defendant-petitioners moved the trial court under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the exparte decree; and the said exparte decree was set aside in Misc. Case No. 52 of 1975.

3. Thereafter the suit was again decreed exparte in preliminary form for Tk. 1,99,418.87 with costs by order No. 77 dated 19-4-78 by Mr. M.I. Khan, Subordinate Judge, 2nd. Court, Chittagong and the ordering portion runs thus:

"That the suit be decreed exparte with cost for. Tk. 1,99,418.87 in the preliminary form. The defendants are directed to pay Tk. 1,99,418.87 (one lakh ninety nine thousand four hundred and eighteen and paisa eighty seven) to the plaintiff within two months of this decree failing which plaintiff may realise the decretal amount by sale of the mortgaged properties".

4. Thereupon the defendant-petitioners moved an application under Order 9 Rule 13 for setting aside the exparte decree dated 19.4-78 but ultimately the said Misc. Case No. 320 of 1978 under Order 9, Rule 13 was dismissed On 24-6-78 for non-prosecution. The plaintiff on 1-8-78 filed a petition under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction of the judgment and decree passed on 19-4-78 in the Suit on the ground stated in the petition and copy of the petition was served upon the defend-ant petitioners. The defendant also filed hazira on 2-8-78 when the application under section 152 C.P.C. came up for hearing.

5. By order No. 83 dated 2-8-78 Mr. .M.I. Khan, the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd. Court, Chittagong after hearing the parties and perusing the plaint, judgment and decree, dated 19-4-78 allowed the amendment of the judgment and decree holding that there has been an accidental slip and omission in the ordering portion of the judgment dated 19-4-78 and directed the correction of the decree in the following terms:-

"That the suit be decreed exparte with cost for Tk. 1,99,418.87 (one lakh ninety nine thousand four hundred and eighteen and eighty seven paisa) in the preliminary form and for pendentilite interest at the rate of Tk. 11 % per annum on the decretal amount till realisation of the full decretal dues. The defendants are directed to pay the decretal amount with costs and pendentility interests at the rate or 11 % per annum on the decretal amount till realisation of the decretal clues within two months of this decree, failing which plaintiff may realise the same by sale of the mortgaged properties. If the decretal dues be not satisfied by sale of the mortgaged properties, then the suit be decreed personally against defendant No.2 for realisation of balance decretal dues. Let the judgment dated 19-4-78 and decree thereon be corrected accordingly under 'section 152 of the C.P.C."

6. Being aggrieved by the said order No. 85 dated 2-8-78 the defendant petitioners moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioner  submits  that from the decree passed in pursuance of Order No. 77 dated 19-4-78 it clearly shows that the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in preliminary form for Tk. 1,99,418.87 with costs only making it payable within two months of this decree failing which decretal amount was to be realised by sale of the mortgaged properties and there was no mention of granting any further relief by way of awarding interest or any personal decree in case the decretal amount could not be satisfied by the sale proceeds of the mortgaged properties and after the decree is passed the court became functus officio in the matter of materially amending the decree under section 152 of the C.P.C. He has also referred to section 152 C.P.C. which runs as follows:-

"Clerical or arithmetical mistakes in judgments, decrees or orders or errors arising therein from any accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected by the court either of its own: motion or on the application of any 'of the parties."

8. Relying upon this section he submits that the amendments made are neither clerical nor arithmetical mistakes and as such the exercise of the power by the court under section 152 C.P.C. by amending the judgment and decree is illegal as it does not come under the purview of section 152 C.P.C. Further Mr. Roy Chowdhury referred to sub-section 2 of section 34 C.P.C. which runs thus:-

"Where such a decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest on such aggregate sum as aforesaid from the date of the decree to the date of the payment or other earlier date the court shall be deemed to have refused such interest, and a separate suit therefore shall not lie."

9. Relying upon this provision of law Mr. Roy Chowdhury argues that since the relief by way of granting further interest on the aggregate sum has not been specifically given in the judgment and decree, it will be deemed to have been refused by the court. In this connection he has referred to the case of Thirugnanavalli Ammul V. P. Venugopala Pillai and others reported in A.I.R. 1940 (Madras) at page 29 wherein a Division Bench of the Madras High Court also held:

"Where a decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest from the date of the decree to the date of payment and the decree follows the judgment, the court must be deemed to have refused it."

10. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff' opposite party argues that the earlier decree dated 13-5-75 shows that the suit was decreed with interest and in the plaint and also in the deposition there is a prayer for interest. He submits that taking these facts into consideration it can be said that it is a clerical mistake that the court did not mention about the prayer granting interest in the judgment and subsequently in the decree is an accidental slip or omission in the ordering portion of the judgment and the learned Subordinate Judge, was of the same opinion when he allowed the application under section 152 of the C.P.C.

11. We have perused the petition, the decree dated 19-4-78 and the order No. 85 dated 2-8-78 where the application under section 152 C.P.C. was allowed by the trial court. It seems to us that after the decree was signed, the court became functus officio in respect of further amending the judgment and decree and that the said court had no other power except the power granted to it under section 152 C.P.C. 'In this case the grounds stated in the petition and the ground for allowing the petition stated by the learned Subordinate Judge in amending the decree is not covered by the provision under section 152 C.P.C., rather it violates the provision of Sub-section 2 of section 34 of the C.P.C.

12. Thus, we find substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners and hold that the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally in exercise of his jurisdiction by passing the order No. 85 dated 2-8-78. Accordingly the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order No. 85 dated 2-8-78 is set aside and the judgment and decree passed on 19-4-78 before the said amendment passed in Mortgage Suit No. 63 of 1974 stands valid.

<u>Mohammad Habibur Rahman, J: I concur.</u>

<u>14. I may add that in the present case the plaintiff prayed for payment of money which included the principal and the interest prior to the date of institution of the suit and the trial court decreed the suit in preliminary form for the aggregate sum. The grant of interest from the date of suit to the date of decree as well as from the date of decree to the date of payment under Section 34(1) C.P.C. is entirely in the discretion of the court (See AIR 1942 P.C. 61; AIR 1961 S.C. 990). Ordinarily interest for the period during which the suit was pending and future interest is not refused except for sufficient reasons. But where the judgment and decree is silent on the point of payment of further interest on the aggregate sum from the date of decree or from any other earlier date, in terms of Section 34(2) C.P.C. the interest must be deemed to have been refused. Section 34 C.P.C. is applicable only where the decree is for a definite sum of money. But in respect of interest from the date of institution of the suit to the date of preliminary decree Order 34 C.P.C. in the matter of suits under that order leaves no discretion to the court. There is thus no inconsistency between the provisions of Section 34 and Order 34 C.P.C. in the present case since the preliminary decree is for a definite sum of money and the judgment and decree passed in the preliminary form on 19-4-78 are silent regarding the payment of further interest from the date of decree to the of date payment, the court must be deemed to have denied it and in no manner it can be said to the a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error in the judgment and decree arising from any accidental slip or omission in order to give jurisdiction to the court under Section 152 C.P.C. to modify, vary or amend the judgment and decree already passed. If the plaintiff petitioner was aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed in the preliminary form without incorporating any interest, an appeal could have been preferred. The remedy certainly did not lie in filing an application under section 152 C.P.C. in the instant case.</u>

<u>15. The case reported in AIR 1961 Orissa 18 is distinguishable as in that case the judgment made a provision for future interest from the date of judgment, omission to include the pro-vision in the decree clearly arose from accidental slip and the court at any time had jurisdiction under section 152 C.P.C. to incorporate it in the decree.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Nurul Islam Chowdhury, Advocate, with M. Fazlul Karim, Advocate ------- for the petitioner.

parties:
Saleh Ahmed
Vs.
Md. Zakaria
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Jalil, J.:- This Rule obtained by the decree-holder petitioner on an application U/S. 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, calls in question an order passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Misc. Case No. 47/74 as order no. 126 dated 6-8-78 directing the decree-holder to proceed with the execution case by determining the location of holding no. 339 i.e. the suit property with further direction not to dispossess the 3rd party opposite party Md. Zakaria from holding no. 339A in execution of the decree passed in Other Suit No. 59/71/50/69.

2. The present petitioner obtained a decree for ejectment against Md. Ilias Majhi in Other Suit No.50/69 on contest. That decree was put to execution in Other Execution Case No. 10/73 for eviction of judgment debtor Ilias Majhi. It appears that the decree holder went to take possession through process of the court but could not get possession due to resistance and filed an application to get delivery of possession with the help of the police on the ground of resistance by the judgment debtor and his men. In that pending execution case the present opposite party Md. Zakaria, a 3rd party filed an application under Order 21 Rule 99 and 100 and U/S. 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for not allowing the decree holder to execute the decree without determining the location of holding no.339 on the allegation inter alia, that the decree holder already obtained possession of the suit holding no.339 Madarbari P.S. Doublemoorings. District Chittagong out of Court but now under the garb of the decree he is trying to evict the 3rd party-opposite party from his holding no. 339A and so it is necessary to ascertain the decretal property before issuance of the writ of delivery of possession. It was further contended in that application that Municipal holding no.339A is a separate and distinct holding which is situated in the extreme north of R.S. plot no.1919 intervened by a common passage in between Municipal holding no. 339 and 339A. It was further alleged that the 3rd party opposite party filed a separate suit no. 58/74 in the 2nd Court of the Munsif, Chittagong for permanent injunction. It is admitted by both the parties that the said suit has been decreed against the petitioner by which the petitioner is restrained by perpetual injunction from dispossessing the plaintiffs of that suit (3rd party opposite party) from holding no. 339A, Majhirghat, Chittagong and from disturbing his possession therein and that decree was affirmed by the appellate court in Other Appeal No. 168/706 and we are informed by the petitioner that against the said appellate decree a second appeal is pending but there is no stay order.

3. The decree holder contested the said application by filing a written objection denying the material allegations and asserting inter alia, that the provisions of Order 21 Rule 99 and 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure have no application to the present case and that the application was filed malafide and the decree holder has no intention to take possession of holding no. 339A as his decree is directed against holding no.339 only and the 3rd party has no right to file any application in the execution case filed against another person, that is judgment debtor. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the prayer of the 3rd party and passed by impugned order.

4. The impugned order as it stands, that is, "O.P.I is directed to proceed with the execution case by determining the location of holding no. 339 as described in the agreement in persuance of which the decree in question was passed. He is further directed not to dispossess the petitioner from holding no. 339A in execution of the decree of other suit 50/69", seems to be harmless as it only directed the decree holder to take possession of the suit property after determining its location, and as the decree holder according to him, does not intend to take possession of any other land, there is no question of causing prejudice to him.

<u>5. But a question has arisen in this case as to whether the executing court has jurisdiction to pass such order at the instance of a 3rd party who has no locus standi at this stage. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate has taken us through the provisions of Order 21 Rules 99 and 100 wherefrom it appears that the executing court may pass such order in case of resistance but that order must be on an application filed by the decree holder under Order 21 Rule 97 of the same Code. The 3rd party cannot file such application but he may file an application if evicted under Rule 100 of the said order and the executing Court may investigate into the matter and restore the applicant in possession. This position of law is also not challenged by Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned advocate appearing for the 3rd party-opposite party; but his case is that his application and the impugned order passed there on are covered by Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as at the present stage when he has not been dispossessed he cannot take resort to provisions of Order 21 Rule 100 and so section 151 is the only section under which the court may grant appropriate relief under its inherent jurisdiction. He has cited some decisions on that point. The first one is PLD 1959 Lahore 511. In that case (Mst. Sahib-un-nissa and others V. Mst. Mahmooda Begum) a 3rd person who is not a party to the decree applied to the court executing the decree U/S. 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the application was allowed and a single Judge of West Pakistan High Court held that when the party has not yet been dispossessed it is a matter of discretion with the court whether it would or would not determine the question beforehand. Next Mr. Rahman cited a case reported in 25 DLR 5. This case was in connection with a matter U/S. 53A of the Transfer of Property Act which is not applicable to the present case. As against that Mr. M. Fazlul Karim has cited a case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 185 Punjab Ali Pramanik and others V. Mohd. Mokarram Hossain) and submits that where specific relief is available, inherent power of Courts U/S. 151 can not be invoked; the said case arose out of an application for setting aside sale and their lordships were pleased to observe-</u>

<u>“Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code, as it stands, empowers a Court, which has held an auction sale, to set aside the sale on an application made, amongst others, by a person whose interests have been affected by the sale, on the ground that there has been material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the said sale. If the ground for impugning the sale is fraud in publishing or conducting the sale then, according to the terms of the rule, the proceeding is to be initiated by a person as has been named in the said rule and recourse cannot, certainly, be taken to section 151 of the Code for the purpose of evading or circumventing the conditions laid down therein. If the ground of challenge is a kind of fraud other than that contemplated in the said rule, which vitiated the proceeding altogether, recourse to section 151 of the Code will also not be ordinarily appropriate, as a properly framed suit under the general law will undoubtedly be a more appropriate remedy in such a case.</u>

<u>"In the present case the decretal suit property has been described in the decree as follows-</u>

<u>“District Chittagong, Mouza East Madarbari P.S. Doublemoorings within Chittagong Municipality, Ward D holding no.339 comprising northern godown east to west 85 and north to south 25 with pucca flooring, roofing and fencing with C.I. sheet situated in the northern part of R.S. plot no 1919.”</u>

<u>And admittedly the 3rd party opposite party does not claim any interest in the decretal property. His claim is against holding no. 339A which is not admittedly the suit property and the present decree holder petitioner does not claim any interest against the property.</u>

<u>6. In our opinion the remedy of the 3rd party is available in a separate suit and the principle of law decided in 29 DLR (SC) 185 is applicable to the present case and the 3rd party may come to the picture in the execution case filed by a different person under Order 21 Rule 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure after eviction. The inherent power U/S. 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be invoked at the instance of 3rd party who is neither a party to the suit nor to the decree sought to be executed. Moreover he admittedly does not claim any interest in the suit holding but in a different holding and questions the identity of the suit land and has filed the application in apprehension of being dispossessed from his land. His such apprehension may be a cause of action for a separate suit for permanent injunction. Admittedly a separate suit had already been filed and a decree of permanent injunction has already been passed against the decree holder petitioner and so he cannot go to holding no. 339A. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman submits that if without ascertaining the location of holding no. 339 the decretal land, the decree holder dispossesses the 3rd party opposite party from holding no. 339A identifying it to be holding no.339 then multiplicity of legal proceeding shall be cropped up and the learned court below rightly passed the impugned order which has not prejudiced the decree holder, rather it would prevent the multiplicity of legal proceeding and would settle all the dispute once for all. We have already observed that the order of the executing court is harmless but every order must be passed with jurisdiction vested by law which is lacking in the present case. In this view of the matter the order cannot stand being passed without jurisdiction and is liable to be set aside. Before we part with the case we must observe that it is the duty of the executing court to give delivery of possession of the decretal property to the decree holder and he may pass necessary order if he finds that the ascertainment of the suit property by local investigation is necessary in order to see that the decree of the court is correctly executed although he cannot pass such order on an application of a 3rd party who has no locus standi in law at this stage before being evicted.</u>

7. The Rule is therefore made absolute and the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge complained of is set aside. Parties however shall bear their respective costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 7-6-77 passed by  the High Court in Civil Revision Case No. 1177 of 1876).
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. This appeal by special leave arises out of a judgment passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1177 of 1976 discharging the Rule and upholding the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge rejecting the prayer of the appellant for hearing of the miscellaneous Case under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Respondents 1-3 instituted a suit being T.S. No. 344 of 1969 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca which was Renumbered as T.S. No. 56 of 1972 on transfer to the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca, for partition of the email property described in the schedules of the plaint by metes and bounds against the co-sharers.

3. Appellant and the respondents 4 and 5 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement and prayed for separate sahams in the suit property position that late Khan Bahadur Sadeq Khan who was the owner of the property described in the schedules 'A', 'B', 'C' and 'D' in 16 annas share and owner of schedule 'DI' to the extent of annas share and they further admitted that the late Khan Bahadur Sadeq Khan died leaving behind 4 sons and 2 daughters as stated by the plaintiff-respondents 1-3. It was contended in the written statement that the appellant subsequently purchased 2/5th share of the respondents 4 and 5 of the property described in the Schedule 'A' & 'B' to the plaint and as such his share in Schedule 'A' & 'B' comes to 3/5th share while his share in Schedule 'C' and 'D' stands at 1/5th share and in Schedule 'D I' at l/l0th share by inheritance and If6th by purchase from co-sharers totalling  4/15th shares therein. It is denied that the respondents 1 and 2 demanded partition of the suit property for the same was not acceded to as alleged in the plaint.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in the preliminary form and an Advocate Commissioner was appointed for partitioning the suit property by metes and bounds. It is alleged by the appellant that the Advocate Commissioner without going to the locality submitted a report behind the back of the appellant and he did not grant any saham to the appellant in respect of the Schedules 'A' & 'B' property although he bad admittedly and according to the preliminary, decree 3/5th share therein.

5. The learned Judge by his order dated 10.7.75 passed the final decrees ex parte in accordance with the Advocate Commissioner's report and making the said report part of the final decree.

Being aggrieved by the ex parte final decree They admitted the factual the appellant filed an application in the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was numbered as Misc. Case No. 76/15.

6. The appellant also filed an appeal under section 96(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure being First Appeal No. 15/1977 in the High Court against the aforesaid final decree passed exporter which is pending for hearing.

7. Later the appellant prayed for hearing of the aforesaid Misc. Case No. 76/75 but the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 1.6.76 stayed further proceedings of the Miscellaneous Case holding, inter alia that the appellant had already filed an appeal to the High Court against the final decree and "no purpose will be served by prosecuting the Miscellaneous Case at this stage as the matter is sub judice before the High Court Division" and stayed the Miscellaneous Case and further liberty was given to the parties to raise the question of maintainability of Miscellaneous Case. Another prayer was made on 26-6-76 for hearing of the Miscellaneous  Case and the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer of the appellant for hearing of the Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

8. Being aggrieved by that order the appellant moved the High Court and obtained the Rule in Civil Revision No. 1177/76. A Division Bench of the High Court on consideration of some decisions discharged the Rule agreeing with the view that was expressed in 19 DLR (Dacca), 81:

"The view that we have taken amounts to this, that although an application under Order 9, rule 13 is maintainable, yet when the points involved in the suit have been re-agitated by a party by way of an appeal has been decided, the original decree is not merely merged in the appellate decree, but the patent fact which, of necessity, must stare one in the face is that to allow the party the luxury of further prosecuting his application under Order 9, rule 13 would be unconscionable".

The learned Judges agreeing with the view discharged the Rule.

Leave was granted, to consider whether an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of a suit decreed ex parte is barred on the filing of an appeal from the ex parte decree or hearing of such application requires to be postponed till 'the hearing of the appeal.

9. Mr. S.R. Paul, the learned Counsel for the appellant contended that the learned Judges of the High Court had fallen into error in not appreciating that the remedies under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil procedure and that of under section 96(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure though concurrent are entirely distinct in their scope. It was further, submitted that the attention of the High Court was not drawn to the case of Sajeda Khatun Vs. Mostafa Khatun; reported in 28 DLR 221.

10. An ex parte decree is passed when the suit is called for hearing and the plaintiff appears but the defendant does not. appear then the Court may proceed ex parte III accordance with the procedure laid down under Order 9, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 13 provides for setting aside the ex parte decree passed against the defendant. This procedure is an original proceeding independent of the suit. The only points for consideration in this proceeding are; (a) Whether there was due service of summons, or (b) Whether there was sufficient cause for non-appearance at the hearing. The Court if satisfied, that such grounds are well founded may make an order setting aside the decree "as against him". There is a proviso added to the rule, under which, where, the decree is of such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendants only, it may be set aside against all or any of the other defendants also. Apart from this remedy as provided by rule 13, an ex parte decree can be challenged; (i) by an appeal under section 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure, (ii) by filing an application for review under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, The scope in review is very narrow (Chajuram vs. Neki 26 CWN 697 PC).

11. An ex parte decree can also be set aside by a regular suit if it is provided that there was supression of summons and defendant was prevented from defending the suit by reason of fraud (Nirsan v. Kishan, AIR, 1931 Patna, 204 (FB) Haricharan vs. Dwarika, AIR 1961, Patna, 88).

12. An the aforesaid remedies are concurrent. This has precisely caused much anxiety to the Courts as to the implication when a party has pursued the remedies simultaneously, that is, by filing application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also by filing an appeal before the Appellant Court against the ex parte decree. In the instant case this was done.

13. There has been divergent opinion in cussed this sub-continent over this question. It appears that one view is that the defendant against whom an ex parte decree has been passed may apply under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set it aside and also at the same time prefer an appeal from it and the proper Court to hear the application is the Court which passed the decree and not the Appellant Court vide Damadar vs. Sarat, 13 CWN 846, Kumud vs. Jatindra, 15 CWN 399, Kalimuddin vs. Ashakuddin, 28 CWN 795, Mathura vs. Ram 37 Allahabad, 208, Humani vs. Azizuddin 39 Allahabad, 143. The reason is that the matter to be considered in a proceeding under this rule is entirely distinct from the matter to be considered in an appeal from the ex parte decree, the one being concerned with the due service of summons or the prevention of appearance for sufficient cause and the other would be determination of the merits of the controversy between the parties. In 28 CWN 795 this point has been dealt with exhaustively.

14. The High Court of Calcutta Allahabad, Nagpur and Judicial Court of Oudh have held that where an appeal is preferred from an ex parte decree and the decree is confirmed or otherwise disposed of in appeal, the Court which passed the ex parte decree has no longer any power to entertain an application to set aside. This view was as taken in Dhonai vs. Tarak, 12 CLJ 53, Kika Bari vs. Sufia, AIR 1937. Nagpur, 381, Giridharlal vs. Deputy Commissioner AIR 1929, Oudh, 35. The reason is that the decree of the Lower Court is merged in that of the Appellate Court. To Gazaraj vs. Swaminath, 39 Allahabad, 13. The point, merger of the decree of the first Court in the decree of the Appellate Court has been exhaustively, discussed.

15. If this application however is heard before the disposal of the appeal and if the same is allowed and the ex parte decree set aside then the defendant has no reason to prosecute his appeal. On the other hand, if the appeal is dismissed during the pendency of the application and the decree of the trial court is merged in the decree of the Appellate Court, the trial court loses its jurisdiction to hear the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure (51 Calcutta, 715).

16. Difficulty arises when in a suit there are many defendants and the defendants who have been duly served with summons may not have any reason to apply under this rule whereas the defendants who were not duly served with summons or have been prevented by any other sufficient cause from appearing the question is whether they can be denied this remedy for filing an application for setting aside the ex parte decree as against them. Where the applicant is no party to the appeal either as appellant or respondent and the Appellate court has not adjudicated upon his case, the decree of the first court does not merge in that of the court of appeal. The question whether the decree of the first court of first instance has merged into that of the court of appeal will depend upon the facts of each case. The proviso to the rule has taken care where the decree is of such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendant only, then it is provided that it may be set aside as against all or any of the other defendants.

17. In a case where the petitioner is the same who has filed the petition under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also filed an appeal against the ex parte decree the preponderant view is that the petitioner can pursue his remedy under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is not the question of indulging any luxury" but it is the remedy that has been provided by law. It is not the question whether the scope in Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is larger than that of appeal because the remedies are distinct as has been rightly contended by Mr. Pal, the learned Counsel. In one case evidence is to be led on the point of non-service of summons or absence due to sufficient reasons, whereas in the appeal the decree can only be challenged on the ground that it is erroneous either in fact or law. The jurisdictions, are different The scopes are different and it is not correct, with respect, to say that having pursued one remedy the petitioner should not be allowed "to indulge in the luxury of pursuing the other remedy". The remedy under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure disappears only upon the disposal of the appeal and on merit when on the principle of merger the Court of first instance loses its jurisdiction to hear the Miscellaneous Case under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree against him. The law in the subject has been correctly expounded in the case of Sajeda Khatun Vs. Mostafa Khatun, (1976) 28 DLR 221 which has also discussed the decision noticed above.

<u>18. On a review of the decisions and the discussion on the question set out, the following propositions seem to be well settled:</u>

<u>1. Where a defendant against whom an exparte decree is passed applies under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set it aside and at the same time prefers an appeal from it, the Calcutta High Court has held that notwithstanding the pendency of appeal the original court may proceed with the application. Damodar Vs. Sarat Chandra 13 CWN 846 and Kumud Nath vs. Jathindra Nath, 38 Calcutta 394. The Allahabad High Court has also taken the same view. Mathura vs. Ram Charan, 37 Allahabad, 208; Gajaraj vs. Swaminath, 39 Allahabad, 13; Humani vs. Azizuddin, 39 Allahabad, 143. The extreme position taken by Madras High Court in Sankar vs. Subdrajan, 30 Madras, 535 has not been followed by other High Courts.</u>

<u>2. Where the ex parte decree has been confirmed or otherwise disposed of on appeal the court which passed the ex parte decree has no longer any power to entertain an application to set it aside, even though the application was made before the appeal was filed Mathura vs. Ram Charan , 37 Allahabad, 208.</u>

<u>3. The same principle will hold good even if the appeal has been preferred by a party other than the defendant against whom the decree was passed ex parte provided the decree was one and indivisible. Dhonai Sikder v.s. Tarak Nath, 12 CLJ 53.</u>

<u>4. But it will not affect the case of the defendant against whom exparte decree was passed and whose claim was not subject matter of appeal although he might be made party as respondent in the appeal. Abdul Jalil Bhuiyan vs. Majibar, 12 DLR 581.</u>

<u>The two remedies are concurrent subject to the doctrine of merger set out above.</u>

<u>19. We, therefore, find that the High Court has fallen into an error in taking the view about the nature and scope of the two remedies. No opinion has been expressed as to the merit of Miscellaneous Case. The petitioner can legitimately pursue his remedy under order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure notwithstanding his filing of appeal which is pending subject to the limitation that the appeal itself is not disposed of in the meantime on merit whereupon he loses his right to pursue the Miscellaneous Case because on the principle of merger the decree of the trial court merges into that of the appellate court.</u>

<u>The appeal is, therefore, allowed with costs. The decisions of the courts below are set aside. The Miscellaneous case before the court below shall proceed as usual.</u>

End.
