full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J : This revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of defendant No. 1 appellant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 20-1-2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.3, Kishoreganj, in the Other Appeal No. 104 of 1999 in affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-5-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Kishoreganj, in the Other Class Suit No. 212 of 1993 in decreeing the suit.

2. The opposite party Nos. 1 to 5 Rabindra Chandra Saha and others as plaintiffs filed Other Class Suit No. 212 of 1993 in the Court of Subordinate Judge for declaration of Title in respect of "Ka" scheduled land, for the recovery of "khas" possession after evicting the defendant No. 1 Ayesha Khatun, demolishing and removing the dwelling house of the defendant No. 1 thereon and for the declaration of the kabala deed No. 2373 dated 5-5-1969 executed by the defendant No.2 in favour of defendant No. 1 as illegal, collusive, ineffective, created by false personification and not binding upon the plaintiffs and for further declaration that no part and parcel of the suit property was declared as vested property.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, inter alia, is that including other land, the alleged 0.21 acre of land belonged to Nabin Chandra Saha in khas and the rest of the land belonged to Gobinda Chandra Saha and Guruchandra Saha and in settlement survey Maliki Khatian No. 86 was published in the name of  Nabinchandra and Khatian No. 88 in the name of Gobinda Chandra and others; that in the said Khatian, one Ragunath Chandra was shown as permissive possessor in the remark column and after the survey the said Ragunath Chandra left for elsewhere, delivering the possession of the suit land in favour of Nab in Chandra Saha and others and by  an amicable settlement Nabin Chandra Saha got the entire land of suit plot with other land in his saham and other co-sharers got other land, that while possessing in such way Nabin Chandra died, leaving his only son, Jagabandhu  Saha, who inherited the same and as per provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the khas Khamar title was converted into Raiyati jote title under the Government; that Jagabandu used to possess the suit land by erecting dwelling house which was a simple thatched hut but the remaining portion of land was an unused plot of land,

4. It is further stated that the defendant Nos. 1 to 5 namely, Rabindra Chandra Saha and Gopinath Saha, son of Jagabandhu Saha, Prodip Kumar Saha, Netai Chandra Saha and Narayan Chandra Saha, son of Anil Chandra Saha, proposed to Jagabandu Saha to rent the same on monthly basis for running the business of a carpenter by constructing a structure on about 2 decimals of land; that Jagabandu accepted the proposal and permitted them to use the land and to do their business as monthly tenant but after some period they became defaulters for a few months rent and about 4 years before the liberation war, they handed over the possession of the hut in lieu of the arrear rent in favour of Jagabandu Saha and went away elsewhere. It is further contended that subsequently the husband of the defendant No. 1 namely, Khondaker Golam Ahmed served in the police department and on transfer he came to Bajitpur and took the house from Jagabandu as a monthly tenant and in the meantime the War of Liberation started and Jagabandu Saha was killed, leaving 3 sons i.e the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and Anil Chandra Saha, the predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 3 to 5, who inherited the property and used to possess the suit land, keeping the husband of the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, as a monthly tenant of the house on 02 decimal; that while possessing the land in this way, the husband of the defendant No. 1 Ayesha Khatun, died, leaving his widow and her son, Babul Khondaker, who remained as tenant; that husband of the defendant No.1 at his own cost re-constructed the old cracked house on the land of schedule No.2 and used to possess therein and that in the meantime Anil Chandra Saha died, leaving 3 sons, the plaintiff Nos. 3 to 5, who inherited their father's share of the property. It is also contended that due to a reckless movement and association with antisocial activities of the son of defendant No.1, she left the house and started living with her daughter permanently and thus the plaintiffs took possession of the aforesaid land; that with a view to grabbing the suit land, the defendant No.1 filed a suit being No. 86 of 1990 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Bajitpur,and through conversation with other villagers, the plaintiffs came to know about the other suit No. 86 of 1990 in which the plaintiffs impleaded themselves as defendants and contested the suit; that although Jogesh Chandra Sutradhar did not inherit the suit land, beyond the knowledge of Jogesh, the defendant No.1 created a forged deed dated 15-5-1969 by false personification showing Jogesh Chandra Sutradhar as vendor in favour of the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, as purchaser which the plaintiffs for the first time came to know from the plaint of the suit filed by the defendant No.1 and on 8-1-1998 the plaintiffs obtained the certified copy of the RoR record and became aware of the fact that in absence of Jagabandu Saha, the tenant, Jogesh Chandra Sutradhar and others collusively and illegally entered their names in RoR and kept this in secret; that the said record was wrongly prepared in the names of an interestless person and no portion of the suit land is enlisted as enemy property; that the husband of the defendant No.1 also obtained a false lease in VP case No. 31 of 1978-79 narrating that the suit land was enlisted as enemy property which also created no right and title; that long after the filing of Other Suit No. 86 of 1990, the defendant No.1 Ayesha Khatun with a view to establishing her illegal claim firmly, constructed a thatched hut on the land of schedule No.2 land and dispossessed the plaintiffs forcibly. In these circumstances, the plaintiffs were constrained to file the suit.

5. The defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, who is now dead, contested the suit by filing a written statement, denying the material allegations of the plaint.

6. The case of' the defendant No. 1 Ayesha, inter alia, is that out of the entire land, a portion of suit land measuring 0.21 acre was recorded in the name of Nab in Chandra Saha in CS khatian No. 86 and the rest of the land in the name of Gobinda Chandra Saha and others in Khatian No. 88; that Gogan Chandra Sutradhar, the father of the defendant Nos.2 to 5, took pattan of the unused suit land and lived there by erecting a dwelling house and subsequently he died, leaving 4 sons namely, Jogesh Chandra, Mohonabashi, Mohananda and Nirananda and with the enactment of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, they became tenants of the Government and while possessing the same adversely, the SA record was correctly prepared and finally published in the names of the defendant Nos. 2 to 5; that while the defendant Nos. 2 to 5 were possessing the entire land by an amicable settlement, Jogesh Chandra Sutradhar got the suit land in his saham and by registered deed No. 2373 dated 15-5-1969 transferred the same in favour of this defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun who since 1969 had been living thereon by erecting a dwelling house and paying rent to the government; that thereafter, since the land is situated within Bajitpur Municipality, the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, opened a holding in her name and paid the municipal taxes and present record was also prepared in her name. It is further contended that while she came to know about the enlistment of 75% of the land as enemy property, she filed Other Suit No. 86 of 1996 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Bajitpur in which the plaintiffs were subsequently added as defendants and her husband was also buried in the same suit land. It is further contended that the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, became astonished to know the claim of the present plaintiffs that Jogesh Chandra by an amicable settlement got the suit land 60 years ago and the plaintiffs got the suit land by inheritance, and that taking the advantage of the helpless condition of the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, the plaintiffs brought this suit on false grounds which is liable to be dismissed.

7. At the trial, the plaintiffs examined 3 (three) witnesses in support of their case. PW 1, Rabindra Chandra Saha, is the plaintiff himself. PW 2, Aftabuddin, is a neighbour of the plaintiffs and PW 3, Jalal Uddin, is also another neighbour of the plaintiffs.

8. The contesting defendant No.1 examined 5 witnesses in support of her case. DW 1 Panna Begum is the daughter of defendant No.1, DW 2 Jogesh Chandra Sarker is the deed writer, DW 3 Nur Miah and DW-4 are the neighbours of defendant No.1 and DW 5 is the Advocate Commissioner.

9. On behalf of the plaintiffs, Exhibits 1, 1(Ka), 2, 3, 4 and 4(ka) are filed. Exhibit 1 and 1(Ka) are the CS khatians, Exhibit 2 and 3 are the RoR khatians, Exhibit-4 is the certified copy of the plaint in Other Class Suit No. 213 of 1993 and Exhibit-4 (ka) is the certified copy of the order sheet of the suit.

10. Defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, filed 5(five) rent receipts of Municipal Tax which are marked Exhibit Ka, Ka(1), Ka(2), Ka (3) and Ka(4). She also filed 2 Dakhilas of lease marked Exhibit 'Kha' and 'Kha(1)' and also filed 4 government Dakhilas. On behalf of the defendant, Advocate Commissioner's report and connecting papers were filed which are marked Exhibits X and X(1).

11. The learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Kishoreganj, framed the following issues:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its Plesent form and manner?

2. Is there any-cause of action of this suit?

3. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get decree as prayed for?

4. Were the plaintiffs dispossessed from Kha scheduled land?

5. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get possession in respect of kha scheduled land?

6. To what relief, if any, are the plaintiffs entitled to?

12. The learned Subordinate Judge considering the facts.and circumstances of the case and evidence

on record by his judgment dated 31-5-1999 decreed the suit deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiffs.

13. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the trial Court, the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, Kishoreganj; being Other Appeal No.104 of 1999 and the said appeal was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj who by his judgment and decree dated 22-1-2002 dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment of the trial Court.

14. It is against the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 20-1-2002 that the heirs of the original defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, as petitioners, moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

15. The learned Advocate for the defendant- petitioners did not appear to support the contention of the petitioners. The contention of the petitioners, as it appears from the revisional application, is that the learned appellate Court delivered the judgment without considering the facts of the case and material evidence on record and that the judgment of the appellate Court is perverse and liable to be set aside.

16. Mr Subash Chandra Saha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs-opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the learned Additional District Judge carefully considered the material evidence on record and dismissed the appeal, affirming the judgment of the trial Court and consequently, the impugned judgment does not suffer from any illegality or legal infirmity to justify interference by this Court in revision.

<u>17. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties cited the decisions in the case of Chan Mohamood (Md) and others vs Md Hossain Ali being dead his heirs 1 (Ka) Md Sekander Ali and others reported in 3 BLC 364; in the case of Kochi Mia @ Khocha Mia vs Suruj Mia being dead his  heirs Md Fazlur Rahman and others reported in 51 DLR (AD) 57, in the case of Zamir Uddin Ahmed vs Ziaul Huq and others reported in 49 DLR 622, in the case of Aroti Rani Paul vs Sudarshan Kumar Paul and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 73 and in the case of Jamaluddin vs Saleha Khatoon and others reported in 3 MLR (AD) 284 in support of his contention.</u>

18. Now the moot point that calls for our determination is, whether the learned Additional District Judge committed any error of law in passing the judgment dated 20-1-2002 which has occasioned failure of justice.

19. It is admitted that the suit land measuring 32 decimals appertaining to RoR plot No. 928 of RoR khatian No.416 corresponding to settlement plot No. 995 of settlement khatian No. 86 and 88 of Mouza Bajitpur under Kishoreganj District originally belonged to Nabin Chandra Saha in khas and the rest of the land belonged to Gobinda Chandra Saha and Guru Chandra Saha and in settlement survey Maliki khatian No. 86 Exhibit-1 was published in the name of Nobin Chandra and Khatian No.88 Exhibit 1(ka) in the name of Gobindra Chandra Saha and others.

20. The case of the contesting defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, is that her predecessor-in-interest Gogan Chandra Sutradhor, took pattan of the suit land from the superior landlords and possessed the same, erecting huts thereon; that Gogan Chandra Sutradhor died, leaving Jogesh Chandra, Mohonbashi, Mohananda and Nirananda who are defendants Nos.2 to 5; that SA khatian was prepared in the name of defendants Nos. 2 to 5; that thereafter, Gogan Chandra Sutradhar got the suit land by family partition who transferred the land in question to defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, by a kabala No. 2373 dated 15-5-1959 and thus, she has been possessing the same mutating her name and paying rent to the government.

21. The further contention of the defendant No.1 is that she filed Title Suit No. 86 of 1990 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Bajitpur, for declaration in respect of the suit and for declaration that the enlistment of the suit land as enemy and non-resident property is illegal and the suit was subsequently transferred to the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Kishoregonj and the suit was ultimately dismissed for default vide order No.39 dated 6-2-1994.

22. It also appears from the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party that later on the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, managed to take temporary settlement of the suit land from the government in the name of her husband.

23. On the other hand, the contention of the plaintiffs-petitioners is that the suit land admittedly belonged to Nabin Chandra who died, leaving Jagabandu who inherited the same. It is the specific case of the plaintiffs that the defendant Nos.  2 to 5 were the monthly Bharatia under Jagabandu. It appears that Jagabandu was killed during the Liberation War who left 3 sons the plaintiffs Nos.1 and 2 and Anil Chandra Saha, the predecessor of plaintiff Nos. 3 to 5 who inherited the property and possessed the same, keeping Khandoker Go!am Ahammad, the husband of the defendant No.1 as tenant and later on Khandoker Golam Ahammad died, leaving a widow defendant No.1 and son namely, Babul Khondaker.

24. Thus it appears that both the plaintiff and the contesting defendant have the specific case of their own.

25. Now let us see what is the law regarding the burden of proof Section 101 of the Evidence Act lays down the provision of the Burden of Proof which runs thus:

"101. Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist.

When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof Iies on that person."

26. The burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it. It is reasonable and just that the suitor, who relies upon the existence of a fact, should be called upon to prove his own case. The party on whom the onus of proof lies must, in order to succeed, establish his case and he cannot on failure to do so, take advantage of the weakness of his adversary's case. He must succeed by the strength of his own right and clearness of his own proof. Here in this case both the plaintiffs and the contesting defendant have made out two distinct cases which each of them has to prove his respective part.

27. Now let us see how far the plaintiffs-opposite parties have succeeded in proving the case.

28. The contesting defendant No.1 admitted in his written statement that the suit land originally belonged to Nobin Chandra Saha who died, leaving the only son, Gogobondu Saha, who inherited the suit land. DW 1, Panna Begum, also admitted in her deposition that Nabin Chandra Saha was the original owner and the plaintiffs are his subsequent heirs. The plaintiffs have also submitted the CS Khatian No.86 of Nabin Chandra Saha Exhibit-1. The plaintiffs have also adduced corroborative and reliable evidence in this respect. So, it is evident from the above discussion that the suit land including 'Kha' scheduled land belonged to Nobin Chandra Saha, the predecessor of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs inherited the same by inheritance.

29. The plaintiffs emphatically deny that plaintiffs predecessor as superior landlord leased out any land to Gogan Chandra Sutradhar, the predecessor-in-interest petitioner, and that the Kabala No.2373 dated 15-5-1959 executed by Jogesh Chandra Sutradhar in favour of defendant No.1 Ayesha Khatun passed no title to the vendor.

30. The definite case of the contesting defendant No.1 is that Gogan Chandra Sutradhar took lease from superior landlord, that is, the predecessor of the plaintiffs; that RoR was prepared in the names of the sons of Gogan Chandra Sutradhar and that the contesting defendant No.1 acquired title in the 'Kha' scheduled land by virtue of Kabala No. 2373 dated 15-5-1959.

31. In the instant case, the proof of pattan taken by Gogan Chandra Sutradhar is a very important factor upon which the whole case of the contesting defendant relies. Without the proof of this point, the entire case of contesting defendant falls down. If the title of Gogan Chandra Sutradhar is not proved, the title of the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, by virtue of Kabala No. 2373 dated 15-5-1959 will also not pass and which will prove the defendant No.1 or her heirs, who are petitioners Nos.1(a) to 1(e), as trespassers in the 'Kha' scheduled land.

32. Now let us see how far the contesting defendant No.1 has succeeded in proving his case.

<u>33. In the written statement, it is simply stated that Gogan Chandra Sutradhar took lease from superior landlord but it is not stated how, when and from whom the said lease was taken. All these are the material facts which ought to have been written in the written statement. As regards that object of pleadings, in the case of Ganesh Trading Co vs Moji Ram reported AIR 1978 SC 484, the Supreme Court has observed;</u>

<u>"Provisions relating to pleadings in the civil cases are meant to give to each side intimation of the case of the other so that it may be met, to enable Courts to determine what is really at issue between parties, and to prevent deviations from the Courts which litigation on particular causes of action must take."</u>

<u>34. The object of pleadings is to bring parties to definite issues and to prevent surprise at the hearing. A party is entitled to know the case of his opponent so that he can meet it. The sole object of pleadings is to ascertain the real disputes between the parties, to narrow down the area of conflict and to see where two sides differ and to prevent miscarriage of justice.</u>

35. Rule 2 of Order VI of the Code of Civil Procedure lays down the fundamental principles of Pleadings. It reads as under:

"2. Every pleading shall contain, and contain only a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim or defence as the case may be ..... "

36. In this instant case, the particular of lease of Gogan Chandra Sutradhar from the superior landlord is a material fact which ought to have been stated specifically. The contesting defendant alleges that her predecessor got the 'Kha' scheduled land by way of lease and the contesting defendant in order to succeed is to prove such assertion both by documentary andoral evidences. But the contesting defendant No-1, Ayesha Khatun, neither disclosed the particulars of the lease nor did she prove it by documentary or oral evidence. The contesting defendant did not file any document of the lease. The contesting. defendant filed two zamidari Dakhalies marked Exhibit 'Kha' and 'Kha' (1) wherein the names of the tenants were written as Mohandrao Sutradhar and Jogesh Chandra Sutradhar whereas in the written statement, it was shown that Gogan, the father of defendant Nos.2 to 5, took the lease from superior landlord. These material discrepancies clearly indicate the falsity of the lease.

37. DW 2 Panna Begum, daughter of defendant 1, clearly deposed that she did not see any paper of the lease or she is not in a position to file any paper of lease.

38. In view of the above discussion, we are of the view that the contesting defendant No.1 has totally failed to prove the story of the lease on the basis of which her title orginated. Since the lease taken by Gogan, father of defendant Nos.2 to 5, from superior landlord has not been proved, the record of ROR in the names of defendant Nos.2 to 5 have no foundation and consequently the kabala executed by Gopinath, one of 4 brothers, has been proved false and fraudulent through which no title was passed to the contesting defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, or to her heirs, the present petitioners.

39. It further appears from the record that the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, filed a case being No. 86 of 1990 for declaration of title in respect of the 'Kha' scheduled land in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Bajitpur, impleading the plaintiffs of this suit as defendants and the said suit was subsequently transferred to the Subordinate Judge and ultimately, the suit was dismissed for default. It further appears from evidence on record that the contesting defendant No.1 who was plaintiff in that suit did not take any legal steps against that order for dismissal.

40. Since the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatun, did not take any legal step against that dismissal order, she is debarred from raising the same issue in this case. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the doctrine of res judicata or rule of conclusivenes of judgment, as to the point decided, in every subsequent suit between the parties. The doctrine of res judicata is that no man should be vexed twice for the same cause. The principle is founded on justice, equity and good conscience. The Doctrine of res judicata is often treated as a branch of law of estoppel. The rule of constructive res judicata is nothing but a Doctrine of Estoppel. As the defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatoon, did not take any legal step against the dismissal order of suit No. 86 of 1990, she is at least barred by the Doctrine of Estoppel from raising her claim of ownership in respect of "Kha' scheduled land.

41. It appears from the submission of the learned Advocate of the opposite parties that the husband named Khandaker Golam Ahmmad of the contesting defendant No.1, Ayesha Khatoon, took lease from admitting the 'Kha' scheduled land as abandoned property and, on the other hand, the defendant No.1 claims that her predecessor took the 'kha' scheduled land by way of pattan and thus she blows hot and cold in the same breath. All these circumstances go against the defendants- petitioners.

42. The learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Kishoreganj, on appreciation of the entire evidence, very prudently held that the contesting defendant failed to prove her title and possession in the suit land and, on the other hand, the learned Subordinate Judge reasonably held that the plaintiffs have succeeded in proving their case and thus the learned trial Court decreed the suit declaring the kabala No. 2373 dated 15-5-1969 as false and fraudulent with a direction to evict the defendant No.1 from the 'Kha' scheduled land.

43. The appellate Court, assessing the evidence on record, correctly affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court holding the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land excepting the possession of the 'Kha' scheduled land for which he passed order for eviction and not treating the suit land as vested property.

44. Both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court appear to have discussed each witness both for the plaintiffs and for the defendant and also the documents in coming to their respective decisions that the plaintiffs have proved their title and possession in the suit land, treating the same as not vested property and directing to evict the defendant No.1 from the 'kha' scheduled land. Furthermore, both the Courts concurrently held that the contesting defendant totally failed to prove the lease, foundation of SA record and the kabala No. 2373 dated 15-5-1969. The concurrent findings of the Courts appear to be well reasoned and supported by both oral and documentary evidences.

45. The revisional Court is to see only whether the lower appellate Court committed any error of law in his decision occasioning failure of justice. Firstly, the revisional Court is to see whether the appellate Court committed any error of law and secondly, such finding has.resulted in any failure of justice. Erroneous finding of fact is a different thing from an error or defect in the procedure. If the appellate Court had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal, in spite of that it hears the appeal or it is found that the findings of the appellate Court are  vitiated by any error of law or of procedure which affected the merit of the case, in such a situation, the appellate Court committed an error of law. High Court Division's power does not include the power to review the evidence to come to a finding of its own. High Court Division's power to interfere with the findings of fact of the appellate Court is limited to misreading and non-reading of material evidence and non-consideration of important documents affecting the merits of the decisions. In all other cases, findings of fact arrived at by the lower appellate Court, which are supported by evidence on record, is immune from attack in revision.

46. The term "occasioning failure of justice" has a far-reaching significance. It invests the High Court Division with wide power not only to go into the question of law but also the question of fact and, if necessary to assess evidence for its own satisfaction, to see to what extent such failure of justice has been perpetuated. Revisional power is discretionary. It is to be exercised only to secure the ends of justice. The revisional Court may call for the record in order to scrutinize whether the appellate Court has committed any error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The primary object of this jurisdiction is to uphold the ends of justice.

<u>47. In exercise of the revisional power vested in this Division mentioned hereinbefore, it appears that the appellate Court appears to have interrogated each witness both for the plaintiffs and the defendants and also the documents in coming to its conclusion that the plaintiffs have proved their title and possession in the suit property and the fact and circumstances of the case and evidence on record safely indicate that neither the appellate Court nor the trial Court committed any error of law in coming to their respective findings. So, the High Court Division as a revisional Court has hardly any jurisdiction to set aside such concurrent findings of the Courts below, rather such findings should be upheld to secure ends of justice.</u>

48. Since the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge as well as that of the learned Additional District Judge are never vitiated by misreading and non-reading of any material evidence or misconstruction of any important document materially affecting the ultimate decision in the Court, therefore, judgments of the Courts below do not suffer from any illegality either in fact or in law resulting in error in the decisions occasioning failure of justice.

49. In such view of the matter, we find no merit in this revision which must fail.

50. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment of the leaned Additional District Judge is upheld and the suit is decreed.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 36 of 1977
lawyer:
M. H. Khandker, Senior Advocate-----------For the Petitioner. 
Mian Abdul Gafur, Advocate, insructed by B.C. Pandey, Advocate-on-Record. Md. A. Aziz, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Haji Abdul Motalib Sowdagar----------Petitioner.
Vs.
Faiz Ahmed Chowdhury and others----------Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 7-1-77 passed by the High Court in S. M. A. No. 28 of 1976).
full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J.—This petition for special leave which arises out of an execution proceeding appears to illustrate the adage that the trouble of a decree-holder begins with the passing of the decree in his favour.

2. Respondents secured a decree on 19-4-67 in a suit for ejectment from the premises in suit against the petitioner as a monthly tenant in respect of the said premises and the decree was affirmed by the appellate court on 24.2.68. Respondents, thereafter, put the decree in execution on 20-5-68 in O.C. Execution Case No. 190 of 1968 which was, however stayed during the pendancy of the Second Appeal which was preferred by the petitioner to the Dacca High Court against the appellate decree mentioned above. The Second Appeal was dismissed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh on 8-1-74. When after the disposal of the Second Appeal, the proceeding of the execution case was resumed, an objection was filed by the petitioner on 12-3-74 in the said execution case under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. II of 1974. The objection taken therein was that the structures in respect of which the tenancy was created having been destroyed by fire during the pendency of the suit, the suit premises had become non-existent and as such the decree had became in executable.

3. On 13-4-74 an application was made on behalf of the petitioner in the said Miscellaneous Case for a local investigation without which, it was stated in the said application, the decree could not be executed. The executing Court rejected the prayer for local investigation on the view that it was not necessary at that stage. The High Court Division being moved under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the said order refused to exercise its revisional jurisdiction in the matter. There was an application for special leave to appeal being C. P. No. 142 of 1974 to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court wherein it was contended that there could not be any execution of the decree without a local investigation inasmuch as the identifying marks of the premises in. suite had been completely obliterated and the premises itself had ceased to exist as a result of the destruction of all the structures standing on the suit premises. The Appellate Division dismissed the petition for special leave with the following observation:

"We do not think that there is any substance in this contention of the learned Counsel. There is, no doubt, some reference to certain structures in the description of the holding as given in the decree in question but the description is also with reference to survey number, and municipal holding numbers. A decree for ejectment in respect of a tenanted holding containing certain structures cannot be defeated by demolition of the said structures and raising certain new structures in their stead. However, whether the decree has become non-executable because of such demolition and new construction, without a local investigation, is to be decided in the proceeding under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is pending before the Executing Court. If the Executing Court on a consideration of the objection raised by the judgment-debtor petitioner in the said proceeding comes to the view that for a proper execution of the decree a local investigation is necessary, there is no bar to the taking of the appropriate action by the Executing Court."

4. Thereafter an Advocate Commissioner was appointed, who submitted a report and the Executing Court- dismissed the petitioner's objection under section 47 of the Code on holding that the schedule of the suit premises as given in the execution case tallied with the decretal land of the, premises and that there could be no bar to the execution of the decree. On an appeal against the said order of the Executing Court, the Court of the subordinate. Judge held that the decretal land had been correctly mentioned in the execution petition and that there was no substance in the objection raised by the petitioner.' On a Second Appeal High Court the learned Single Judge who heard the appeal dismissed the Second Appeal summarily relying upon the concurrent finding of the Courts below that the disputed land had been correctly described in the execution petition and was also sufficiently identified.

5. Mr. K. H. Khandker, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the judgment-debtor petitioner, has strenuously argued that on the destruction by fire of the huts in respect of which the tenancy had been created the decree has become non-executable inasmuch as the subject matter, for the possession of which the decree was obtained, has become non-est. The tenancy was in respect of the huts only, learned Counsel submitted, and had nothing to do with the land on which the said huts stood and so there was nothing left to be taken possession of on the disappearance of the said huts, although the judgment-debtor was very much on the same site by constructing some new huts thereon. The argument seems to be of no substance on the very face of it. But Mr. Khondker with great persistence tried to add some amount of plausibility to such a patently wrong proposition by reference to some case law and the English principle relating to a statutory tenant.

6. The basic contention of the learned Counsel that the petitioner's tenancy consisted merely of the huts independently of the land on which the said huts stood appears to be based on some misconception. As a theoretical proposition it may not be an impossibility to have a tenancy of a hut or a room completely independent of the land on which the structure stands and it may be said, in case of a decree against the tenant in respect of such a hut or room, that the decree may become inexecutable on the destruction of such a hut or room, because with the disappearance of the hut or room in respect of which possession has been directed by the decree to be delivered, there remains nothing left to be complied with under the terms of the decree, as the possession of the tenant automatically comes to an end with the disappearance of the tenanted but or room in such a case. A tenancy of a room or apartment in a multi-storeyed building, which is incapable of being used or possessed by the tenant in any manner after its destruction, may be one of that sort of tenancy, but that is not the position in the instant case.

7. Learned Counsel has placed before us the description of the subject matter of the tenancy as given in the schedule to the plaint of the suit as well as of the decree passed therein, which has been quoted in paragraph 1 of the petition for leave. On a perusal of this description it becomes clear that the suit as well as the decree passed therein were in respect of the land within specified boundaries together with certain structures. In the local investigation which was held for the identity of the decretal premises the Advocate-Commissioner delineated the decretal premises with reference to the survey plots and it is the finding of the Courts below that the decretal land has been correctly described in the petition for execution. We have also examined the description of the premises as quoted in the petition for special leave and we find that it comprised a part of R. S. Plot No. 4953, appertaining to Khatian No. 3695 of Mouza Bakalia, known as Chaletai, with three huts standing thereon, which is the same as the new Municipal holding No. 264, and also the new Municipal holding No. 1863, surrounded on the north by the premises of another, Bharatia, Syed A. Majid. Sowdagar, on the south by that of the other bharatia, Rahman Brothers, on the east by Rajakhali Khal and on the west by the road. It is obvious that the subject matter of the tenancy comprised both lands and huts and as such on the destruction of the huts the entire subject Matter if the tenancy was not destroyed nor did the possession of the tenant in respect of the decretal premises automatically come to an end with such destruction.

8. Learned Counsel has cited a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Golamar Rahman Sowdagar Vs. Sm. Emartannissa Begum, in (1970) 22 DLR 126 P.L.D 1957 Dacca 372: where a decree for recovery of possession on a declaration of title was affirmed by the High Court on the view that the monthly tenancy in question having been in respect of a but only was extinguished as such as the subject matter of the tenancy was completely gutted by fire and that the tenant who constructed a new but at the old site was not entitled to claim that his tenancy still subsisted at his option as contemplated in Section 108(e) of the Transfer of Property Act.

9. Mr. Khondker has also referred to a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of A. Motalib Vs. Mst. Rezia Begum, 22 D.L.R. (SC) 134 where the decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Golamar Rahman was distinguished on the ground that the tenancy in that case was exclusively of a hut and so the subject matter of the lease could be said to have been destroyed as a whole and it was held that when a tenancy was in respect of some structures as well as of land the tenancy subsisted at the option of the tenant under section 108 (c) of the Transfer of Property Act, although all the structures were destroyed.

10. Learned Counsel has contended that it is the decision of the Dacca High Court, rather than the decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court referred to above, which is applicable to the facts of the case and that the subject /matter of the tenancy, in view of the said decision, must be deemed to have come to an end on the destruction of the structures, as there has been nothing left in respect of which the decree may be executed.

<u>11. We have already noticed that the tenancy in question was in respect of the land together with certain structures and as such if any of the aforesaid two" decisions is sought to be applicable to the instant case it is the decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court which may be regarded to have some relevance. We are, however, not concerned in this case as to the conditions under which a tenancy may 'be extinguished, but we are to see here whether a decree, which has been obtained for recovery of possession of a Premises on the finding that the tenancy in question had already been extinguished has become inexecutable on the destruction of the structures which stood on the said premises. Such a decree may be inexecutable if the subject matter for the possession of which the decree has been made is completely destroyed, as in that event nothing may be left which may be taken possession of in executing the decree. In the instant case the tenant was in occupation of the land and structures as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint and the part of the land which was in possession of the tenant was covered by the structures and the remaining part was vacant. On the destruction of the huts the tenant continued to remain in possession of the land including the portion on which structures stood. In such a case, it is extremely difficult for the Court to accept the submission of the learned Counsel that on the destruction of the huts there was nothing left for the judgment-debtor to comply with and that the decree 'has become infructuous. It is not necessary for the disposal of this petition to decide Whether in view of the definition of "premises' as given in section 2(6) of East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, .1953, which means any building or part of the building or any hut or part of the but let, including the grounds appertaining to such building or 'hut or part thereof, there can be a tenancy of huts or structures independent of the land on which such structures stand, as has been held by the Dacca High Court in the case of Golamar Rahman Sowdagar and others, because, as we have already found in the instant case, the tenancy in question specifically comprised both land and structures.</u>

<u>12. Mr. Khandken, learned Counsel for the petitioner, has also referred to Halsbury's Laws of England Vol. 32, 3rd Edition paragraph 1586 page 806, where the position of what has been known in England a Statutory tenant has been explained. During the war time there had been in England certain legislations which are collectively known as Rent Restrictions Acts, for giving protection to or mitigating the hardships of certain categories of tenants, whose premises had been destroyed or damaged in consequence of the war. Under the English law, as has been stated in the said paragraph, a tenant who retains possession of the premises by virtue of the Rent Restrictions Act, is known as a Statutory tenant and his position is to be distinguished from that of a contractual tenant. Such a tenant is entitled to retain possession of the premises even after their contractual tenancy has been lawfully determined by notice to quit or otherwise and they are liable to be ejected only if the conditions laid down in the Rent Restrictions Acts are satisfied. Mr. Khandker has also cited two decisions of the English Court, namely, Ellis & Son Ltd. Vs. Sidman 1948(1) All. E.R. 461 and Eastend Dwellings Co. Ltd. Vs. Finsbury Borough Council 1951 (2) All, ER. 587., which dealt with the cases of a Statutory tenant whose rented premises were destroyed by enemy action. 'These cases which were decided on the basis of certain specific legislative enactments as are in force in England have no manner of application to the instant case. A lawful decree of the Court directing the judgment-debtor to remove himself from and vacate possession of the premises of which he is still admittedly in possession cannot be said to have been rendered inexecutable only because certain structures have been destroy act or demolished and certain new structures have been put up thereon. This Court pointed out the correct position of law in its order dated 19th December, 1975 rejecting Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 141 of 1975. The Courts below were right in rejecting the petitioner's plea. There is no substance in this petition which is dismissed.</u>

End.

lawyer:
M. Nurullah, Advocate, instructed by S.M. Huq, Advocate-on-Record------------For the Appellant.

parties:
Golam Hafez Mia. -------- Appellant.
Vs.
Khadem Ali Meah -------Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated the 27th July, 1970 passed by the Dacca High Court in Second Appeal No. 1114 of 1967).
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, J.:-In this appeal interpretation of some of the provisions of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 are involved.

Facts material for the appeal are that dispute between plaintiff-appellant, Golan Hafez Mia, and defendant respondent, Khadem Ali Meah centres round the land belonging to Nalini and his wife Sarala. They left the country for West Bengal in 1962. Their rayati holding fell in arrears of rent which prompted the Government Acquired Estate to start four certificate proceedings. They are certificate case Nos. 138/1961-62, 185/1961-62, 187/1961-62, and 1970/1962-63. The holding comprising 1.72 acres of land was sold on 22-19-1962. It was purchased by the plaintiff, and he took delivery of possession on 4-10-62, Dispute between two parties cropped up when plain-tiff who had mututed his name in the Government Acquired Estate, found that the defendant on the basis of an ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 730/62, had got his name entered in the record of rights. Defendant got the ex-party decree, as his name was omitted from the record of rights. His claim is that in Baishak 1350 B.S. corresponding to April 1973, he got settlement of the land from Nalini and Sarala, on the basis of Lakhik and has been in possession since then. The suit of the plaintiff was for declaration only. The suit was contested on various grounds; one was that the plaintiff did not acquire a valid title in the certificate sale, and the other was that he was not in possession of the property.

<u>2. The trial court h yid against the plaintiff in that there was no proper service of certificate of notice under section 7 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, and as such the sale was a nullity and plaintiff acquired no title. He however found possession in favour of the plaintiff. The trial court held that the decree in Title Suit no. 730 of 1962 in favour of the defendant was fraudulent and void. There was an appeal and a cross-appeal before the first appellate court. He concurred with the trial court on the question of want of title of the plaintiff. But as regards possession he reversed the finding of trial court and held, the defendant was in possession of the land and the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act in the absence of a prayer for consequential relief. The first appellate court dismissed both the appeal and the cross-appeal.</u>

3. The plaintiff alone took a second appeal to the Dacca High Court and a bench heard the appeal and concurred with the decision r of court of appeal below with the modification that non service of notice under section 7 of the Act, rendered the sale voidable and not a nullity. A prayer was made before the High Court to allow the plaintiff, to amend his plaint by adding the prayer for recovery of possession, but it was refused and the appeal dismissed.

4. The plaintiff moved the Appellate Division and obtained leave on two points; the High Court was in error in refusing the prayer for amendment of the plaint, in order to remove the bar of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act ; the second is that, the High Court having accepted the concurrent findings of Title Suit no. 730 of 1962 was fraudulent and void and he did not acquire any title to the land on the basis of his alleged settlement, the Court was in error in the interpretation of s. 20 of the Public Demands Recovery Act by holding that the plaintiff did not acquire any title on the footing of the auction sale in the certificate proceeding in which the defendant was not a party.

<u>5. Of the two points, we propose to deal with the second question first. Before entering into the construction of the section, the finding of the High Court is to be looked into in order to ascertain the fact in its proper context. Both the plaintiff and the defendant claim title from Nalini and his wife. The plaintiff's claim is that by virtue of his auction purchase, Nalini's title was extinguished and vested in him. The defendant's claim is that long before the certificate sale, he in 1943 took settlement of the land, and is in possession of it, and so his title has not been affected by the certificate purchase of the plaintiff. The Courts below have concurrently found that the defendant has failed to substantiate his acquisition of title on the footing of settlement, and that the ex-parte decree obtained by him was fraudulent and void. This finding was not in challenge before the High Court. On the acceptance of this concurrent finding as to defendant's title, the observation of the High Court regarding plaintiff's title on the interpretation of section 20 of the Act seems to be out of place. The question before the High Court was what title was acquired by the plaintiff in the certificate sale. And having found that the defendant was on the land without any title, the High Court was in error in going to the question of title acquired by the plaintiff under section 20 of the Act, because defendant's claim of title through the certificate debtors had failed. But the defendant being in possession, the question to be determined is, whether plaintiff has a better title to recover possession from him.</u>

6. Since leave has been granted to consider the question, we propose to deal with it, in the proper perspective. We first propose to deal with relevant provisions of the Act, and see what title an auction purchaser acquires in a certificate sale, in terms of the provisions of the Act, and whether the finding of the High Court on the imperfect acquisition of title by the plaintiff, is correct. We also propose to deal with some of the rulings of the Dacca High Court on the question which requires restatement. To understand what title is acquired on a certificate sale some of the salient provisions of the Act are to be looked into.

7. A certificate proceeding can be started before the certificate officer for the recovery of any dues described in the Act, as in the nature of public demand. We are then to look at section 7, 8, 14, 20, and 36 of the Act to see the consequences following the filing of the certificate.

<u>8. Section 7 says that when a certificate has been filed the Certificate Officer shall serve upon the certificate debtor in the prescribed manner a notice in the prescribed form, After service of the notice ; when a period of 30 days has elapsed, and no objection has been taken in terms of the Act, the Certificate Officer under section 14 will proceed with the attachment and sale, or sale without previous attachment of any property, or attachment of the decree, or arrest and detention of the certificate debtor, as the case may require. The Certificate Officer, as the language of the Act stands, can follow all or any of the modes prescribed above, having regard to the special provisions of any enactment concerning the certificate, In this case the procedure by sale of the holding of the certificate debtor was adopted in terms of rules 23 and 46.</u>

<u>9. The consequences following before and after the sale may now be considered, The consequence following from the service of notice under section land before the sale, is contained in section 8. It says, that private sale of the property of the certificate debtor situated in the district in which the certificate is filed, shall be void against any claim enforceable in execution of the certificate, and that the amount due from time to time, in respect of the certificate shall be a charge upon the immovable property of the certificate debtor, wherever situated. The notice form given in Appendix to the Act in Schedule II, shows that the certificate debtor is prohibited from alienating any immovable property, or any part thereof. The effect is that of attachment of the property, and so rule 23 says, that when the property to be sold is an immovable property of the certificate-debtor, no attachment need be made before the sale. On the service of notice under section 7, the consequences following from it are first: any private transfer of any immovable property in the district where certificate is filed, is void, and secondly, the certificate dues become a charge upon the immovable property of certificate debtor through the country.</u>

<u>10. We now turn to sections 20 and 36 to see what consequence follow after the sale in execution of a certificate. Section 20 consists of 4 sub-sections. We are concerned with two of them, sub-sections (1) and (3), and other two sub-sections are not material for our consideration. Sub-section (1) says, that when a property is sold in execution of a certificate, there shall vest in the purchaser merely the right, title and interest of the certificate debtor at the time of the sale, even though the property itself be specified. Sub-section (3) is an exception to sub-section (1), and it begins with a non obstante clause. The relevant part says: notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), or any other law for the time being in force where the tenure or holding is sold in execution of a certificate, for arrears of rent due in respect thereof, the tenure or holding, shall, subject to the provisions of section 90 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, where that section is in force, pass to the purchaser with the power to annul encumbrances with the restriction provided by the Act. This is the material part of the section relevant for our purposes excluding the immaterial portions.</u>

<u>11. The substance of the two sub-sections may be considered by drawing an analogy from the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act, in that the effect of the sale in execution of a certificate under sub-section (1), is that of a money decree, and that under sub-section (3) of a rent decree in certain cases. Under the former, the right title and interest of the certificate-debtor on the date of sale, and under the latter the tenure or holding will pass to the purchaser with the right to annul the encumbrances. Ordinarily the right title and interest of the certificate-debtor at the time of the sale vest in the purchaser. He steps into the shoes of the certificate debtor, and claims through him. All lawful liabilities created on the and by the certificate debtor before period of the service of notice under section 7, or the attachment, will bind the purchaser. If the certificate debtor had no subsisting interest on the date of the sale it is a nullity. These are the incident of a money-decree.</u>

<u>12. A certificate sale held in default of payment of rent, and on the compliance with the requirement of the principles of representation of the landlord and the tenant, the tenure or holding passes with the certificate sale. It has the effect of a rent decree. If the doctrine of representation is not fulfilled, it will have the effect of money decree. The consequence of a rent decree, is different from that of a money decree. The purchaser acquires a right in the property adversely to the right of the certificate debtor. He gets a paramount title, which extinguishes the rights of the certificate debtor, or any one claiming through him, subject to some interests described in the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 20. The purchaser, of course, has the right to annul all encumbrances mentioned in the sub-section.</u>

13. Turning to the facts of the present case, we find that the certificate proceeding was initiated for the realization of arrears of rent, due to the Government Acquired Estate from Nalini and his wife. The consequences of the certificate proceeding therefore came under sub-section (3) of section 20. The plaintiff purchaser acquired a paramount title in the certificate sale. The certificate sale under sub-section (3), we have already observed, corresponds to rent decree in some cases, and the purchaser acquires an absolute title in the holding, except the protected interest described in the proviso to the sub-section (3), but with the right to annul the encumbrances in the manner prescribed under the Act. We are not concerned with any protected interest here. The defendant, no doubt claimed an under rayati right by virtue of a settlement from Nalini and his wife, the certificate debtors. But his claim has not succeeded, On the contrary, the ex-parte decree obtained by him in Title suit No. 730/62 on the basis of his settlement, has been found by the Courts below to be fraudulent and void, The defendant, therefore, has been found bereft of any legal title, or interest capable of protection under sub-section (3) of section 20. The High Court was in error in not looking at the true character of the certificate sale, and erroneously proceeded solely on the basis of sub-section (1) of section 20 of the Act, ignoring sub-section (3). Even under sub-section (1) the purchaser, as in a money decree, acquires the right, title and interest of the certificate debtor on date of the sale. The defendant however claimed a subordinate interest under the certificate debtors, but his claim was negatived by the courts below, His claim does not stand under any of the two sub-sections The concurrent findings of the two courts are that the defendant acquired no valid title in the certificate land, The certificate debtors being the sole tenants, and the plaintiff the sole purchaser of the certificate sale, he, under S. 20 (1) of the Act acquired the right, title and interest of the certificate-debtors, and in the present case the entire interest in the holdings in question, and the holdings also passed to the plaintiff under section 20(3) with right to annul the encumbrances.

<u>14. We now turn to the other part of the validity of the title of the plaintiff, on the basis of the sale, held on non-service of notice under S. 7. This calls for the consideration of section 36. The relevant portion for discussion may be set out: It says: Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, a sale of immovable property in execution of a certificate, shall not be held to be void, on the ground, that the notice required by section 7, has not been served; but, a suit may be brought, in a Civil Court to recover possession, of such property or to set aside such sale, on the ground, that such notice has not been served, and that the plaintiff has sustained substantial injury, by reason of irregularity : Provided, that no such suit shall be entertained: if instituted more than one year from the date on which the possession of properly was delivered to the purchaser, or if certificate debtor had appeared in the certificate proceeding or has applied to the certificate officer under section 22 or section 23 to set aside the sale.</u>

15. It is to be remembered that prior to the introduction of section 36 of the Act in 1913, there was conflict of judicial decisions on the effect of sale, in consequence of non-service of notice. One set of view was, that non-service of notice rendered the sale a nullity, and the other was, that it was an irregularity, and so the sale was voidable. The controversy has now been set at rest by section 36. It says that if notice required under section 7, has not been served, the certificate sale shall not be void, and subject to the proviso to section 3 6, the sale may be set aside, on the ground that such notice has not been served, and the plaintiff has sustained substantial injury due to the irregularity.

<u>16. The language employed by the Legislature is direct and negative. Attempt to put the language in positive terms, as many of the judicial decisions have done, will turn out to mean, that non-service of notice under section 7, makes a certificate sale voidable and not void. Though it is a convenient way of expressing the meaning of the section, it seems to us that it does not convey the true import. The language employed is negative to emphasise an affirmative. It first says, that for non-service of notice, the certificate sale shall not be void. By this negative language, what is being affirmed, is that the sale will be valid, subject to certain conditions given in the section. The condition is that the certificate debtor and his privy, can get the certificate sale set aside, by instituting a suit on ground of non-service of notice, within one year of the date of delivery of the properly, and that substantial injury has been sustained by him, by reasons of irregularity, and that the certificate debtor did not appear in the certificate proceeding, or apply for setting aside the sale under sections 22 or 23 before certificate officer.</u>

<u>17. The true import of the section is that the sale in a certificate proceeding for non-service of notice under section 7 is valid against the whole world for all times, and as against the certificate debtor, after a period of one year, from the date of delivery of properly to the purchaser, if no proceeding for setting aside the sale has been started in the meanwhile. The position is two fold: such sale is valid as against the whole world, except the certificate debtor, for all times, and against the certificate debtor, it is voidable for a limited period, and valid after the prescribed period. The purchaser may claim a valid title against the certificate debtor as well after the lapse of the period under section 36.</u>

<u>18. The language of section is such, that even a certificate debtor cannot challenge a certificate sale by way of defence, in a suit filed by the certificate purchaser to establish his title, nor can such title be collaterally challenged in another suit. We find that this view has been held by the two Division Benches of the Calcutta High Court, in Ananda Chandra Naudy vs. Anion Singh, 33 C.W.N. 305; and Sri Bansi Gopal Jin vs. Uday Chan A.I.R, 1954. Calcutta 113. Fraud; however, raises a different consideration as a vitiating factor, but that is not for our consideration in this case. We, therefore, find that the courts below were in error in allowing the defendant to raise by way of defence, the issue of non-service of notice in the certificate sale in the suit filed by the plaintiff, the certificate purchaser.</u>

19. We now propose to consider some of the decisions of the Dacca High Court, cited before us which require reconsideration of some of the legal propositions stated therein. First we take the case of Mohammad Moslem Ali Molla vs. Sk. Azaharali, P.L.R. 1957 Dacca 6, a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court. In that case, the dispute arose over a town property in the Dacca City situated at Bonogram lane. The plaintiff claimed the property on the basis of purchase from the certificate debtor, Kamini Kumar Mazumdar by a registered kabala dated March 23, 1952. The defendant resisted the claim, on the footing of purchase of properly in a certificate sale, held on 10th July, 1952. It is to be noted that the plaintiff purchased the properly after notice under section 7 of Act was said to have been served on June 6, 1951. The question principally turned on the voidness of the purchase of the plaintiff in terms of S. 8 of the Act. Incidentally section 36, and other sections of the Act were considered. Another question was the maintainability of the suit under section 37 of the Act. The High Court on evidence, held that there was fraud before, and after the sale, and so the title was found in favour of the private purchaser, the plaintiff. The conclusion of the High Court on the facts found by it, cannot be taken exception to, but while dealing with the question of non-service of notice under section 7 of the Act, an observation has been made, that rule 6(b) cannot be resorted to for service of notice under S. 7, and that the service of notice under rule 6(b) is non-service in the eye of law. We think, that this statement of law as to the interpretation of section 7, on the question of service of notice, is not sound. Section 7 says that when a certificate has been filed, a certificate officer, shall cause to be served upon the certificate debtor, in the prescribed manner, a notice in the prescribed form. The prescribed manner is to be found in rule 2 to 9 contained in Schedule II of the Act. A reading of the rules shows, that there must be an attempt to serve the notice directly on the certificate debtor in person. But there is also the alternative provision for service, by way of substituted service, if the attempt at personal service fails. That is contained in rule 6(a) and (b). It is to be observed that clauses (a) and (b) have been so worded; as to make them alternative subordinate clauses of the principal clause, embodied in rule 6, so that when the condition of the principal clause of rule 6 is satisfied, then one of the alternate clauses (a) or (b) can be resorted to, if the requirement of the alternative clauses, is fulfilled. Both the clauses prescribe the different modes of substituted service, For the application of rule 6(b), all that is necessary, is that, if there be land affected by the notice, alternative method of service under this clause can be resorted to. It is further to be remembered, that for the sale of immovable property affected by the certificate, specific rules have been provided in rules 23 and 46. It is also to be noted that in terms of section 8, immediately on the service of notice under section 7, transfer of immovable property of the certificate debtor within the district where certificate is filed, is prohibited amounting to an attachment of the properties ; and all his properties, wherever situated, are charged with certificate dues. In this view of the matter, so much of the decision in Mohammad Moslemali Molla's case which says, that rule 6(b) cannot be resorted to for service under section 7 of the Act, is not correct. For substituted service of notice under section 7 of the Act, both the alternate clauses (a) and (b) of rule 6 can be resorted to, according to the facts of each case.

<u>20. The other decision of the Dacca High Court, which calls for attention, is a decision of 4 single Judge in the case of Tarangini Devi vs. Govinda Mallik 9 D.L.R. 57. The decision arose out of a suit for setting aside the certificate sale, and the plaintiff claiming that her interest in the certificate sale had not been affected. A question arose, whether non-service of notice under section 7 makes the certificate sale a nullity. The learned Judge referred to the case of Puma Chandra vs. Dinabandha Mukherjee I.L.R. 34 Cal. 811, a decision of a Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court, and held that the non-service of notice under section 7, renders the certificate sale a nullity. It is to be noticed, that another Single Bench of the Dacca High Court, in the case of Abtabur Rahman vs. Madan Mia 19 D.L.R. 333. has not only taken a contrary view, but has dissented from the view taken in Tarangini Devi and held that non-service of notice under section 7, does not render the sale a nullity. We find that the Single Judge in Tarangini Devi, following the authority of Purna Chandra, held the sale to be a nullity because of non-service of notice. We have already referred to the legislative interference to settle the conflicting judicial decisions on this question. In Purna Chanda's case an observation of the Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court, is there calling for legislation, not only to resolve the conflict of decisions, but also to protect the auction purchaser from undue harassment and to safeguard his auction purchase. We have already given our interpretation to S. 36. We therefore find that Tarangini Devi 19 D.L.R, 57 is not a correct statement of law, whereas in Abtabur Rahman a correct view has been taken, in that non-service of notice does not render the sale a nullity. It is a valid sale unless set aside in the manner and within the recede prescribed by section 36.</u>

<u>21. We may now turn to the facts of the present case. The Trial Court has held that the notice under section 7, was not served personally upon the certificate debtor, but it was served on the land under rule 6(b), and such service is no service of notice at all, The Court of appeal below affirmed this finding, following the case of Tarangini Devi, and held that, it was a case of non-service and so the sale was void. It appears that the certificate proceeding was started by the Government Acquired Estate, for realisation of arreas of rent. Section 20(3) of the Act says, that when a proceeding under the Act, is taken for execution of a certificate for arrears of rent, the tenure or holding is to be sold, which means that the land is affected by the notice, and therefore, rule 6(b) can be resorted to, if personal service has failed. The order sheet of the certificate proceeding clearly shows that personal service of notice under section 7 of the Act had failed, and thereafter service of notice under rule 46 read with rule 6 (b) was resorted to. The Courts below were in error in not regarding this service as good service under section 7 of the Act. The learned Judges of the Dacca High Court, upon the facts found by the Courts below held that it was a case of non-service of notice, which makes a sale not void but voidable. The High Court committed a second error in so finding because two reasons: first, validity of a certificate sale cannot be challenged on the ground of non-service of notice under S. 7 by way of defence, and secondly, even if there has been non-service of notice, the certificate sale is valid, unless it set aside in the prescribed manner and within the period contained in S. 36 of the Act. Apart from the two grounds, the High Court perpetuated the error of the Courts below in treating the substituted service under rules 6 (b) as non-service.</u>

<u>22. We now take the second ground of the leave order: whether the High Court was justified in refusing the plaintiff-appellant's prayer for amendment of the plaint to and the prayer of recovery of possession. The reasons given by the High Court were, that the move was belated, and the plaintiff purchased the holding of 1.72 acres, at a sum of Rs. 95/. Mr Nurullah citing the case of Keramat Ali Vs. Muhammad Yunus, 51 DLR (S.C) 120 has submitted that the reasons for refusal do not find support from recognised judicial authority. We find the submission of Mr. Nurulla, is well founded. The Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the cited decision, has repeated the principle laid down by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, It is the consistent view of judicial authorities, that amend Bents of the pleadings are allowed, even when a legal right had accrued to the other party, if special circumstances of the case outweigh such consideration. In exercising this power, the Court would no doubt, be reluctant to allow such an amendment, which would have the effect of totally altering nature of the suit; or take away a valuable right accrued by lapse of time, but where in the circumstances of the particular case, it would be plainly inequitable to refuse such a relief, the court will not hesitate to act. The Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the cited case allowed the amendment of the plaint. The learned Judges of the High Court were of the view, that the prayer was belated, but overlooked the fact that obviously, the prayer was made at a time when prima facie, the other side might not have acquired any right by lapse of time. Secondly, the prayer did not change the nature of the suit. What was prayed for was more of a consequential relief following the declaration of the title. The second reason of the High Court, though not articulated, is the low price given for the certificate purchased land, Mere low price in the absence of any proof of fraud, cannot be a ground for denial of a legitimate prayer. In our judgment, therefore, the High Court was not justified in refusing the prayer for amendment of the plaint.</u>

<u>23. We therefore conclude that the plaintiff has acquired a valid title by his auction purchase, and the defendant cannot challenge by way of defence the validity of the certificate sale on the ground of non-service of notice under section 7, The substituted service under rule 6(b) is due service of notice under the said section, The findings of the Courts below that the defendant has failed to establish his settlement from Nalini and Sarala and that the ex-parte decree of his Title Suit No 730 of 1962 is fraudulent and void are affirmed.</u>

24. In the result the appeal is allowed. with the above finding, the decisions of the courts below are set aside in part, and the case remitted back to trial Court for allowing the plaintiff- appellant to amend his pleading, by adding the prayer for recovery of possession on payment of proper court fees. The defendant shall be at liberty to file additional written statement, the court below shall decide the question of the recovery of possession by the plaintiff, and the ancillary question of adverse possession of the defendant, if so raised. The question will be decided on the evidence on record. The court shall, however, be at liberty to allow such additional evidence, if the parties pray and the court thinks fit to allow. The prayer for amendment if not made within three weeks of the arrival of the records in the court below, the shall be dismissed with cost. The cost of this appeal shall abide the result of the suit.

End.
