full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against an order of a Bench of the High Court Division, dismissing summarily an application filed by the appellant under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, challenging the validity of the two orders passed by the Court of the Subordinate Judge of Khulna in a proceeding under Order 33, Rule 1 of the Code, instituted by Respondent No. 1, by which the proceeding in execution of a decree obtained by the appellant against Respondent No. 1 and 2 was stayed.

2. The appellant instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Khulna, being Title Suit No. 1000 of 1966 for specific performance of a contract for sale of land against Respondents No. 1 and 2, the two brothers, who appeared in the suit and filed two separate written statement's, but both of them having failed to appear at the time of the hearing the suit was decreed exparte on 18-4-68. Respondent No. 1 thereafter filed an application for setting aside the said exparte decree under order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure being Miscellaneous Case No. 187 of 1968, which was ultimately dismissed for default. An appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 107 of 1969 which was filed by Respondent No. 1 against the aforesaid order of dismissal of the Miscellaneous Case was also dismissed for default on 1-4-70. Respondent No. 1, however started a proceeding being Miscellaneous Case No. 237 of 1970 under Order 41 rule 19 of the Cede for the restoration of his Miscellaneous Appeal, which was earlier dismissed for default, but the said Miscellaneous case also was dismissed for default on 26-6-71. The said Miscellaneous Case was, however, subsequently restored to the under the provision of President's Order No. 12 of 1972 and was ultimately allowed on 29-11-72 restoring the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 107 of 1969 to file. The appellant having moved the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code against the said order of restoration, a Rule being Civil Rule No. 160 of 1972 was issued and the said Rule was ultimately made absolute on 11-4-74, setting aside the order of restoration of the Miscellaneous Appeal and dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 237 of 1970. The appellant, in the meantime, got the requisite deed of sale executed and registered through Court in Title Execution Case No. 69 of 1970 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Khulna, and thereafter started Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1971 in the same Court for obtaining delivery of possession of the decretal land under the decree for specific performance of contract, the proceeding of which was stayed pending the disposal of Miscellaneous Case No. 237 of 1970 and of Civil Rule No. 160 of 1970. After the disposal of the Civil Rule by the High Court the order of stay was vacated and the proceeding in the Title Execution case was resumed.

3. On 18-3-75 Respondent No. 1 filed an application under Order 33, rule 1 of the code for permitting the appellant to sue as a pauper for setting aside the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No. 1000 of 1966 on 18-4-68 and the said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 95 of 1975 without any examination of the said applicant in person. On the same day an order was passed in the said Miscellaneous case, staying further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1971. A petition of objection having been filed to the said order of stay by the appellant, the learned Subordinate Judge passed another order on 2-6-75, staying the proceeding in the Execution Case till the disposal of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case on the alleged grounds of ends of justice and balance of convenience.

4. The High Court Division, being moved under section 115 of the Code against the said two orders of stay, refused to interfere with the said two orders on the view that the learned Subordinate Judge had given sufficient reasons for passing the said orders and summarily rejected the appellant's application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. Special leave to appeal was granted to consider the principle under which a Court may pass an order staying the progress of a collateral proceeding and also the question whether the impugned orders of stay of the execution case were correctly passed.

6. For a proper understanding of the questions involved in this case it is necessary to examine the nature of the claim raised, in the proposed suit sought to be prosecuted by Respondent No. 1 as a pauper under Order 33, rule 1 of the Code. The claim in the said suit is stated to be one for setting aside the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No. 1000 of 1966 and the grounds, as alleged in the proposed plaint, are, in brief, that there was no agreement for sale of land between the appellant and Respondent No. 1, that the appellant could not produce any credible evidence in support of his false claim, that because of certain circumstances the said Respondent could not appear at the time of the hearing of the suit and that the said Respondent was a simple-minded illiterate man, who could not appear also in Miscellaneous Case No. 187 of 1968 and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 107 of 1969, both of which had been dismissed in the absence of both the parties.

7. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, learned .Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant, who is the decree holder in the execution case, has submitted that, having regard to the averments made in the proposed plaint in the suit, for the prosecution of which in foil pauper is permissive has been sought by Respondent No. 1 under Order 33, rule 1 of the Code, the said suit, on the face of it, is not maintainable and the learned Subordinate Judge trying the Respondent's application under Order 33, rule I of the Code exceeded his jurisdiction in staying the execution proceeding till the disposal of the Miscellaneous case under Order 33 of the Code. Learned Counsel has further submitted that there are no provisions in the Code empowering the Court to stay, in the circumstances of the case, the progress of the proceeding in execution of a valid decree of a Court and that, in view of the facts of this case, the Court cannot be held to be justified in invoking his inherent jurisdiction to do justice for the purpose of staying the proceeding of the execution case.

There having been no appearance on behalf of the Respondent in this Case, we have ourselves tried to examine the question rather closely.

8. One of the basic principle underlying the judicial procedures followed in this country is the conclusiveness of the final decision of a Court in a suit or other judicial proceeding relating to a disputed question of right so far as the parties to the said suit or proceeding are concerned subject to the scrutiny by a superior court, if so provided by law. The correctness or propriety of such a decision cannot be raised by any parties thereto in any collateral proceeding or a proceeding in, execution thereof. Another principle of equal importance is the exclusive jurisdiction of a judicial tribunal over the proceedings arising or pending before it subject to some kind of control by superior courts as provided by law. According to the said principle, a proceeding in execution pending before a Court can be stayed or otherwise interfered with by the said court or by a superior court under certain conditions prescribed by law. The question of stay of any execution proceeding ordinarily arises when the correctness or propriety of the decree or the order under execution is put under a challenge, in a superior court by way of appeal.

<u>9. Provisions have been made in rule 5 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure for stay of execution of a decree or order on a sufficient cause being shown, in case of an appeal preferred against the said decree or an order by the appellate Court, and before the filing of the appeal but before the expiration of the period of limitation for filing such appeal, by the Court which passed the decree or order. According to the said provision, stay or execution of the decree or order shall not, however, be granted as a matter of course. Before granting such stay, the Court concerned shall have to be satisfied, as has been provided in sub-rule (3) of the said Rule (a) that substantial loss may result to the party applying for stay unless the order is made, (b) that the application has been made without unreasonable delay and (c) that security has been given by the applicant for the due performance of such decree or order as may ultimately be binding upon him. These provisions make it abundantly clear that ordinarily the mandate of the Court as contained in the decree or order under execution shall be carried out and that the execution of the said decree or order shall not be interfered with merely because an appeal has been preferred against it. The party praying for stay shall have to make out a special case for stay of the execution in terms of the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 5 as has been mentioned above. Rule 6, sub-rule (2) of Order 41 provides for stay of sale of immovable property in execution of a decree against which an appeal has been preferred, by the Court which passed the decree, under certain conditions as to giving security or otherwise as the Court thinks fit, till the disposal of the appeal.</u>

10. The provision of Order 21, rule 26 of the Code seems to be ancillary to the provisions of Order 41, rules 5 and 6 of the Code and makes provision for stay of execution of decree by a Court to which the decree has been sent for execution in order to enable the judgment-debtor to obtain the necessary order of stay of execution or any other order relating thereto from the Court which passed the decree or the Court having appellate jurisdiction in respect of the decree or the execution thereof.

<u>11. From the provisions referred to above, the principle which appears to have weighed with the legislature in making those provisions appears 10 be clearly expressed therein showing that ordinarily a decree-holder should not be deprived of the fruits of his decree even though the correctness of the decree has been challenged or intended to be challenged in an appeal to a superior Court for final determination of the question. The Court concerned has no doubt been given discretion to stay the execution proceeding till the disposal of the appeal but it shall have to be satisfied on sufficient cause being shown by the appellant as to the propriety of such stay and a rigorous test has been laid down in sub-rule (3) of rule 5 of Order 41 requiring the satisfaction of the court on the conditions mentioned therein.</u>

12. Mr. N. U. Haider, learned Counsel for the appellant, has contended that, no appeal against the decree under execution having been preferred, the only manner in which the Court trying the application of the respondent under Order 33, rule 1 in Miscellaneous Case No. 95 of 1975 could have stayed further progress of the execution proceeding was by an order in the nature of temporary injunction restraining the decree-holder from proceeding with the said execution, but that such an order could have been passed only when the Court was satisfied that all the conditions for granting such as injunction as to prima facie case, irreparable injury to the judgment-debtor and balance of convenience had been in existence. Learned Counsel has submitted that the proposed suit being not maintainable on the face of the averments made in the application of the respondent under Order 33, rule 1 of the Code, there was no prima facie case in favour of the respondent and the learned Subordinate Judge acted without jurisdiction in staying the executing proceeding without coming to necessary findings for the said purpose.

<u>13. It is no doubt correct that when a Court wants to stay the proceeding in execution of a decree, the validity of which is under investigation in an independent suit instituted in a court of co-ordinate jurisdiction, it can do so only by restraining the decree-holder, if he is a party before it, by means of a temporary injunction in exercise of its inherent powers under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as the Provisions of Order 39 of the Code do not generally apply in terms of such a case. Since such an action can be taken in exercise of its inherent power, the Court shall have to be satisfied about the justice of the case, namely, that the general conditions for granting temporary injunction as have been laid down by the judicial authorities are in existence.</u>

14. We do not, however, think that it is a proper case where the provisions of Order 39 relating to temporary injunction, read with section 151 of the Code, are attracted. It is the provision of Order 21, rule 29 of the Cede which appears to have relevance for the purpose of stay of the proceeding in execution in the instant case. The provision of this rule is to the following effect:

"Where a suit is pending in any Court against the holder of a decree of such Court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the Court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise, as it thinks fit, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided."

15. This is the specific provision as to stay of a proceeding in execution of a decree in a suit brought by the judgment-debtor against the holder of the decree, pending in the same Court. The nature of the suit as has been referred to in the said rule in a very general term, has not been sufficiently explained, but it is obvious that it must necessarily be of those kinds which when decided, would affect the execution or the manner of execution of the decree which is being sought to be executed. The suit may be one for nullifying the earlier decree altogether or may be one which, though unconnected with the earlier decree, is what has been referred to as a cross-decree in rule 18 of Order 21 of the Code. In the former case, the earlier decree becomes null and void and as such the execution proceeding also becomes a nullity ; in the latter, the validity of the execution proceeding is not affected but the decree under execution becomes liable to be adjusted in the manner as laid down in the said rule 18 of Order 21 of the Code. In the event of full or partial execution of the decree, therefore, the subsequent passing of a decree in the later suit in both cases is likely to lead to multiplicity of litigations, causing harassment, unnecessary expenses and waste of time to the parties concerned. There is no doubt, therefore, that a very salutary provision has been made in the said rule 29 of Order 21. Since the suit is pending in the same Court in which the proceeding in execution has been laid, there is no difficulty for the Court to stay the execution in an appropriate case till the decision in the pending suit, as it will be staying the proceeding of its own Court. There is no necessity for such a Court for taking recourse to the provisions relating to temporary injunction for restraining the party concerned from prosecuting the proceeding.

<u>16. It may, however, be contended that the aforesaid provision of rule 29 of Order 21 cannot be invoked in the instant case as a mere application for permission to sue as a pauper is pending decision as to whether such permission would at all be granted and there has not as yet been any suit pending in the Court where the execution has been laid. There is no doubt that the said provision is not attracted in terms in this case, as formally there cannot be any pending suit within the meaning of the Code before the application for permission under Order 33 has been allowed. But since the application of the judgment debtor for permission to sue for setting aside the decree under execution as a pauper itself shall be numbered and registered as a suit and shall be deemed to be the plaint in that suit in accordance with the pro-vision of rule 8 of Order 33, the principle underlying the provision of Order 21 rule 29 of the Code may very well be invoked in the instant case in the interests of justice under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the purpose of stay of execution of the decree, for the setting aside of which the application under Order 33 has been made, if the Court is satisfied that the exercise of its inherent powers is likely to advance the cause of justice or prevent an abuse of its process.</u>

<u>17. The authority which has been given to a Court under Order 21, rule 29 of the Code, to stay an execution proceeding is, no doubt, discretionary and there are no express provisions in the rule making the use of such authority subject to certain positive conditions, as have been made in Order 41, rule 5 of the Code, but the condition in Order 21, rule 29, that the order of stay is to be made on such terms as to security or otherwise as the Court thinks fit makes it abundantly clear that the Court shall have to apply its judicial mind in making the order of stay for the purpose of protecting the interests of the decree-holder. Moreover, it is a settled principle, that the discretion of a court, the exercise of which is likely to affect a valuable right of a person acquired under the law of the country, must be exercised judicially and for the said purpose, the Court must be satisfied that there are very good reasons for withholding from the holder of the decree the fruits thereof, even though for a temporary period. The fundamental consideration is that the mandate of the Court as contained in a decree must not be lightly ignored or evaded to the prejudice of its holder. But if from the facts of the case the Court is satisfied that there are good reasons to suppose that the judgment-debtor is likely to succeed in his suit and that in case of such success the execution of the decree against him may result in multiplicity of litigations, entailing costs and harassment to the parties concerned, the Court may, as the Rule provides, stay the execution of the decree, on such terms as to security or otherwise, as the court thinks fit till the decision in the said suit. In the case of a proceeding under Order 33 of the Code, which has not as yet ripened into a suit, the same principle may be followed by the Court for the purpose of staying an execution proceeding in exercise of its inherent powers.</u>

18. It does not appear that the Court of the Subordinate Judge applied its judicial mind at all to the facts of the case for the ascertainment of the conditions under which a lawful decree of a court may justifiably be stayed till the decision of the pending proceeding. The Court appears to have mechanically passed the order of stay without being satisfied as to whether the execution of the decree could appropriately be stayed in consonance with the principle of justice of the case. If the Court concerned properly examined the nature of the allegations made in the application of Respondent No. 1 under Order 33, rule 1 of the Code, impugning the correctness or propriety of the decree under execution, it could very easily see that the suit contemplated in the said application, which seeks to undo the impugned decree on the ground that it was obtained on the basis of a false claim in the absence of the said respondent who was prevented by illness from contesting the suit, had, prima facie little chance of success and that in the said circumstance the stay of the execution proceeding was not likely to serve the ends of justice. The order of stay granted by the Court is, therefore, clearly unsustainable.

The appeal is, therefore, allowed and the orders of stay passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside. There shall, however, be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree dismissing a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. The plaintiff, dinned to be a co-sharer and an attorney for other co-sharers and as such, was in possession of the disputed land and has been dispossessed by the defendants who had neither title nor possession in the suit land. According to the plaintiff, the defendants dispossessed him on 7.12.66. The instant suit was filed on 10.5.67.

2. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 denying the material allegations made in the plaint. According to the contesting defendants, the plaintiff was not in possession of the disputed land and the same vested in the custodian as Enemy Property. It was further centered that the suit was bad for defect of parties and was barred by limitation and under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The defendants contended that they have been possessing the land on taking settlement from the custodian of Enemy Property. Issues were framed reflecting the contentions of the parties who adduced evidence in support of their respective cases.

3. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit holding inter alia that it is an admitted fact that the defendants entered into the suit properties on 7. 12.66 and it is also an admitted fact that the present plaintiff filed T. S. No. 83 of 1966 in the court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet for the suit properties along with other properties, but in that suit the present defendants had not been made parties. The learned Munsif was of the view that the "plaintiffs has got no locus standi to file the suit because his very foundation of claim has been removed. Moreover the parties of T. S. No 83 of 1966 are necessary in this suit. So, the suit is bad for defect of parties according to me. Defendant No.3 is unable to show me that he was given possession of the suit properties by the custodian of the Enemy Properties on the date of his entry in the suit properties. His alleged leases are subsequent to the date of entry. So, according to me he entered into the suit and illegally and by dispossession"

According to the learned Munsif Ext.B, the certified copy of the plaint in T.S. 83 of 1966 indicates the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land as an attorney and not as a co-sharer.

4. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule contends that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in dismissing the suit; According to the learned Advocate, the learned Munsif, having found possession of the plaintiff within six months of the date of the suit and also that the defendants entered into the suit land illegally and by dispossession, acted illegally and with material irregularity in refusing a decree in favour of the plaintiff upon erroneous views and misconceived grounds. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman has pointed out with reference to the pleadings and the evidence on record that the plaintiff was a co-sharer along with others in respect of the suit properties. He was also acting as an attorney of the co-sharers. The learned Munsif was of the view that since the power of attorney executed by the co-shares ceased to be a valid document after promulgation of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964, the plaintiff had no locus standi to present the interest of the absentee co-sharer as their attorneys According to Mr. Rafiqur Rahman the plaintiff's assertion that he was in possession of the suit property as a co-sharer was not negative by any evidence of the defendants. In the absence of any evidence indicating partition of the properties by metes and bounds, the interest of a co-sharer remains unaffected and it is not liable to be defeated at the instance of trespasser. The mere fact that the plaintiff was also an attorney for his co-sharers did not wash out his individual character as a co-sharer in possession of the suit land. In the circumstances, Mr. Rahrnan contends that the learned Munsif acted illegally in the exercise of jurisdiction in holding that the very foundation of the plaintiff's claim has been removed by Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. Mr. Rahman further contends that Ordinance No.1 of 1964 was void and dead for all purposes.

5. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties contends that the learned Munsif, although wrote but a cryptic judgment, was perfectly within his jurisdiction in refusing the decree for recovery of possession since the property in suit was enemy property. According to the learned Advocate as soon as this was brought to the notice of the Court that the disputed property was an Enemy Property, the court lost its jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter. There is no finding by the learned Munsif that the property in question is Enemy Property. The documents filed by the defendants do not indicate that at the material time the custodian was in possession of the suit property. The learned Munsif did not find the Custodian or the defendants in possession of the suit land before the dispossession. Further, it is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Khan that the mere allegation that the disputed property is Enemy Property ousts the jurisdiction of the Court. Mr. Khan could not cite any authority in support of his contention.

6. Mr. Khan next contends that the learned Munsif was correct in holding that She suit was bad for defect of parties. The instant suit is against defendants allegedly dispossessed the plaintiff on 7.12.66. The alleged act of dispossession is an independent act giving rise to the cause of action for the instant suit. The persons who dispossessed the plaintiff are the only necessary parties in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of khas possession. The contention that the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 83 of 1966 on 24-5-66 against certain officers of the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan and as such, these impleaded in Title Suit No. 83 of 1966 are necessary parties in the suit appears to be misconceived. The cause of action for the said Title Suit No. 83 of 1966 was completely different and had no connection whatsoever with the subsequent suit filed on 10.5.67 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. It could not be pointed out by Mr. Khan that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, these officers of the erstwhile Province of East Pakistan are necessary parties to the present action. In that suit the instant defendants were not impleaded since there was no overt act by these defendants when the cause for that suit arose. Mr. Khan has further urged that the defendants entered into possession of the suit land days before the alleged date of dispossession on the assurance of some officers of the then Government. There is no material on record to support this contention. In the written statement filed by the defendants, it has been stated that the application of the defendants for settlement was under investigation. It has been clearly stated that the defendant No. 1 entered into possession of the suit properties on 8.12.66. In the affidavit in opposition before this court it has been stated that" this deponent filed applications before the Sub-Divisional Officer, Moulvi Bazar on 30.11.66 stating that the suit homestead is lying vacant and the same may be settled with this deponent. That on receipt of this application, the Sub-divisional Officer, Moulvi Bazar asked this deponent to occupy that house provisionally pending final allotment by the authorities to whom his application has already been forwarded and as such on 7.12.66 the petitioners' family entered into the house and has been staying thereafter reconstructing the house." Thus from the written statement as also the affidavit-in-opposition, it appears that before 7.12.66 the defendants were not in possession of the disputed property which is a homestead and a tank. Mr. Khan has also drawn the attention of the court to Exhibit E, a Memo granted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dated 192-68 granting settlement in favour of Shamsur Rahman from 1-1-67 to 31.12.67. This appears to be the basis of defendants entry into the suit land. This document conclusively indicates that before 19.2.68 the day on which it was issued, Shamsur Rahman was not authorised in law to enter into possession of the properties in suit. In the circumstances the finding of the learned Munsif that the defendant entered into the suit land illegally and by dispossession is proved by Ext. E the basis document of the contesting defendants. There is nothing on record to indicate that on or before 7.12.66 the suit property was in possession of the custodian as Enemy Property and that the defendants acquired lawful authority to enter into the same. It is necessary to remember the language of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act which is in the following terms:-

"If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immoveable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him any, by suit recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit"

<u>7. It, therefore, appears that on the date of dispossession the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff "otherwise than in due course of law". The subsequent acquisition of title if any, by way of lease from Enemy Property authority did not validate the illegal dispossession by the defendants. Mr. Khan could not point out any authority in support of his contention that the subsequent lease validated the invalid entry. In the circumstances, Mr. Khan's contentions do not appear to be of substance for maintaining the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif, Mr. Khan however relied upon the decision in the case of Abdul Jameel Vs. Harun 21 D.L.R.(WP)293 where it has been held that before a person can come under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act he has to show that he had actual physical possession of the immoveable property from which he was dispossessed without his consent by the defendants within six months prior to the institution of the suit. There is no finding by the learned. Munsif that the plaintiff was not in actual physical possession of the suit land within six months prior the institution of the suit to Mr. Khan could not point out any evidence to that effect. Since the plaintiff is to succeed on the strength of his own case, he has to prove that he was in actual physical possession of the immoveable property from which he was dispossessed by the defendants. The plaintiff has proved his actual physical possession on or before the alleged date of dispossession and within six months prior to institution of the suit. The defendants, on the other hand, failed to prove that they had any possession on or before the date of dispossession. The learned Munsif has clearly found that the defendants entered into the suit land illegally and by dispossession. Appreciating the inherent weakness of the defence case Mr. Khan ultimately prayed for a remand of the matter to the learned Munsif. In making this prayer the learned Advocate submits that the learned Munsif should write out a proper judgment on application of mind to the materials on record. This indicates that the judgment of the learned Munsif was not a proper judgment based on consideration of the materials on record. There is no grievance that the suit suffered from paucity of evidence. The evidence on record is apparently sufficient for disposal of the instant suit. Thus, on the materials on record, Mr. Khan finds it difficult to press for a remand seriously.</u>

<u>8. The materials on record disclose that the plaintiff's possession as a co-sharer was not disputed. There is no evidence to indicate that the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendants. The learned Munsif has found on consideration of evidence that the defendants "entered into the suit land illegally and by dispossession,." There is no dispute that the suit is in time, as observed earlier, the defendants of Title Suit No, 83 of 1966 are not necessary parties in the instant suit. The learned Munsif refused a decree in favour of the plaintiff because of "legal difficulties." According to the learned Munsif the "legal difficulties" were (1) plaintiff has got no locus standi to file the suit because his very foundation of claim has been removed." and (2) "the parties of T. S. No. 83 of 1966 are necessary in this suit, So, the suit is bad for defect of parties" Mr. T.H. Khan did not challenge that the plaintiff is a co-sharer in the suit land because of the obvious reason that there was no materials before the trial court indicating that the plaintiff was not a co-sharer in possession of the suit land. The trial court did not also characterise him as such. According to the learned Munsif, the power of attorney became invalid due to Ordinance I of 1964 and as such the plaintiff had to locus standi to file the suit. In fact of the instant case, Ordinance I of 1964 has no role to play since the plaintiff is a cc-sharer in possession of the suit land. The part attributed to Ordinance I of 1964 by the learned Munsif is apparently misconceived. Ordinance I of 1964 being a post Constitutional law was violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution and was dead for all purposes. Reference way profitably be made to the case of Abdul Majid Bepari Vs Kashem Ali Maloo XXVII Dacca Law Reports 1 (High Court Division,) where East Pakistan Ordinance I of 1964 (E. P. Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, has been found to be dead for all purposes and void abinitin. In the circumstances, it does not appear that there is any legal bar for the plaintiff in getting a decree for recovery of khas possession after evicting the defendants from the suit land.</u>

9. An application fox additional evidence has been filed in this Court by the opposite parties. In the exercise of revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Court does not require additional evidence for disposal the instant rule.

10. The fact of dispossession having been clearly found by the learned Munsif and this finding being supported by the materials on record the contention of Mr. Rafiqur Rahman that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in refusing a decree to the plaintiff appears to be of substance.

For the reasons stated above, the Rule is made absolute with costs assessed at five gold Mohars. The judgment and decree of the learned Munsif are set aside and the suit is decreed with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This rule under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act is directed against an order dated 10.1.74 of the learned S.C.C. Judge in Misc. Case No. 524/73 under Order 9 Rule 13 and 151, C.P.C. for setting aside an ex-parte decree dated 12.9.73.

2. The plaintiff filed S.C.C. Suit No. 5/73 for ejectment of the defendant who was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit premises. The defendant filed a written statement, but ultimately did not appear on the date of hearing and as such the suit was decreed exparte on 12.9.73. On 15.9.73 an application under Order 9 Rule 13 and section 151 C.P.C. was filed for restoration of the S.C.C. suit on set-ting aside the exparte decree. On the same day, the defendant filed a petition praying for stay of operation of the exparte decree or stay of further proceedings of the execution case, if any, filed by the plaintiff decree holder till the disposal of the Misc. case. The learned S.C.C. Judge stayed further proceedings of the execution case by order No. 21 dated 15.9.73. On the same day, another application was filed by the defendant praying for time to furnish security bond. The prayer was allowed granting time till 25.9.73 for furnishing security bond. The defendant after taking time on various occasions, ultimately furnished security bond on 24.11.73 along with a petition showing cause for the delay in filing the security bond and prayed for acceptance thereof. The plaintiff also filed a petition for rejecting the security bond. An application under section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed by the defendant on 29.12.73 explaining the delay in filing the security bond. The plaintiff filed a counter-affidavit denying the material statements made by the defendant in the petition under section 5 of the Limitation Act. The matter came up for hearing before the learned S.C.C. Judge on 10.1.74.

3. The learned S. C. C. Judge took up the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act together with the counter-affidavit filed by the plaintiff and on hearing the parties, rejected the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act and by the same order dis-missed the Misc. case No. 524 of 1973.

4. According to the learned S.C.C. Judge the application u/s. 5 of the Limitation Act was misconceived and malafide. Since the defendant failed to furnish security bond in terms of section 17 of the S.C.C. Act in time, the application under Order 9 rule 13. C.P.C. was not maintainable. The learned S.C.C. Judge was of the view that "no useful purpose can be served by allowing this petition under section 5 of the Limitation Act." In that view of the matter the application was rejected. The learned S. C. C. Judge also rejected the petition under Order 9 rule 13. C.P.C. being of the view that the same was not maintainable.

5. Mr. Syed J. R. M. Hussain. the learned Advocate appearing in support of the rule contends that the learned S.C.C. Judge was wrong in rejecting the application u/s 5 of the Limitation Act. According to the learned Advocate sufficient cause was made out in the 'application u/s. 5 of the Limitation Act for not furnishing the security bend in time. The learned Advocate further contends that noncompliance of sub-section (1) of section 17 of Small Cause Courts Act does not vitiate an application under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. Since in a suit for ejectment under S.C.C. Act, the defendant is not required to deposit in court the amount due under the decree.

6. The question whether section 17(1) of the S.C.C. Act has any part to play in a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. arising out of an ex-parte decree in a suit for ejectment of the defendant appears to be of considerable legal importance. Section 17(1) of the S.C.C. runs as follows:—

"The procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall, save in so far as is otherwise provided by that Code or by this act, be the procedure followed in a Court of Small Causes Act in all suits cognizable by it and in all proceedings arising out of such suits:

Provided that an applicant for an order to set aside a decree passed ex-parte or for a review of judgment shall at the time of presenting his application, either deposit in the Court the amount due for him under the decree or in pursuance of the judgment, or give such security for the performance of the decree or compliance with the judgment as the Court may, on a previous application made by him in this behalf, have directed".

Controversy arose over the interpretation of above provision and divergent views were expressed. The first view or the wide view was expressed in the Full Bench case of Gedi Mal Vs. Hana Mal AIR 1931 Lahore 334. According to this view the expression: "at the time of presenting his application" is incompatible with the words "as the Court may direct." Accordingly, it was held that the provision of section 17(1) must be taken as merely directory or recommendatory and not mandatory and the court has discretion to extend the period for making the deposit or furnishing security. The second view is that the provisions contained in the proviso to section 17(1) are mandatory. According to this view the legislature intended to make it a condition precedent to the granting of a fresh trial to any applicant that he should, at the time of his making the application, deposit the decretal amount or furnish security for the payment of the same and an application is not entertainable unless the amount was deposited or security furnished along with the application. According to this view the failure to deposit or furnish security along with the application cannot be cured by subsequent compliance. In the case of Jogi Ahir Vs. Bipin Dayal Singh I.L.R. 18 Calcutta 83, it was held that the requirement of the proviso to section 17(1) of the S. C. C. Act is a condition precedent to the granting of a new trial. In the case of Sri Bhagawat Chaudhury Vs. Balkaran AIR 1922 Allahabad 29, it has been held that the application to set aside an exparte decree unaccompanied by deposit required by the proviso to section 17(1) of the Act amounted to non-compliance with the requirement of law and the same was not cured by subsequent deposit within the period of limitation prescribed for setting aside an ex-parte decree. The case Vembu Amal Vs. Esakkin Pillai AIR 1949 Madras 419 also indicates that the requirements of section 17(1) of the act are mandatory. The third view is available in some of the earlier cases decided by the Calcutta High Court. In the case of Bashiruddin Vs. Sanaullah 15 C.W.N. 102 it has been held that if the deposit is made or the security is furnished before the application was rejected and within time prescribed by the law of limitation for making an application, such deposit or security may be regarded as substantial compliance of the requirements of law. In the case of Jagadish Pramanik and others Vs. Mahadev AIR 1953 Allahabad 758, it has been held that the security bond if presented after the expiry of the period of limitation, the application for setting aside the exparte decree must be rejected since it amounts to non-compliance with the provision of section 17(1) of the Act. Relying upon the decision in the case of Abdul Sheikh Vs. Md. Ayub 24 C.W.N. 380 it was held in the case of Misa Pramanik Vs. Khatu Saner 24 C.W.N. (2 D.L.R.) 67 that on the last date of limitation an application was filed without deposit or furnishing security and the security was furnished after the expiry of limitation, the application under Order 9 rule 13 was barred by limitation. In the case of Jagadamba Prasad Vs. Ram Das AIR 1943 Allahabad 228, it has been held that the proviso is mandatory and either the deposit of the decretal amount or the security as directed by the court upon a previous application must be made for that purpose. In the case of Kripa Sankar Bramha AIR 1955 Allahabad 282, it has been held the requirements of section 17(1) of the Act are evidently complied with if the application for setting aside the exparte decree is accompanied by either cash deposit or security bond to safeguard in the interest of the decree holder.

<u>7. On a careful consideration of the views variously expressed by the different High Courts before and after the amendment of 1935, it appears that the requirements of the proviso to section 17(1) are mandatory and either deposit of the decretal amount or security for performance of the decree or compliance with the judgment as the court may direct on a previous application made by the applicant in that behalf, at the time of presenting the application for setting aside an exparte decree are the essentials to be complied with. In respectful agreement with the view expressed in the Full Bench decision of Madras High Court in the case of Kalapati Feda Pitchamma and another Vs. Chiravella Pedammeyya and another AIR 1935 Madras 380. it may be saki, that the proviso "only cut down the very wide discretion which the courts have under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C., in setting aside exparte decree and in imposing terms upon the petitioner. Under the above proviso the petitioner should either deposit the decree amount or give security. No other alternative such as that no condition need be imposed at all is allowed."</u>

<u>8. Mr. Hussain, however, contends that by the amendment of 1962 a suit for ejectment was brought within the scope of the S.C.C. Act. According to the learned Advocate there may not be any amount due under the decree in a suit for ejectment of a monthly tenant and as such a deposit contemplated under section 17(1) of the Act is not called for. Evidently in a suit for ejectment there is no amount due under the decree except the costs if any, but section 17(1) of the Act is comprehensive enough to require security "for the performance of the decree or compliance with the judgment as the court may, on a previous application made by him in this behalf, have directed". It is difficult to conceive that the defendant has nothing to perform under an exparte decree or to comply with the judgment. Since in a suit for ejectment of the defendant, the exparte decree directs the defendant to vacate the premises, the defendant thus becomes bound under the decree for its performance or compliance with the judgment. In that view of the matter in a suit for ejectment of the defendant although a deposit of the decretal amount may not be necessary, but a security for the performance of the decree or compliance with the judgment appears to be the mandate of the proviso to section 17(1) of the Act. In the circumstances, Mr. Hussain finds it difficult to press his contention further.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Hussain has however, argued that in the facts and circumstances of the case the learned S.C.C. Judge should, have held that due compliance of section 17(1) of the Act has been made since the defendant has already furnished security bond in the court and by an application u/s 5 of the Limitation Act, has prayed for condonation of the delay. The record discloses that the application under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. was filed on 15.9.73 and an application was filed for time to furnish security bond: and that application was allowed granting time upto 25.9.73 for furnishing security bond. The security bond was however, furnished on 14.11.73 upon a direction by the court to show cause why the Misc. case should not be rejected for the default to furnish security bond. In the application u/s. 5 of the Limitation Act, the circumstances for the delay in filing the security bond have been sufficiently explained. In paragraph 3 of the petition it has been clearly stated that due to the wrong advice of his former advocate, the security bond was not furnished along with the application and time was prayed for filing the security bond. In paragraph 4 it has been stated that the said advocate returned the brief to the defendant only on 24.11.73 and on that very day the defendant engaged another learned advocate who, on inspection of the record, advised the defendant to furnish security bond forthwith. In the circumstances, the delay was caused. The reasons for the delay have been elaborately and frankly disclosed by the defendant in the said petition. In the affidavit-in-opposition, the material facts have been controverted and it has been slated that the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay in filing security bond was not maintainable. Mr. Hussain, the learned Advocate has placed the petition for condonation of delay and contends that in the facts and circumstances bonafide disclosed therein, the compliance with the requirements of section 17(1) of the Act by furnishing a security bond in court for performance of the decree has been made. The applications dated 15.9.73 and 29.12.73 clearly indicate the bonafides of the defendant. It further appears from the record that the defendant was misled due to the wrong advice of his former advocate which resulted in filing security bond on 24.11.73. It is evident that the moment the defendant was advised by the learned advocate engaged afresh, he took appropriate steps to remedy and rectify the technical non-compliance of the requirements of the statute. Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply in terms for extension of the time prescribed for furnishing security but the principle behind it may be applied in the facts and circumstances of the instant case for the reasons that the defendant was misled by the wrong but bonafide instruction and advice of the learned advocate and that the defendant acted in good faith and there is nothing on record to indicate that there was any negligence and deliberate disregard to act in terms of law. Reference may be made in the case of Kunwar Rajendra Bahadur Singh Vs. Rai Rejeshwar Bali and others 41 C.W.N. 1189 in support of the view that in the circumstances of a particular case the elastic concept of sufficient case may be extended and applied. In the above case their Lordships of the Privy Council observed "Mistaken advice given by a legal practitioner may in the circumstances of a particular case give rise to sufficient cause within the section though there is certainly no general doctrine which saves parties from the results of wrong advice". It may be remembered that the expression sufficient cause does not admit of a legal or logical definition. It has always to be construed with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case.</u>

10. The application under Order 9 rule 13, C.P.C. was filed on 15.9.73 and was in time. The application for extension of time relates to the filing of the security bond. In the facts and circumstances indicated above the learned S.C.C. Judge should have accepted the security bond furnished by the defendant on 24.11.73 and thereafter dispose of Misc. case No. 524 of 1973 on merit.

For the reasons stated above, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost.

The impugned judgment and order of the learned S.C.C. Judge are set aside and the application for acceptance of the security bond upon extension of time is allowed.

The learned S.C.C. Judge is directed to accept security bond and to proceed with the Misc. case No. 524/73 under Order 9 rule 13 read with section 151 C.P.C. according to law. The learned S.C.C. Judge is further directed to dispose of the said Misc. case as expeditiously as possible.

Send down the records at once.

End.
