lawyer:
Sultan Ahmad, Deputy Advocate-General 
A.M. Mahmudur Rahmaan, A.A.G. Ismailuddin Sarkar, A.A.G.---------For the Appellant. 
M. Hafizullah, Nurul Islam----------For the Respondents.
parties:
Bangladesh ------------ Appellant.
Vs.
Unamarayen S.A. Panama and others --------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
K. M. Subhan, J.—This appeal by the Government is from the judgment and order dated 16.5.77 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge of the 3rd Court, Chittagong, in Money Suit No. 42 of 1977.

<u>2. The Government, as plaintiff, filed a money suit against the defendants, for recovery of Tk. 1,01,47,500.00 for damage caused to 5109 Metric tons of wheat, carried by defendants due to contamination by sulphur. In that suit an application under Order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was also filed upon which the impugned judgment and order was passed on its final hearing.</u>

2. <u>The learned Subordinate Judge held, that the application filed by the Government was not in conformity with the requirements of order 38 rule 5 and also because of the judgment in the case of M/s. United Venture Navigation Co. Ltd. Vs. Samudrajatra Shipping Lines, 28 D.L.R. 231 the learned Subordinate Judge vacated the earlier order of conditional attachment before judgment.</u>

3. Mr. Sultan Ahmad, the learned Deputy Advocate General, appearing on behalf of the Government appellant submitted that a reading of the application would show that it was in conformity with the requirement of Order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and further submission of the learned Deputy Advocate General, was that the principles in the decision reported in 28 D.L.R. 231 were wrongly applied to the present case by the learned Subordinate Judge.

4. Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant-respondents has, on the other hand, contended that in the application filed by the Government there is no statement to the effect that there was any intention on the part of the defendants to delay or to defeat the decree, that there is no allegation that the defendants were trying to remove the lighterage concerned from the jurisdiction of the court concerned. The second contention of Mr. Hafizullah is that there is another remedy available under the provisions of Private International Law and as such the application under Order 38 rule 5 was misconceived. Lastly, Mr. Hafizullah submitted that the lighterage concerned is a foreign ship and as such the processes under the said rule 5 were not available for attachment of this lighterage.

<u>5. Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate for these propositions has fully relied upon the decision reported in 28 D. L. R. 231. These submissions were made by the learned Advocate particularly in view of the fact that the agent was within the jurisdiction of the court where the suit was filed.</u>

6. The application was filed by the Government in which, it is true, that specifically no mention was made that there was an intention to delay or to defeat a decree, if passed, on the departure of the mother ship Maersk Commander. In this connection it is necessary to quote paragraph No. 2 of the application which runs as follows :

"That the defendants have no properties and assets to the knowledge of the plaintiff except the property described in schedule below to meet the claims in suit and they have removed their ship Maersk Commander from Chittagong Port i.e. from the jurisdiction of this Court and they failed to furnish the guarantee as promised by them to meet the claims to UNDP W. F. P. and unless the Schedule lighterage vessel is attached, the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss." In the plaint itself in paragraph 5 statements were made about the meeting between the officials of the defendants and the officials of the plaintiff, when on 22-2-77 a decision was taken for providing bank guarantee promptly to the tune of US Dollar 1.2 million plus US Dollar 76,500 equivalent to Tk. 1,91,47,500/- as cost of damage and extra charges in favour of the WFP to meet the loss suffered by the plaintiff, the ultimate consignee, on account of damage caused by mixture of sulphur. It is also in the said paragraph No. 5 that a further decision was taken that on the failure to grant bank guarantee promptly the official of the WFP informed the defendants that the lighterage vessel concerned will be detained to meet the losses suffered by the plaintiff, the ultimate consignee.

Paragraph 5 of the plaint is set out below: "5. That the plaintiff's official had a meeting with officials of the defendant No. 1 and 2 and other held on 19.2.77 and in the meeting the defendant No. 1 and 2 offered the said lighterage vessel as guarantee to meet the loss although the plaintiffs. officials demanded bank guarantee to meet their claim to the said damage and subsequently another meeting was held on 22-2-77 wherein it was decided to provide Bank guarantee promptly of US Dollar 1.2 million plus US 76,500 dollars equivalent to Tk. 1,91,47,500/- as cost of damage and extra charges in favour of World Food Programme to meet the loss suffered by the plaintiff, the ultimate consignee on account of damage of wheat caused by mixture of sulphur and it was also decided that on their failure to grant bank guarantee promptly the official of the W.F.P. (World Food Programme) informed the defendants that the lighterage vessel concerned will be detained to meet the losses suffered by the plaintiff the ultimate consignee."

In the written-objection filed by the defendants no specific reply has been given to the allegations made in paragraph 2 of the petition filed under the said rule 5. In paragraph 5 of the written-object ion it has been stated that defendants are not the owners of the said lighterage which was conditionally attached before judgment. It has been further stated in the said paragraph 5 of the written-objection that the said ship is owned to the knowledge of the plaintiff, by another company and defendant No. 1 by an arrangement with her owner was utilising her for the purpose of carrying cargo from the other ship, from the outer anchorage to the inner port. In para 6 it has been admitted that defendant No. 1 has no property or assets in Chittagong. A mere denial has been given about the properties owned by defendant No. 2 in the following terms:

"6. It is admitted that the defendant No. 1 has no property or asset in Chittagong but it is denied that the defendant No. 2 has no property or asset within the jurisdiction of this Court as alleged in paragraph 2 of the application. The defendant No. 2 is a Limited Company located within the jurisdiction of this court." In paragraph 7 it has been stated thus: '7. It is false that these defendants were under any obligation to furnish any guarantee or that these defendants made any promise to 171.eet any claim to UNDP or WFP as further alleged in paragraph 2 of the said application."

7. It may be mentioned, as we are informed by Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate, that no written-statement has been filed by defendants in this case. In the written-objection, we have failed to find any statement of properties owned by defendant No. 2. There is an evasive denial of the allegation that defendant No. 2 has no properly. There is total absence of a statement or nature of properties owned by defendant No. 2. The only argument with respect to the properties owned by defendant No. 2 as made by Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate, was that the defendant No. 2 was a private limited company. We do not understand how the defendants being a private limited company improves it financial standing when specific allegation is made with regard to non-ownership of any property by the particular defendant. The Sea Customs Act requires the agent of a foreign carrier to be a limited Company. We wanted a list of properties owned by defendant No. 2 or the authorised and paid-up capital of this private company, but Mr. Hafizullah made no attempt to furnish the list of properties. He, however, submitted that the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company which detail the capital structure of the company were at Chittagong where the company has its registered office.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge in course of his judgment has found a prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff in the following terms:

"Considering this report of examination of the samples of the wheat in question it can be held that the plaintiff has a prima facie case in the suit."

The learned Subordinate Judge having found a prima facie case of the loss allegedly suffered by the plaintiff, found that the provisions of Order 38 rule 5 were not complied with. Placing reliance upon the said decision reported in 28 D.L.R. 231 the learned Sub-ordinate Judge found that the prayer could not be granted. In this connection, it is necessary to set out the provisions of Order 38 rule 5 which runs as follows:

"5(1) Where, at any stage of a suit, the Court is satisfied, by affidavit or otherwise, that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any to that may be passed against him,—

(a) is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property, or

(b) is about to remove the whole or any part of his property from the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, the Court may direct the defendant, within a time to be fixed by it, either to furnish security, in such sum as may be specified in the order, to produce and place at the disposal of the Court, when required, the said properly or the value of the same, or such portion thereof as may be sufficient to satisfy the decree, or to appear and show cause why he should not furnish security ;

(2) The plaintiff shall, unless the Court otherwise directs, specify the property required to be attached and the estimated value thereof.

(3) The Court may also in the order direct the conditional attachment of the whole or any portion of the property so specified."

9. It has been argued by Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate that nowhere in the application filed by the Government appellant, the malafides of the defendants have been mentioned. Mr. Sultan Ahmad, the learned Deputy Advocate General, in this regard submitted that the very mention of the mother ship's departure from the jurisdiction of the court as also the allegation of no property being owned by defendant No. 2 is sufficient for alleging malafides on the part of the defendants.

<u>10. In the said decision reported in 28 D.L.R. 231 a Division Bench of this court in the facts of that case which was filed by an agent against his foreign principal observed as follows:</u>

<u>"When the ship, said to be belonging to the defendants, which are foreign companies, is about to leave the port, where it had discharged some cargoes, in the normal course of its business, it is difficult to presume that the ship's departure for another port was with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of any decree, which may be passed against the said defendants. In this circumstances we do not, therefore, think that having regard to the provisions of Order 38 rules 5 and 6 of the Code the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in passing the impugned order."</u>

<u>It is obvious from this observation that the intention of delaying or defeating the decree was presumed by their Lordships in this decision from the facts and circumstances of that particular case. We do not think that this observation is made in absolute terms to be applied to each case, and it does not require the authority of any decision to hold that intention being in abstract, has to be gathered from the attending facts and circumstances of each case. The conclusion arrived at in this observation by their Lordships shall be applicable to the facts and circumstances of that case, records of which were before their Lordships and the presumptions that were drawn by their Lordships from those facts are but for that case. In the instant case we have already set out the allegation s made in paragraph 5 of the plaint and paragraph 2 of the application, a positive statement was made that the mother ship registered in a Latin American country having discharged the cargo left the jurisdiction of Chittagong court for a foreign destination and defendant No. 2 the agent of .defendant No. 1 has no property to satisfy the decree, if any, passed by the court. In these circumstances, the inevitable presumption from the departure of the mother ship and the failure of defendant No. 2, the agent or defendant No. 1 the carrier, to set out a list of properties owed by defendant No. 2 is that the intention was but to delay or defeat the execution of any future decree passed in favour of the plaintiff. It may also be mentioned that in the normal course of business a foreign ship does not call on a foreign port unless it is chartered for the purpose.</u>

11. We have also noted that there is an allegation of an agreement between officials of plaintiff and defendants that a bank guarantee shall be furnished, in default it was pointed out that the authorities of WFP would have the lighterage attaches', for any default in furnishing bank guarantee. We have also noted that in the written-objection, written-statement having not been filed, there is merely an evasive denial and no specific statement of the plaintiff with regard to the properties owned by defendant No. 2 has been made, particularly when it was admitted that defendant No. 1 owned no properties within the jurisdiction of Chittagong court. The malafides, is also patent, as there is denial in the written-objection of defendant No. 2's liability to furnish any bank guarantee.

12. It is also urged by Mr. Hafizullah that there is no allegation that defendants were trying to remove the lighterage concerned from the jurisdiction of the court. We do not find anything in the written-objection to hold that there was any intention to keep the lighterage within the jurisdiction of the Chittagong court till the finalisation of the suit. Furthermore, the lighterage is registered in Panama and as such it is not necessary to allege that the lighterage will be removed from out of the jurisdiction of the Chittagong court, particularly when in the normal course of business, she is bound to sail away from Chittagong port being a foreign vessel, after discharge of her cargo and is not likely to call on Chittagong port.

13. How reference to defendant No. 2 being a private limited company, we do not see, improves its financial position. A private limited company by itself is no guarantee that it owns properties. Defendant No. 2 who is an agent of the carrier defendant No. 1 having been licensed by the Government as, of statutory necessity, to be a limited company. The mere statement that defendant No. 2 is a private limited company, in our opinion, does not warrant a conclusion otherwise than what we have drawn, namely, that the intention, in this particular case, of the mother ship's departing from the jurisdiction of Chittagong port and non-furnishing of a list of properties owned by the defendant No. 2 is to delay or defeat the future decree. We have looked not only to the allegations made in the application filed by the Govt. but also in the plaint. Thus we hold that the application if read with the plaint suffers from no infirmity in so far as requirements of Order 38 rule 5 are concerned.

14. It is necessary to mention the principle correctly laid down by the Pakistan Supreme Court though under different facts, in the case of Mohiuddin Molla Vs. The Province of East Pakistan, 14 D.L.R. 112, Their Lordships held at page 115 thus:

"The Court has inherent jurisdiction to preserve the property of the Judgment-debtor in order that it may be available for realization of the decretal amount. The principle has been recognised in Order VXXVIII, rule 5 of the Civil Procedure Code which empowers the Court to attach the property of the defendant in order that any decree that is passed in the suit may be satisfied by sale of the attached property. If the Court has power to attach the property of the defendant at a time when there is only a possibility of a decree in favour of the plaintiff, it will be anomalous to hold that after he has actually secured a decree the Court cannot act to protect his interests just because the execution of the decree has been postponed. The jurisdiction of the Court to attach the property of the defendant truly arises from the fact that the Court has power to grant relief. A power to grant relief necessarily implies power to sake all such steps as may be needed to ensure the grant of relief to the plaintiff. Full relief is not granted to a plaintiff by a paper decree. It is only when the decree is satisfied that he gets full relief and the Court has power to pass all such orders as may be required for the satisfaction of the decree unless any such order be expressly or by necessary implication prohibited. Order XXXVIII, rule 5, should be regarded as a provision which recognizes a power rather than a provision which confers a power. The Civil Procedure Code, generally speaking, does not create new powers but regulates the exercise of power already possessed by the Court. Even before the Civil Procedure Code was enacted the Civil Court possessed powers of the kind mentioned in the Civil Procedure Cede. It possessed these powers because the Civil Court has jurisdiction to determine and protect civil rights and for the protection of those rights the exercise of such powers is essential."

<u>15. Next we come to the point raised by Mr. Hafizullah that under the private international law, a remedy is available and as such an application under Order XXXVIII rule 5 is incompetent. In support of this argument Mr. Hafizullah has relied upon an unreported decision of a Division Bench of this Court, to which one of us was a party, in Civil Revision No.648 of 1971. United Aircraft Corporation & 217-C-ther Vs. Pakistan International Airlines, decided on 29-7-76. For this proposition also Mr. Hafizullah has placed reliance upon the said decision reported in 28 D.L.R: 231. In paragraph 19 of the said decision reported in 28 D.L.R. 231 their Lordships have observed as follows:</u>

<u>"We do not think that the plaintiffs will be without any remedy in respect of any transactions involving foreign companies. This kind of difficulty is likely to arise in many cases. But even then the Private International Law recognises remedies which may be taken recourse to in an appropriate case in order to enforce the judgment which may be passed in the suit. But even if the apprehension of the plaintiffs is well based, such kind of difficulty, in our opinion, is not a sufficient ground for taking re-course to the provision of Order 38 rule 5 and 6."</u>

<u>This observation with utmost respect we must say has been made in general terms without looking into the provision of section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides as follows:</u>

<u>"44A.-(1) Where a certified copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed Pakistan as if it had been passed by the District Court.</u>

<u>(2) Together with the certified copy of the decree shall be filed a certificate from such superior Court stating the ex-tent, if any, to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted and such certificate shall, for the purposes of proceedings under this section, be conclusive proof of the extent of such satisfaction or adjustment.</u>

<u>(3) The provisions of section 47 shall as from the filing of the certified copy of the decree apply to the proceedings of a District Court executing a decree under this section, and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13.</u>

<u>Explanation 1.—"Superior Courts" with reference to the United Kingdom, means the High Court in England, the Court of Session in Scotland, the High Court in Northern Ireland, the Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Lancaster and the Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Durham.</u>

<u>Explanation 2.—"Reciprocating territory" means the United Kingdom and such other country or territory as the Central Government may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, declare to be reciprocating territory for the purpose of this section; and "superior Courts", with reference to any such territory, means such Courts as may be specified in the said notification.</u>

<u>Explanation 3.—"Decree", with reference to a superior Court, means any decree or judgment of such Court under which a sum of money is payable, not being a sum payable in respect of taxes or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalty, and</u>

<u>(a) with reference to superior Courts in the United Kingdom, includes judgments given and decrees made in any Court in appeals against such decrees or judgments, but</u>

<u>(b) in no case includes an arbitration award, even if such award is enforceable as a decree or judgment."</u>

<u>16. This clearly refers, as was observed in the said unreported judgment in Civil Revision No. 648 of 1971 to a reciprocal arrangement between the states concerned. We enquired, in vain, of Mr. Hafizullah, if there was any reciprocal arrangement between Bangladesh and the Republic of Panama under whose flag the mother ship Maersk Commander, as well as the lighterage that has been the subject of attachment order, are selling. In the said unreported decision a point was raised by Mr. Hafizullah the learned Advocate when he was arguing that case of the petitioner in the said revisional application, about the ineffectiveness of a decree passed by a foreign court. It has been observed in that judgment that section 44A lays down that there must be a reciprocal arrangement between this country and the foreign country concerned. There is nothing on record of this case nor produced, by either of the parties to show that there is a reciprocal arrangement between Bangladesh and Panama. Furthermore, it is well settled now that if a litigant has more than one remedy it is firstly open to him which remedy he shall take re-course to and the obvious choice is on such remedies as are available quickly and easily. Even if a remedy is available under the provisions of Private International Law, as we have already pointed out, the remedy is subject to reciprocity between the Stales concerned and it is bound to be more expensive and time consuming. The remedy available under Order 38 rule 5, needless to say, is much more easily and effectively available. Thus, in the circumstances, we find no substance in the point urged by Mr. Hafizullah, in this regard also.</u>

17. Lastly, it has been argued by Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate that the lighterage concerned being a foreign ship cannot be attached. We must frankly say that this argument is bewildering to us. Mr. Hafizullah could not found this argument on the basis of any provision of law. But again reliance was placed upon an observation in the decision reported in 28 D.L.R. 231. In the said decision their Lordships have observed as follows:

"It is pertinent to observe that it is extremely doubtful if the provisions of Order 38 have any application in the case of a defendant who does not usually reside, or whose property is not normally situated, within the jurisdiction of the Court concerned."

In this decision their Lordships themselves have expressed doubt in this proposition. Apart from this Mr. Hafizullah could not refer to any provision of law or for that matter any decision of any recognised court which has allowed immunity to foreign property in such elastic terms as Mr. Hafizullah wants us to apply. Immunity is available under the Public International Law to persons and properties of classified persons and mentioned in the list which is usually filed by foreign missions and International Agencies. Immunity may also be granted by specific statute as has been given, in the Contract Act, but we do not find anything in the Code of Civil Procedure, permitting such immunity to legal processes. The lighterage concerned is well within the jurisdiction of Chittagong Court and there being no provision of law we find it difficult to accept the proposition formulated by Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate because such proposition leads to encroachment on state sovereignty.

18. Before we conclude it is worthwhile mentioning that we enquired of Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate, if defendant No. 2 was willing to furnish any security in place of the lighterage that was the subject-matter of attachment. It must be observed that Mr. Hafizullah did not give any definite reply to this, nor could we gather anything from his argument that there was such willingness on the part of defendant No. 2 to furnish security or bank guarantee instead.

19. In this view of the matter we allow the appeal and set aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. The connected rule being Civil Rule No. 639 (fm) of 1977 is made absolute. We make no order as to costs in both appeal and the rule. A revisional application was filed wider section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the Government-appellant, but in view of our judgment there is no necessity of passing any order in the revisional application.

A. T. M. Afzal, j.—I agree.

End.

lawyer:
B. N. Chowdhury—For the Petitioner 

P. K. Bose—For the O. P.
parties:
Bipin Chandra Ray------ Petitioner
Vs.
Bunchuki Barmani ------ Opp.-Party
full_judgment:
The petitioner being defendant No. 1 in Other Suit No. 228 of 1977 has obtained this rule challenging the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge, Rangpur in Other Appeal No. 84 of 1980 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the Munsif, Nilphamari in Other Suit No. 228 of 1977 which was decreed in favour of the plaintiff opposite party. The plaintiff brought the suit for a declaration that defendant No. 1 was not the adopted son of her father Sree Kanta.

 2. The plaintiff's case was that Sree Kanta died in 1377 B.S. leaving a widow Khata Barmani and the only daughter namely the plaintiff. Upon his death his widow namely the plaintiff's mother inherited the lands of Sree Kanta in life interest and subsequently upon death of Khata Barmani in 1380 B.S. her only issue and daughter namely the plaintiff inherited the said lands of her father Sree Kanta in life interest. Plaintiff has her only son namely pro-defendant No. 2 who is due to inherit the land of Sree Kanta in absolute right upon death of plaintiff. The plaintiff's mother Khata Barmani having no male member in the house brought the defendant No. 1 as a permanent servant on yearly wages for looking after and managing the landed property. In course of time she also got the defendant No. 1 married and continued to employee defendant No. 1 as servant and his wife as maid servant. Being satisfied with their services she also gifted away some lands to him by two registered deeds dated 12-4-69 and 21-4-69 which were in fact obtained by the defendant No. 1. Upon death of her mother the plaintiff also exercised her life interest in the lands as legal heir of her father by employing defendant No. 1 as bargadar and plaintiff also along with her son transferred some lands to the defendant No. 1 for constructing his dwelling hut. On the other hand the plaintiff had transferred some lands to one Jogi Barmani and Jogi Barmani grew potato in the said land which was wrongfully plucked away by another Joyhari and others for which Jogi Barmani brought a Criminal Case. In that case Joyhari claimed right by purchase from defendant No. 1 and also cited the defendant No. 1 as his witness when defendant No. I deposed on 26-6-75 stating that he was the adopted son of the plaintiff's father. This false claim of the defendant No. 1 threatened the plaintiff's heirship and thus gave a cause of action for this suit. 

3. The defendant No. 1 denied the case of the plaintiff and also denied the right and possession of the plaintiff in respect of the lands left by Pran Kumar. His case was that in his infancy he was adopted as son by Pran Kumar after observing all the required formalities and since then he has continuously remained in the house of Fran Kumar and upon his death he has legally inherited all the land of Sree Kanta in absolute right and has been in continuous possession thereof. He also asserted that the plaintiff was all along aware of the adoption. So the present suit is without any cause of action and also barred by limitation. It was also stated that the suit is not maintainable in the present form as no consequential relief was prayed. The learned Munsif upon a threadbare discussion of all the oral and documentary evidence found that the defendant No. 1 was not the adopted son of Sri Kanta and that defendant No. 1 for the first time claimed to be the adopted son of Sri Kanta while he deposed in the Criminal Court on 26-6-75 when the plaintiff for the first time came to know of it and the suit having been filed on 22-8-77 that is within 6 years of the knowledge was within time. He also found the suit to be maintainable. Upon such finding he decreed the suit. 

4. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge concurred with all the findings of the learned Munsif on points of fact as well as law after considering all the evidence and accordingly affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner at the outset conceded frankly that he will not challenge the finding of fact as to defendant No. 1 having not been adopted by Pran Kumar and the plaintiff's knowledge relating to the point of limitation. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury pressed before this Court only two points of law. The first point submitted by him was that the present suit being a suit for a negative declaration was not maintainable according to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. His contention was that section 42 only entitles the plaintiff to seek positive declaration of his own legal character or right to property and it does not entitle him to seek a negative declaration either in respect of the legal character or title to any property of any other person. 

5. On the other hand Mr. P. K. Bose, the learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that there is no bar in respect of negative declaration and that all that section 42 requires is that the declaration should be concerning the legal character of the plaintiff, be it in the positive manner or in the negative manner. 

6. For a proper decision on this point of law it will be useful to reproduce the workings of section. 42 of the Specific Relief Act which is in the following language: "Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right to any property, may institute a suit against any per-son denying, or interested to deny his title to suet, character or right, and the Court may, in its discretion, make there-in a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not, in such suit, ask for any further relief". From a reading of the aforesaid provision it is found that section 42 of the Specific Relief Act entitles a person to come to Court for a declaration if the person is entitled to tither (1) any legal character (2) or any right to any property and if any other person denies or is interested to deny his title to such character or right. 

7. In the present case the plaintiff has not come to seek any declaration in respect of any right to property as the plaintiff does not mention any schedule of suit property nor does it bear any prayer for declaration of plaintiff's right in respect of such property. On the other hand the only relief claimed in 'the suit is a declaration that the defense No.1 is not the adopted son of plaintiff's father Sri Kanta. This certainly shows that the plaintiff had brought the suit only for declaration of a legal character though in a negative way. 

8. Apparently it seems that plaintiff had not sought a declaration of her own title to the legal character in as much as she has only sought for declaration that defendant No. 1 is not the adopted son of her father Sri Kanta. But plaintiff has well explained in the plaint the 'purport and substance of her prayer which amounts to declaration of her own legal character that is her heirship though in life interest from her father and mother. It is an admitted fact that plaintiff's father Sri Kanta died leaving a widow Khata Barmani and only daughter plaintiff and plaintiff has her only son the pro-defendant No. 2. So according to Hindu law of inheritance upon the death of her father her mother inherited the property in life interest and upon death of her mother she inherited the said property of her father in life interest and upon her death her son pro-defendant No. 2 will inherit the same property in absolute right. In such a situation if defendant No. 1 is an adopted son of plaintiff's father Sri Kanta as the defendant No. 1 has claimed thereby denying the plaintiff's legal heirship of her father that will destroy the plaintiff's legal character as heir of her father. So the declaration sought by the plaintiff in the way that defendant No. 1 is not the adopted son of plaintiff's father Sri Kanta actually though indirectly amounts to declaration of plaintiff's own legal character. 

9. The real purport of the suit and the actual substance of the relief prayed has to be considered in order to see if the requirement of section 42 is fulfilled or not. The apparent form and language of the plaint are immaterial but the real purport and import and substance of the suit and the claim of relief have to be considered. 

10. In this case though apparently there is a negative declaration sought by the prayer for a declaration that defendant No. 1 is not the adopted son of plaintiff's father -but this, in the facts and circumstances narrated the plaint tantamount to a declaration of plaintiff's own legal character as a legal heirs of her father. So  merely because a negative declaration has been sought that cannot be any ground to hold that the suit does not come within the ambit of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The said section does not really bar a negative declaration as such if otherwise its condition and terms are fulfilled as it has been found in this case. By seeking declaration in a negative way namely that, “Defendant No. 1 is not the adopted son of her father" plaintiff has in substance claimed declaration of her title to a legal character as legal heir of her father. Mr. P. K. Bose cited a decision in the case of Josoda Sal Ys. Mongal Ghani reported in 45 CWN Page 470. . 

In that case plaintiff sought a declaration that defendant Josoda had not any right or title in the mortgaged property at the date of the mortgages. Objection was taken as to the maintainability of the suit under section 42. It was held that "in seeking for a declaration which negatives Josoda's claim to any share in these properties the plaintiff in substance asserts his own right and seeks for a declaration in respect thereto. 

"It was also held that" in determining whether the suit is for a declaration of the character contemplated by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, it is the substance and not the form which has to be regarded. Where a person in substance asks for a declaration that he has mortgage rights to the whole sixteen annas of a property and asks it in the form of declaration that the defendant has no right, or title in the said property, the relief prayed for is not outside the purview of section 42." In the case of Chinneasami Mudaliar Vs. Ambalavana Muldaliar reported in IL.R Madras page 48 in similar facts and circumstances the same view was taken. 

12. In that case plaintiff brought a suit for declaration that defendant was not his adopted son and it was held that where an adoption alleged to have made by the plaintiff has been set up under such circumstances which would operate to the prejudice of the plaintiff if he would not take steps to have it declared not true he is entitled to seek such declaration. Besides that these are several cases in which nega Live declaration have been held to be maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

13. In the case of Waryam Singh Vs. Mahtab reported in 26 PR 1903 it has been held that a suit lies for declaration that plaintiff is not the wife of the defendant. 

14. In the case of Secretary of State Vs. Dhobu Ram reported in ER ( 1944 ) Lahore page 168 it has been held that a suit for a declaration that certain person does not belong to a certain caste can be allowed under section 42. Thus in consideration of the facts of the present case with reference to the requirements of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act I find that inspite of the prayer for a negative declaration the suit is maintainable and that the objection of Mr. B. N. Chowdhury does not stand. Thus the conclusion of the courts below on this point was correct. 

15. The second point raised by Mr. B. N. Chowdhury on behalf of the petitioner was that the suit is barred under section 42 on the ground that no consequential relief by way of recovery of possession was sought. He submitted that this suit practically related to the lands of plaintiff's father which were admittedly in the possession of defendant No.1 and in such position the plaintiff was repaired to seek consequential relief and she avoided that only to evade the payment of adveloram court fees. His further contention was that under section 42 plaintiff was bound to seek all the relief necessary upon the cause of action narrated by her. As against that Mr. P. K. Bose, the learned Advocate for the O. P. submitted that this suit did not seek declaration of any right to property and so no property in the shape of land etc. being involved it was not necessary to seek any consequential relief. It is a settled principle of law that if any plaintiff seeks any declaration of any right to property and he has no possession therein he is bound to seek consequential relief by way of recovery of 'possession but in this case as I have already observed no declaration has been sought in respect to any right of property. On the other hand it is a suit merely for a declaration: relating to and concerning the legal chas; meter of the plaintiff.in respect of her legal heir-ship: of her father: So no right to property being involved the seeking of consequential relief relating to the possession of such pro4 petty does not arise. So this contention of Mr. B. N. Chowdhury also fails. 

In the result, it is found that the judgment and decree passed by the courts below do not suffer from any error of law and there is no scope for revision. 

The Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs. 

End.

case_source: In the matter of an application under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for setting aside the Judgment and decree dt. 31.10.81 passed by Addl. Dist. and Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in T.A. No. 241/77 affirming those of Sub-Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in T.S. No. 22/72 passed on 22-9-77.
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree, dated 30.12.81, passed by the Additional District. Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in title Appeal No. 241 of 1977 affirming those, dated 22.9.77, passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Suit No. 22 of 1972. 

2. The plaintiff-petitioner and the defendant No. 22 who was originally plaintiff No. 2 filed Title Suit No. 22 of 1977 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal impleading the opposite parties and defendants for declaration that the compromise decree, dated 16.4.70 passed in Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal, was fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the auction sale held on 21.12 62 in Certificate case No. 60/61.62 was fraudulent, collusive, and ineffective with regard to the plaintiff's title to the suit land . 

3. The plaintiff's case, inter alia, was that the suit land in the 'Ka' schedule of the plaint originally belonged to Ushabala Chakraborty the defendant No. 15. The plaintiff, Hashem Ali and his brother Kashem Ali the pro-defendant No. 22 took settlement of the suit land from the said owner, the defendant No. 15. in Baisakh, 1349 B.S. and since then they have been in possession of the same by exercising their title therein. The defendant Nos. 1-21 have got no title and possession of the suit land. But the defendant Nos, 1-7 instituted Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 against the defendant Nos. 8 21 on the false allegations in respect of the suit land & other lands. in that suit the defendant No. 1 claimed title over the suit land on the basis of (Pattan allegedly taken from the defendant No. 15 in. 1354 B.S. and on the basis of auction purchase held in .Certificate Case No. 60K/61-62. But as a matter of fact defendant No. 1 never took pattan of any land from the defendant No. 15 who left this country for India for good in 1349 B.S. No summonses were served upon the defendant in that suit All these were collusively and fraudulently suppressed No notice or sale proclamation was ever served or issued in the Certificate Case. The sale held in the certificate case was fraudulent and collusive. The defendant managed to obtain a sole decree, dated 16.4.70 in the said Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 by practicing fraud upon the court. The Solenama filed in that suit is a forged document the defendant No. 15 never appeared and effected any compromise. Neither the plaintiff nor his brother, the defendant No. 22, was made a party in that suit. The plaintiff came to know about the same in Chitra, 1378 B S. while the defendant No. 1 claimed title over the suit land on the basis of the said illegal sole decree. 

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filling a written statement. His case in brief was that he took settlement of the land of S.A. Khatian Nos. 165, 167 and 168 from the defendant no.15, Ushabala Chakraborty in Baisakh, 1354 B S. and since then he has been possessing the same. He auction purchased the lands of S. A. Khatian No. 169 on 21. 12. 62 in Certificate Case No. 60/ K 1961 62 and thereafter took possession of the same through Court and since then he has been in possession of the same. Thus the defendant No.1 is the owner and possessor of the suit land. The sole decree, dated 16.4 70 passed in Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 and the auction sale held on 21. 12. 62 on Certificate Case No. 60K/ 61-e2 are quite legal and valid. The notices and the sale proclamation were duly issued and served in the Certificate Case. The summons were also duly served upon the defendants of Title Suit No. 109 of 1970. The defendants of the suit duly signed the solenama which is a genuine document. The plaintiff and his brother, the defendant No 22, never acquired any title or possession in the suit land. The suit is not maintainable in the present form. The plaintiff has no locus-stand to file the suit; the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

5. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, the trial court, dismissed the suit with the finding that the plaintiff has got neither title nor possession in the suit property; that the plaintiff has no locus standi to fife the suit and that the suit is not maintainable and it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The trial court further found that the plaintiff has failed to establish that the impugned decree and Certificate sale were illegal, collusive, fraudulent and void. 

6. The plaintiff-petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree preferred Title Appeal No. 241 of 1977 which was also dismissed by the Additional District Judge 3rd Court, Barisal. On consideration of evidence on record the appellate court recorded the following finding:-'As the plaintiff has got no title or possession in the suit laud and as he has not made any prayer in this suit for declaration of title and for any consequential relief either in the Arm confirmation of possession or recovery of khas possession so it can be safely said that the plaintiff has got no locus-standi to bring the suit and that suit is nor maintainable in its present form" Being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of the appellate Court, the plaintiff petitioner moved a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

7. I have gone through the judgments of the courts below and perused the record of the case. I also do not find any point of law involved in this case to set aside the above concurrent findings of the courts below which are based on consideration of the evidence on record. 

8. Mr. Md. Nizamul Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner contended that though the plaintiff has failed to prove his right, title and interest in the suit land, yet he is entitled to a part decree as the defendant has failed to prove that the compromise decree, dated 16.4.70 passed in Title Suit No.109 of 1970 was a genuine document. 

9. Mr. Hamayet Uddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party no.1 on the other hand argued that the plaintiff, having no legal character or right to the suit property, bas no locus-standi to file the present suit and could not claim for passing a part decree. He also argued that the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

10. The present suit. is a suit for Sinters declaration and was filed under the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, which runs as follow-"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to the property, may institute a suit against any persons denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion, make therein a declaration that be is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit seek for any further relief : Provided that no court, shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than mere declaration of title omits to do so. To maintain a suit under this section the following 2 ingredients must be proved :- (I) that plaintiff is entitled to a legal character or right as to the property. (I1) and that the defendant is denying or is interested to deny such character or right .So, the suit must fail if the plaintiff fails to establish his legal character or title which authorises him to ask for the declaratory decree. In the case of Mst. Sabera Khatunn Vs. Mst. Arnena Khatun reported in I SCR (i981) page 127 it has been held by a Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court that :—"Before the plaintiff can be given a declaration under section 42, Specific Relief Act she has to prove before the Court that she had the legal character or the right to property she claimed and unless the plaintiff could prove such legal character or right to property she could not be given any declaratory relief." 

11. The same view has been taken by another Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in the Case of Imanuddin. Parks' Vs. Lilabati Dos reported in 32 D.L R. page 75. Their Lordships of the Division Bench held as follows: — 11The plaintiff has prayed for a declaration to the effect that the decree obtained by the defendant was fraudulent arid collusive and not binding against the plaintiff. The plaintiff having failed to prove her title and having no legal character in the subject matter of the suit land, was not entitled to any declaration with regard to the defendant's decree to which she had not connection". 

12. It is now an established principle of law that the plaintiff is to succeed on the merit of his own case and he having failed to prove his title in the suit property, the plain; tiff has no legal character and as, such he in not entitled to any declaration that the compromise decree obtained by the defendant is fraudulent, collusive, and null and void. 

13. in the present case both the trial court and the appellate court have concurrently found that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title and possession of the suit property and as such he has no locus-standi to file the present suit which is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, evidence on record and the relevant laws, I hold that the plaintiff having no locus-standi to file the present suit, he is not entitled to any declaration against the defendant No. 1 with regard to compromise decree; dated I 6.4-70 passed in Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 and the suit has been rightly dismissed by the courts below. There is no force in the argument of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner. 

The rule, is therefore, discharged with costs. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 24.1.73 passed in F.M.A. No. 67 of 1971)
full_judgment:
Mahmud Husain, J: This petition for special leave to appeal by the judgment-debtor is against the decision of a Division Bench of the High Court Division dismissing Appeal from Original Order No.67 of 1971 arising out of the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dacca in Miscellaneous Case No.185 of 1970. Respondent decree-holder obtained a compromise decree against the petitioner and under the terms of the compromise, the decretal amount of Rs. 66,056.5-6/ pies was payable by the petitioner in annual installment amounting Rs. 8,000/-. The petitioner made payment of two installments amounting Rs. 16,000/- and thereafter defaulted So, the respondent put the decree into execution being the Money Execution, Case No.1 of 1960 in which the respondent certified receipt of payment of Rs. 16,000/- and prayed for recovery of the balance. The petitioner thereafter paid Rs. 10,000/- out of Court. The said Money Execution Case No.1 of 1960 was dismissed for non-prosecution on 15.12.67

	On 1.5.1968 the respondent started a fresh execution case being Money Execution Case No. 12 of 1968. In the application for execution of the decree the column Nos. 5,6 and 7 have not been filled in correctly. (In column No. 5 “Payment or adjustment made, if any with date”). Only Rs. 10,000/- was shown to have been paid. In column No.6 (Previous application, if any, with date and result) “M/Ex.1/60 dated 16.12.67” was noted. In column No.7 (Amount with interest, if any, due upon the decree or other etc.) was filled in as follows:-

	“Claim : Rs. 62,497.56 less Rs. 10,000/- above
		i.e., Rs. 52,497.56
		Cost Rs. 3,558.78
		Interest Rs. 33,630.00
		Ex. Cost Rs. 7.66
	Total-		Rs. 89,694.00”

	The petitioner filed an objection under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 185 of 1970 and stated that the Money Execution Case No. 12 of 1968 was time barred and not maintainable and that the columns in the application for execution of the decree had not been correctly filled in and as such it was not in accordance with law and that notice of execution was not served on the petitioner. The respondent opposed the said Miscellaneous Case by filing written objection and denied the allegations made therein. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the Miscellaneous Case with a direction to substitute the figure in column No. 5 of the application for execution by the figure “Rs. 16,000/- and to take early steps to add the result of the previous execution case in column No.6

	As against that, the petitioner preferred an appeal before the High Court Division which was dismissed. As against that , the petitioner filed this petition for special leave to appeal.

	Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner pressed the following ground:-

	“ I. Because the decree-holder did not disclose certified payments of Taka 16, 000/- in Column 5 of the application for execution and showed and exaggerated amount of principal as well as amount of interest contrary to the terms of the decree in Column 7 thereof, the application was not in accordance with the law at the time when it was presented and in view of the provisions of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Executing Court had no jurisdiction to allow amendments thereto so as to transform it into a fresh application after expiry of the period of limitation.”

	The learned Counsel while developing the points submitted that failure on the part of the respondent to disclose the certified payments of Taka 16,000/- in column 5 of the application for execution is a material defect and the amendment thereto having been made after the expiry of the period of limitation, the execution case is barred by limitation. He drew our attention to the case of Asgar Ali v. Troilokya Nath Ghose reported in I.L.R. 17 Calcutta 631. The High Court Division considered this case as well as other cases referred before them. The above reported case is of the year 1890. So, this citation has no application in this case because of the substitution of the relevant portion of Sub-rule (1) of Order 21, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure made in 1933.

	The words “the Court may reject the application, or may allow the defect to be remedied then and there or within a time to be fixed by it” occurring in Sub-rule (1) of Order 21, rule 17 of the Code of Civil procedure was substituted by the following words:-

	“The Court shall allow the defect to be remedied then and there or within a time to be fixed by it. If the defect is not remedied within the time fixed, the Court may reject the application.

	These substituted words cast a duty upon the court to see that the defect, if any, in the application for execution of a decree is remedied.

	Order 21, rule 17(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure runs thus:-

	“Where an application is amended under the provisions of sub-rule (1), it shall be deemed to have been an application in accordance with law and presented on the date when it was first presented.”

	In view of the above provision, the amendment allowed by the Executing Court takes effect on the date when it was first presented and so no question of limitation arises. We, therefore, do not find any substance in this contention.

	The petition for special leave to appeal is accordingly dismissed.
End.

case_source:
(From the Judgment and order dated 8th of December, 2011 passed by the 
High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7707 of 2008).
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 08.12.2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7707 of 2008 discharging the Rule Nisi. 

The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are as follows:

The original Artha Rin Suit No. 66 of 2006 was filed by Mercantile Bank Limited for realisation of Tk. 53,15,235.76. The appellant was impleaded as defendant No. 8 being a third party mortgagor. She was the owner of the property described in Schedule 6 to the plaint. 
The said suit was decreed ex-parte vide judgment and decree dated 20.06.2007 and the property mentioned in the schedule shown in the decree of the said suit was put to execution on 04.11.2007 in Artha Execution Case No. 153 of 2007. On 22.5.2008 the said property was sold to the auction purchaser, respondent No. 10. Thereafter, the petitioner on 25.09.2008 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 21 of 2008 under section 19 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (the Ain) for setting aside the ex-parte decree passed in Artha Rin Suit No. 66 of 2006 stating, inter alia, that no notice was served upon her and the suit was decreed ex-parte and the summons was returned unserved, but no notice was published in the daily newspapers. The petitioner resided in Dhaka and on 18.09.2008 came to know about the case and enquired about the matter and on 24.09.2008 came to know about the ex-parte decree. The petitioner further stated that she is a third party mortgagor and did not enjoy the credit facility. On 06.10.2010 she submitted a pay order amounting to Tk. 5,41,523.58/ which is 10% of the decretal amount, as required by section 19(3) of the Ain.

The respondent Adalat rejected the application under section 19 vide Order No. 42 dated 07.10.2008 holding that notice was published in ‘the Daily Ittefaq’ and ‘the Daily Naya Diganto’ and that it was not believable that the petitioner was not aware of the suit.

Against the said order dated 07.10.2008 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, 1st Court, Chittagong the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 7707 of 2008 and obtained Rule Nisi on 19.10.2008 and an order of stay of the execution proceeding. At the same time the petitioner was directed to pay 25% of the decretal amount within 3 (Three) months in accordance with law, failing which the Rule would stand discharged. Thereafter, the petitioner went before the Artha Rin Adalat to deposit the 25% of the decetal amount, but the Artha Rin Adalat refused to receive the amount on the ground that the auction purchaser, respondent No. 10 had preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1959 of 2008 against the order of the High Court Division dated 19.10.2008 so far as it related to the order of stay and direction and this Division on 27.10.2008 stayed the order directing payment of 25% of the decretal amount. Hence, the petitioner was unable to pay the 25% of the decretal amount. The civil petition for leave to appeal was ultimately disposed of on 09.02.2009 and this Division directed the parties to maintain statup-quo in respect of the suit land till hearing of writ petition. 

The Rule Nisi issued in Writ Petition No. 7707 of 2008 ultimately came up for hearing before a Division Bench of the High Court Division. Respondent No. 10, auction purchaser filing affidavit-in-opposition contested the Rule. After hearing the parties the High Court Division discharged the Rule Nisi vides judgment and order dated 08.12.2011. 

Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the High Court Division, the petitioner filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 413 of 2012. Leave was granted to consider the following grounds: 

I. That the petitioner executed a power of attorney in favour of respondent No. 5, Md. Saidur Rahman to execute mortgage deed. The petitioner did not authorise Md. Saidur Rahman to appear and conduct the Artha Rin Suit No. 66 of 2006 and Artha Execution Case No. 153 of 2007 on her behalf. Saidur Rahman is also a defendant-judgment debtor in Artha Rin Suit No. 66 of 2006 and Artha Execution Case No. 153 of 2007. Saidur Rahman appeared in the execution proceeding in his personal capacity as such finding of the High Court Division is erroneous and, therefore, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. 

II. That the High Court Division committed error of law in holding that the petitioner’s application under section 19 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is beyond the period of 30 days because the petitioner’s agent had knowledge regarding the suit, decree and execution case, but failed to consider that the agent is acting against the interest of the principal and as such the agent’s knowledge cannot be treated as knowledge of the principal (petitioner).

III. That the High Court Division committed error of law in not considering the fact that limitation being a mixed question of law and fact, the executing Court ought to have given opportunity to the petitioner to adduce evidence and, therefore, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside.

Mr. Shah Md. Munir Sharif, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in the light of the grounds on which leave was granted. He further submitted that the application under Section 19(1) of Ain, 2003 was summarily rejected without giving the appellant any opportunity to prove her assertion regarding date of knowledge about the decree and it is unconscionable to hold that the statement is not believable, which can only be determined through evidence and as such the impugned judgment and order is illegal and liable to be set aside. He also submitted that the High Court Division committed error of law in discharging the Rule upon consideration of so many extraneous facts, whereas for disposal of an application under section 19 of Ain, 2003 knowledge about decree is the sole consideration and the date of knowledge is a question of fact which cannot be ascertained without evidence and thus, the appellant was debarred from a chance/opportunity to prove her statements. He further submitted that the High Court Division committed error in discharging the Rule and thereby maintaining the order of rejection passed by the Adalat, whereas an application under section 19 can only be rejected summarily under section 19(5) of Ain, 2003, i.e. on the ground of non-deposit of security in violation of Section 19(3) of Ain, 2003. He lastly, submitted that the appellant executed a power of attorney in favour of respondent No. 5, Md. Saidur Rahman to execute mortgage deed and manage her property. The said attorney did not and is not in a position to depose about the knowledge of the appellant about the Artha Rin suit or the Artha execution case. Only the appellant is competent to give evidence about her own knowledge. That opportunity having not been given to the appellant, the High Court Division erred in not setting aside the order rejecting her application under section 19 of the Ain.

Mr. Bodroddoza, learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 10 made submissions in support of the judgment and order of the High Court Division. In addition the learned Advocate submitted that the order challenged by the writ petitioner-appellant in writ jurisdiction was an appealable order as per law and thus the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed. He further submitted that the High Court Division as well as the trial Court below rightly decided that notice was duly served as per the provision of the Ain, which is a special law and disbelieved the date of knowledge and device of the knowledge of the appellant, on the basis of the records and since the same is pure question of fact. Thus the order of the trial Court cannot be decided in writ jurisdiction and the High Court Division rightly discharged the Rule Nisi. He also submitted that the attorney of the appellant namely Mr. Saidur Rahman contested the jari case and also filed several writ petitions challenging different orders passed by the Adalat from time to time and as attorney of the appellant was fully aware about the proceedings of the suit and jari case and as such in view of section 229 of the Contract Act, 1872 the writ petition-appellant had sufficient knowledge about the same through her constituted attorney and the High Court Division rightly discharged the Rule. He submitted that the appellant did not raise any allegation or objection against Mr. Saidur Rahman for use or non-use of the power attorney in her application under section 19 of the Ain nor in the writ petition and also she did not cancel the said power of attorney till now and the unauthorized person namely Mr. Shafiqul Islam cannot be entertained by any Court of law and the High Court Division rightly discharged the Rule. The learned Advocate submitted that the property in question was sold in auction to the auction purchaser-respondent No. 10 and after full payment, the transfer deed was executed and registered in favour of the auction purchaser which has created vested rights in favour of the auction purchaser which has created vested rights in favour of the auction purchaser and as such the instant appeal does not have any merit for consideration. He further submitted that the plea of the appellant that the constituted Attorney of the appellant is acting against the interest of the appellant has absolutely no basis on record. He submitted that a proper reading of the power of attorney in favour of Mr. Saidur Rahman shows that the said power of attorney is one coupled with interest and hence irrevocable. The high Court Division after examining the impugned order rightly found that the order is passed in conformity with the evidence on record and the information available in the record of the case and as such the High Court Division did not commit any error of law in passing the impugned judgment and order. He also submitted that the judgment-debtors in connivance with each other filed writ petitions one after another to frustrate the auction sale and the appellant claimed that on 18.09.2008 she for the first time knew about the decree, but the certified copies filed in the writ petition as annexures A to D show that applications for certified copies of those documents were filed on 7.7.2008 and requisites were put in on the same date and those were made ready on 9.7.2008 and deliveries were taken on 1.9.2008 and moreover on 11.09.2008 an affidavit was sworn with those certified copies and the auction purchaser-respondent No. 10 made a clear assertion in his affidavit-in-opposition filed in the writ petition regarding much earlier knowledge of the appellant about the suit, which was not denied by the writ petitioner-appellant by filling any affidavit-in-reply and considering the same the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed. He lastly submitted that it is clear from annexures A to D that the writ petitioner knew about the suit much earlier, though she stated in her writ petition that she initially learnt about the ex-parte decree on 18.9.2008 and on the other hand the auction purchaser-respondent clearly stated in his affidavit-in-opposition that such claim is false and the same has not been denied by the writ petitioner-appellant by filing any affidavit-in-reply and by comparing those annexures and statements it is clear that the writ-petitioner did not come before the Court with clean hand and the High Court Division rightly discharged the Rule which is not liable to be interfered with. 

We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

           The reason given for dismissing the miscellaneous case was that the notice regarding auction had been published in the daily ‘Ittefaq’ and ‘Noyadiganta’ and hence, it was not believable that the petitioner (appellant herein) had no knowledge about the suit. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant-writ petitioner before the High Court Division submitted that in fact the respondent having published the auction notices only in the local newspapers namely ‘Doinik Somokal’ and ‘Doinik Ajker Chattogram’ which is not sufficient for service of notice in accordance with the provision of section 7(a) of the Ain. In reply the learned Advocate for the auction purchaser-respondent No. 10 had submitted before the High Court Division (and also in the concise statements filed on behalf of the respondent herein) that the required notices and summons were duly served. It was further submitted that one Saidur Rahman, constituted attorney of the appellant-Dilruba Morshed, was empowered to sell/mortgage etc. the property and therefore, the provision regarding knowledge in section 19(2) was sufficiently satisfied. 

The High Court Division observed as follows: 

“It also appears that the present petitioner, Mrs. Dilruba Morshed executed a registered Special Power of Attorney on 10.10.2000 in favour of the present respondent No. 5, Alhaj Saidur Rahman, who executed a mortgage deed being No. 662 of 2006 on 05.11.2000 and also executed an irrevocable general power of attorney for selling the mortgaged property in case of default in payment of the borrowed money. It further appears from Annexure-6 of the Supplementary Affidavit-in-opposition that the present petitioner executed a Power of Attorney in favour of the present respondent No. 5 on 10.10.2000 vesting powers to act on her behalf for the purposes by the registered deed No. 5923 dated 10.10.2000 for selling, mortgaging, transferring etc. her property as mentioned in the schedule for the said Deed of Power of Attorney. On the basis of the aforesaid power of attorney Mr. Saidur Rahman executed the aforesaid mentioned deeds in favour of the Bank.”

In addition to the provisions regarding notice by way of publicity in the newspaper, the High Court Division also observed that an attorney of the petitioner respondent No. 5 was fully aware about the proceeding filed by the bank by way of artha rin suit and also artha jari case. The High Court Division posed the question whether in such a given fact it would not be sufficient knowledge on the part of the petitioner (appellant herein) through her constituted attorney appointed by a registered document, which is still valid? With regard to knowledge the High Court Division concluded as follows: 

“As an attorney of the petitioner the respondent No. 5 was fully aware about the proceeding filed by the bank by way of Artha Rin Suit and also Artha Jari Case, in such a given fact, would it not be sufficient knowledge on the part of the petitioner through her constituted Attorney appointed by a registered document which is still seen to be a valid piece of document. Moreover, the publication by way of the public advertisement as to sale of the property of respondent No. 5 for himself and on behalf of the present petitioner can be taken to have sufficient knowledge of the proceedings which were going on against the respondent No. 5 to 10 and also against the present petitioner.”

   With regard to section 19(2) of the Ain, the High Court Division observed that the petitioner would only get relief if she could show that she did not have knowledge of the ex-parte decree passed on 20.6.2007 or knowledge of the Artha Jari Case No. 153 of 2007. The High Court Division held that personal knowledge of the petitioner or knowledge through her constituted attorney would be sufficient for knowledge of the case. 

With regard to knowledge of any party to any particular fact in issue or of the existence of any suit or decree is personal to him or her, that is to say whether a person had or did not have knowledge can only be ascertained by examining that person. Knowledge of any person cannot be imputed on that person through examining his or her agent or attorney. We may state categorically that the date of knowledge is a disputed question of fact which can be determined after taking evidence. 

The suit was decreed ex parte and the appellant who was defendant No. 8 claims that she did not receive notice of the suit. Section 19(2) of the Ain allows the defendant to file an application for setting aside the ex parte decree. Section 19(2) provides as follows: 

“১৯(২) কোন মামলা একতরফা সূত্রে ডিক্রী হইলে, বিবাদী উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রীর তারিখের অথবা উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রী সম্পর্কে অবগত হইবার ৩০(ত্রিশ) দিবসের মধ্যে, উপ-ধারা(৩) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রী রদের জন্য দরখাস্ত করিতে পারিবেন।”

Admittedly the appellant did not file the miscellaneous case within 30 days of the date of the decree. But the law allows her to file the same within 30 days from knowledge of the decree on payment of 10% of the decretal amount within 15 days of the filling of the miscellaneous case. This is provided in section 19(3) of the Ain which reads as follows: 

“১৯(৩) উপ-ধারা(২)এর বিধান অনুযায়ী দরখাস্ত দাখিলের ক্ষেত্রে বিবাদীকে উক্ত দরখাস্ত দাখিলের তারিখের পরবর্তী ১৫(পনের)দিবসের মধ্যে ডিক্রীকৃত অর্থের ১০% এর সমপরিমাণ টাকা বাদীর দাবীর সেই পরিমাণের জন্য স্বীকৃতিস্বরুপ নগদ সংশ্লিষ্ট আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে, অথবা জামানতস্বরুপ ব্যাংক ড্রাফট, পে-অর্ডার বা অন্য কোন প্রকার নগদায়নযোগ্য বিনিমেয় দলিল (Negotiable Instrument) আকারে জামানত হিসাবে আদালতের জমাদান করিতে হইবে।” 

Section 19(4) provides that as soon as deposit is made under section 19(3) the application shall be allowed immediately, the ex parte decree shall be set aside and the main suit restored to its file and number. Section 19(4) provides as follows: 

“১৯(৪)উপ-ধারা(৩)এর বিধানমতে ডিক্রীকৃত অর্থের ১০% এর সমপরিমাণ টাকা জমাদানের সংগে সংগে দরখাস্তটি মঞ্জুর হইবে, একতরফা উক্ত রদ হইবে এবং মূল মামলা উহার পূর্বের নম্বর ও নথিতে পুনরুজ্জীবিত হইবে এবং আদালত ঐ মর্মে একটি আদেশ লিপিবদ্ধ করিবে; এবং অতঃপর মামলাটি যে পর্যায়ে একতরফা নিস্পত্তি হইয়াছিল, ঐ পর্যায়ের অব্যবহিত পূর্ববর্তী পর্যায় হইতে পরিচালিত হইবে।”

The combined effect of sub-sections (2) (3) and (4) of section 19 of the Ain is that if a proper application is made by the defendant for setting aside an ex-parte decree in accordance with law a right accrues to the defendant to have the ex-parte decree set aside. In the present case the only point in issue is whether or not the defendant filed the application for setting aside the ex-parte decree within the time stipulated by law. Admittedly miscellaneous case was not filed within 30 days from the date of the decree, whether or not it was filed within 30 days from the date of the decree. Whether or not it was filed within 30 days from the date of knowledge of the ex-parte decree is a matter to be decided with the help of evidence, adduced by the parties.

With regard to knowledge of defendant No. 8-appellant herein, the High Court Division made certain observations which have been detailed above. It is our considered view that the view taken by the High Court Division that the appellant had knowledge through her constituted attorney is absolutely misconceived since knowledge of any party to the suit is a matter personal to that party. Knowledge can only be ascertained upon taking evidence. There is no evidence on record to indicate that even the attorney was examined to ascertain whether or not this defendant had received notices of the suit. 

In the facts and circumstances discussed above, the appeal is allowed, without, however, any order as to costs. 

The judgment and order of the High Court Division is hereby set aside. The artha rin miscellaneous case is sent back to the Artha Rin Adalat, First Court, Chittagong, where the appellant (defendant No. 8) is to be given an opportunity to prove her knowledge as contemplated in section 19(2) of the Ain by adducing evidence. The Artha Rin Adalat is directed to dispose of the miscellaneous case within four months of receipt of this judgment.

End.
